title: Savannah Guthrie renews NBC contract after 15 years
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.
The move by one of morning television’s most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.
The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.
In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.
Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”
The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
“The world goes on, things appear ‘normal,’ ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”
“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”
Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC’s election coverage, most recently for last week’s midterm elections.

title: Sure, you could eat a decorative gourd. But don’t.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story was originally published in October 2021.
It’s decorative gourd season, Mainers. The knobby, colorful squash may seem too pretty to eat, but you technically could eat this organic autumnal home decor if you really wanted to — it just might not be worth it.
Though ornamental gourds are often labeled as “inedible,” the majority of them are not toxic to humans. However, Rob Dumas, food science innovation coordinator at the University of Maine, said that the tiny, bumpy gourds often used for decoration would taste terrible and be difficult to skin, chop and otherwise prepare.
“I don’t know that those have significant culinary value in the sense that there’s probably not a whole lot to them in terms of flavor,” Dumas said. “You might be able to get away with slicing and roasting those, though you’re going to have a hard time processing some of them just due to their shape and actual flesh.”
There are notable exceptions to the toxicity rule, too. The round green and striped colocynth, for example, has reported toxic effects and is sometimes available commercially for strictly decorative uses. More often than not, though, these tiny gourds will just taste bitter or even have no taste at all.
Dumas said that the types of gourds that are considered decorative have often been selectively bred for certain traits, and flavor is not one of them. Sometimes, though — especially at the grocery store — Dumas said there will be delicious gourds mixed in with the tiny, tasteless ones.
“I think that grocery stores tend to lump a pretty wide variety of squashes and pumpkins into that decorative gourd family,” Dumas said. “All of those weirdly shaped pumpkins and squashes that maybe folks are unfamiliar with, they are actually phenomenally delicious squash. One of the biggest of the decorative squashes is a blue hubbard and blue hubbard is fabulous. It’s like a giant butternut squash.”
In addition to blue hubbard, Dumas said to look out for turban squash, kabocha squash, speckled acorn squash and delicata squash.
Similarly, keep an eye out for small pumpkins. Though big jack-o’-lantern pumpkins often don’t taste great (seeds notwithstanding), some of the smaller pumpkins that are used as decorative are delicious.
“Those little pumpkins are often pie pumpkins or sugar pumpkins and they’re often quite good,” Dumas said. “They can be used in a variety of cooking applications with great results.”
With the wide variety of gorgeous edible squash out there, Dumas suggested rethinking your selection of decorative gourds.
“Rather than perpetuating something that has no culinary value, why not go to a farmstand and buy a selection of pumpkins that are equally visually pleasing and can also feed your family?” Dumas said.
“Then you’re also buying local. Go support a local farm stand, buy some beautiful pumpkins and delicatas, display them thoughtfully in your home and then move them into a basement or a cool closet somewhere and enjoy them throughout the winter.”

title: Family of high school freshman who died after collapsing in class remembers ‘a good kid’
text:
EAGLE RIVER, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Friends and family are remembering the life of an Alaska high school freshman who died from cardiac arrest after suddenly collapsing while playing football in physical education class last week.
Mary and James Curry said their son Levi was born with a heart condition, but had surgery to alleviate it.
“The surgery basically healed it,” James Curry said. “Other than that, he’s just like a normal kid.”
Youth football career
Those who knew Levi best agreed that he was seemingly born to play football, standing 6 feet 3 inches tall at just 15 years old.
“I think 17 years now, and I’ve never had a ninth grader start for varsity, especially on the offensive line,” Eagle River High School football coach Jonathan Wetzel said.
Curry’s family said Levi was named one of the best defensive players in the state on Wednesday.
“I called the coach and he told him, and Levi was so excited about that,” Mary Curry said. “He was really joyful and he called his dad to tell him.”
“I was out of town,” James Curry said. “That was the last conversation I had with him, and it was a good one.”
Remembered for kindness
More than a football player, Levi is remembered by those closest to him for his kindness and positive attitude.
“So many people have come up and shared their positive experiences with Levi, and now it’s proven that he’s just a good kid in general,” James Curry said.
“There was plenty of times that I could be having a bad day at work, and I could get to the ball field and you see him coming up, and his smile would just kind of wash that bad day away,” Wetzel said.
Funeral and community support
Levi’s funeral was held on Wednesday. Nearly 500 people attended to pay their respects and show support for the family.
“It’s just overwhelming, how much he meant to the community or what kind of impact he had,” Mary Curry said.
Levi had several siblings.
“It’s just amazing how many people just showed up for Levi,” Noah, Levi’s older brother, said.
“I wasn’t really surprised because I knew he was popular,” Sarah, Levi’s younger sister, added.
In the days since Levi’s death, support has been pouring in for the family.
“I just kept hearing his grandmother say, ‘Man, there’s just so many people that love Levi,’” Wetzel said. “I was like, ‘Well, he made it easy.’”
According to the Currys, two community members built a custom casket that would fit Levi’s large frame
Levi’s teammates also helped James Curry bury his son.
“The football coach, with the team, dug Levi’s grave by hand, which is something that our church does, which is very special,” James Curry said.
Nothing can ease the pain that comes with losing a child, but thanks to the support from community members, the Currys said their lives are just a little bit more peaceful.
“There’s people that we don’t even know about, that we’ve never even met, that have shown great support,” James Curry said. “For as much peace as we’ve had, we know people must be praying.”
As a family grieves, those who knew Levi are remembering his life as one filled with love.
“He knew how to lead when he needed to and he also knew when the seniors were doing their thing and leading,” Wetzel said.
Organ donation and fundraiser
According to his family, Levi was an organ donor. Hospital staff and donor recipients met to honor him this week.
A GoFundMe has been created by the family to help offset the cost of medical bills.

‘This is real bad’: Witness reacts to Mississippi River ship collision
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - Former Baton Rouge resident Devon Flanagan was working along the Mississippi River in New Orleans early Friday afternoon when a tanker reportedly struck the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat.
The American Heritage eventually tipped over, prompting a massive rescue effort.
Flanagan, who now lives in Metairie, Louisiana, said he saw the U.S. Coast Guard and New Orleans search and rescue teams quickly arrive at the scene. He shot multiple photographs and pieces of video that he shared with WAFB of the accident and the rescues.
“It was pretty frantic,” he said. “I did see quite a few people getting pulled out of the water. From what I saw, I think most people got off. By the time I started to walk up on it, it had officially sort of rolled over, and that’s when I realized it was more of an ‘Oh no, this is real bad.’”
Early reports indicated 129 passengers were on board.
Video shows the Atlantic Asphalt tanker hitting the paddlewheel cruise boat while it appeared to be docked, the Associated Press reported.

title: Noah Kahan at L.L.Bean in Freeport? Not So Fast! Fake Concert Event Has People Fooled 🚨
text:
Noah Kahan Freeport, Maine Concert Rumor Is A Hoax
Over the last few days, you may have come across a Facebook event page promoting a Noah Kahan concert at the L.L.Bean flagship store in Freeport, supposedly scheduled for June 12, 2027.
Sounds pretty exciting, right? Unfortunately, there's one big problem: The event is completely fake.
Hundreds of people responded to the Facebook event, marking themselves as either "interested" or "going." There was even a phony Eventbrite link where people could supposedly purchase tickets.
One of the biggest red flags? Noah Kahan already has a concert scheduled in Buffalo, New York, that very same night!
Read More: 10 Artists Who Have Never Plaed Bangor, Maine, But Should
And considering just how popular the Vermont-born singer has become, it's easy to see how people might get excited about the possibility of seeing him perform right here in Maine.
Kahan recently made history with four consecutive sold-out shows at Boston's Fenway Park in 2026. He's also scheduled to return to Fenway for six shows in 2027, after adding two additional dates due to overwhelming demand.
We reached out to L.L.Bean, and they immediately responded, confirming that this is not an authorized L.L.Bean event.
The company also reported the fraudulent event to both Facebook and Eventbrite.
L.L.Bean added that anyone who made a purchase through the fake event page should contact their bank or credit card company as soon as possible.
This is also a good reminder that you should be careful when clicking on links shared through social media, especially when they're connected to concert tickets, giveaways, or events that seem too good to be true.
Fake event pages can look surprisingly convincing. Scammers may use familiar business names, popular artists, convincing graphics, and links that look like legitimate ticketing websites to get people to hand over their money or personal information.
Before purchasing tickets, always check the artist's official website, the venue's website, and authorized ticket sellers to confirm that the event actually exists.
And remember, just because hundreds of people clicked "Interested" or "Going" doesn't mean an event is real!
If you happened to see the Noah Kahan event pop up in your Facebook feed, hopefully you didn't fall for it. It's always better to double-check before clicking that purchase button!

title: ‘I’d do it a million times’: Man sentenced for killing father of 5 shows no remorse in court
text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) – A man sentenced for killing a California father showed no regret in the courtroom.
Damien Murphy was sentenced Thursday to 32 years in prison for the October 2023 shooting death of William Carney, a Fresno father.
Carney’s family had waited more than three years for sentencing. Loved ones filled the courtroom.
Plea and sentence
Murphy shot Carney in central Fresno in October 2023. Two months ago, he pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter. The plea avoided a first-degree murder conviction and resulted in a lower sentence.
Murphy did not express remorse when the judge gave him the chance to address the court.
Family speaks in court
Carney left behind five children. His family said he was less than one month shy of his 40th birthday.
More than a dozen friends and family members attended the hearing. Five of them addressed the court, including Carney’s mother and his 16-year-old daughter.
Among those who spoke, one family member said: “He could never walk me down the aisle on my wedding day and cry seeing how much I’ve grown.”
Another said: “My life simply no longer holds the happiness it once had. The joy that used to come naturally has been replaced by grief.”
One of Carney’s childhood friends spoke directly to Murphy.
“I can’t hate you because I know you’re suffering more than he is, and that brings me peace of mind,” the friend said.
Judge and defendant
Murphy showed no reaction during more than 20 minutes of statements from Carney’s family, including as the judge described the weight of the crime.
“I hope every second of your 32 years you think about William and his family, and the damage you’ve caused,” the judge said.
The judge then offered Murphy a chance to address the court and Carney’s family.
“I would apologize, but I’m not going to apologize for protecting my family, sir. I’d do it a million times,” Murphy said.
The judge responded: “I hope you change your mind and have some remorse for your actions, and don’t be disrespectful to people you’ve murdered and hurt their family.”
What’s next
Murphy will return to court next month for a restitution hearing. He will not have a chance at probation.

title: Evacuation order lifted after bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant
text:
PEORIA (25News Now/Gray News) - An evacuation order was lifted after bomb teams found a bomb Friday night and rendered it safe at an ethanol plant in South Peoria, Illinois.
Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon made the announcement shortly after 1 p.m. Saturday. Officials ordered the evacuation of a one-mile blast radius of the plant shortly after 7 p.m. Friday.
The police department released the following statement:
“State, Federal, and Local Law Enforcement have done an extensive search of the BioUrja facility. They have found no other items of concern at this time. The evacuation order will no longer be in effect. The street barricades will be removed, and all roads will be opened.
Residents are now free to return to their homes in the area that was affected by this order.
Law Enforcement will continue their investigation into this incident and updates will be provided.
The Peoria Police Department thanks the community for their cooperation during this incident."
Earlier, Dixon said authorities were looking for explosives at the plant, equivalent to 44 1/2 football fields.
Dixon declined to reveal the type of device discovered Friday, only to say the package that was “rendered safe” was a “credible threat. Peoria Mayor Rita Ali confirmed for reporters late Friday night that the device was a bomb.
Dixon also did not provide details of what he said was an extensive criminal investigation. Also participating the news conference were representatives of the FBI, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the U.S. Coast Guard, and the Peoria Fire Department.
Dixon said about 60 to 80 people were housed at the evacuation shelter at Manual High School.
No one sought shelter at EastSide Centre, East Peoria officials said.
East Peoria’s government released the following statement:
“As of 1:00 p.m., the 1-mile evacuation zone has been lifted and our residents can return to their homes and all businesses can resume normal operations. Once again, thank you to the East Peoria community for their continued patience and understanding during this situation. We are proud of our staff’s dedication to public safety and their actions to keep this community safe.”

title: Maine October sales and prices ease
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Realtors across Maine reported fewer sales and lower prices last month. Maine Listing reported sales of single-family existing homes dipped 6.58 percent while the median sales price (MSP) decreased 5.63 percent to $402,500 comparing October 2026 to October 2025. The MSP indicates that half of the homes were sold for more and half sold for less.
“As we move into the fourth quarter, buyer demand has softened as mortgage interest rates are shaping market dynamics,” says Judy Oberg, 2026 president of the Maine Association of REALTORS® and Associate Broker at Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
“Statewide, buyers have more homes to choose from than last year and more room to negotiate. Sellers are facing more competition from other listings and that’s reflected in the median sold prices,” adds Oberg.
According to the National Association of Realtors, single-family existing home sales in October 2026 decreased 8.6 percent, and the national MSP rose 0.4 percent to $421,900 compared to October 2025. Statistics reported from the regional Northeast indicate an October year-over-year sales decrease of 4.1 percent, while the regional MSP was up 3.2 percent to $519,600.
“With more homes on the market, work with a knowledgeable local Realtor to negotiate a competitive offer. Move-in ready homes, priced strategically, are selling,” says Oberg.
Below are two charts showing statistics for Maine and its 16 counties. The first chart lists statistics for the month of October (2025/2026), statewide. title: Albany football deals UMaine its ninth consecutive loss
text:
The University of Maine football team’s nightmarish season continued on Saturday afternoon.
The University of Albany’s Great Danes scored on their first three possessions and coasted to an easy 37-3 win over the punchless Black Bears at Bob Ford Field in Tom and Mary Casey Stadium in Albany.
The Great Danes, 7-4 overall and 5-2 in the Coastal Athletic Association, kept their Football Championship Subdivision playoff hopes alive with the victory.
UMaine fell to 1-9 and 1-6 and suffered its ninth straight loss which is the longest single-season losing streak in program history dating back to 1892.
UMaine had won seven of its last eight games in Albany but the Black Bears fell behind 21-0 in the first 16:26 of the game and could only produce a 42-yard field goal from Omar Aboutoui.
UMaine’s feeble offense entered the game ranked 122nd in points scored (13.3) among 124 FCS schools and 112th in yards per game (288.9).
The Black Bears generated a dismal 162 total yards of offense including only 42 passing yards. They managed to pick up just six first downs the entire game.
Senior quarterback and Princeton University transfer Kai Colon threw a pair of touchdown passes and ran for another and back-up senior quarterback Aidan Semo added a pair of short TD runs for Albany.
Colon’s seven-yard touchdown run opened the scoring just 5:09 into the game as he finished off a nine-play, 84-yard drive on the Great Danes’ first possession. A 38-yard pass from Colon to Tavahri Groves on third-and-10 extended the drive and there was also a roughing-the-passer penalty on Chris Bacon on the same play.
Colon picked up a first down on a third-and-six run later in the drive to set the stage for his TD run.
UMaine then drove the ball to the Albany-48 but, on fourth-and-three, Mike McMaugh’s pass fell incomplete.
Albany took over on downs and two 24-yard completions from Colon to Groves and Jordan Rae moved the ball to the UM-16 and Semo eventually punched it into the end zone with a two-yard run.
The Great Danes made it 21-0 with an 11 play, 55-yard drive capped by Colon’s eight yard TD pass to Groves with 13:34 left in the half.
UMaine put together a 10-play, 54-yard drive but it stalled at the Albany 24 so the Black Bears had to settle for Aboutoui’s 42-yard field goal.
It was the transfer from Division III Curry College’s (MA) first Division I field goal.
Albany added a safety before the end of the half when Bodhi Sabongui blocked Anthony Pecorella’s punt.
Albany added insurance touchdowns in the second half on Semo’s one-yard run and Colon’s 24-yard touchdown pass to Luke McAuliffe with 7:54 remaining in the contest.
Colon completed 20 of 30 passes for 264 yards and also ran the ball five times for 35 more yards. Joey Koch had 12 carries for 50 yards and Rae and Groves each had five catches for 95 and 78 yards, respectively.
Albany had 371 total yards on 66 plays.
Cole Sisson led the defense with eight tackles including a sack and Sam Boyer had six tackles.
McMaugh completed 9 of 20 passes for 36 yards and Caden Drezek completed 2 of 4 for six yards. Nobody caught more than two passes.
Rashawn Marshall was the lone bright spot on offense with 74 rushing yards on 14 carries.
UMaine’s Brayden Isaiah had a game-high 11 tackles including two for lost yards and Sam Oppenheimer had seven tackles. Elijah Alvarado had his first career interception.
UMaine will try to salvage something from the season when it hosts arch-rival New Hampshire on Saturday at 1 in the annual battle for the Brice-Cowell Musket.
Albany will travel to North Carolina A&T for a noon game.

title: Nationwide flight grounding disrupts football games this weekend
text:
Nationwide flight grounding disrupts football games this weekend
The Federal Aviation Administration's decision to ground all flights nationwide Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
The FAA issued a notice that said the ground stop was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
Sports leagues and college football conferences have released statements regarding the situation and how to proceed with scheduled games moving forward.
The first game to move days from Saturday to Sunday is No. 19 Ole Miss at Oklahoma, originally slated to kick off at 4:15 p.m. ET Saturday. It will now take place at noon Sunday.
"Due to the national FAA ground stop impacting team travel, the Big 12 Conference is evaluating potential changes to Saturday's football schedule. The Conference will continue to monitor the travel disruptions alongside its member institutions and provide updates for Saturday's games," the Big 12 Conference said in a statement.
At 8:19 p.m. Friday, the FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop. However, residual effects of the halting of flights for nearly six hours could still be felt in the coming days.
West Virginia, a member of the Big 12, originally was slated to host Kansas Saturday for a 5:30 p.m. kickoff. The WVU athletic department said that game has now been moved up to a 3:30 p.m. start.
"Since Kansas has already arrived for its game against West Virginia, there is the potential for a game time change for the Jayhawks and Mountaineers. The game potentially could move to earlier in the day to fill an open television slot," the university said.
According to On3, there are 19 Division I college football teams that have not yet reached their destination as of Friday night and were planning to fly for Saturday games. Tennessee, Texas, Ole Miss, Baylor, Kansas State, San Jose State, Washington, Minnesota, Florida Atlantic, Utah, Arizona State, Oregon State, UNLV and Colorado State have been grounded. Some of the teams have returned to their respective campuses with no concrete plans to fly out Friday night.
The Arizona State game at UCF in Florida was originally scheduled for 3:30 p.m.; however, as Arizona State did not fly get to fly out as planned, that game will now kick off at 5:30 p.m.
Matt Fortuna of the Sports Business Journal said at least eight teams plan on driving to their destinations, including Alabama, Appalachian State, East Carolina, Georgia Southern, Georgia Tech, Southern Mississippi State, Troy and North Texas.
The Southeastern Conference addressed the travel troubles in a statement, noting that the disruptions are affecting several of its teams.
"The safety and well-being of student-athletes, coaches, and team personnel remain our highest priority," SEC officials said. "They're going to monitor the situation and make decisions as they come."
The Texas Longhorns posted on social media a short video of them boarding their plane before the stoppage began. If they ended up taking a bus to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, the trip for the 6:30 p.m. CT kickoff against the Tigers on Saturday would take about seven hours.
"We are grounded and waiting to see when we can leave,” a Texas team spokesman said.
ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Baylor's game against BYU in Provo, Utah, is likely to be postponed indefinitely if the Bears are unable to fly the 1,225 miles from Waco, Texas, as the Cougars cannot play on Sundays because of religious restrictions in the Mormon faith.
The only NFL teams that have officially landed in their destination for Sunday's games are the New England Patriots and Detroit Lions, who both landed in Munich, Germany, earlier in the week. Their game kicks off at 9:30 a.m. ET Sunday.
For some of the NFL teams, trips via bus would be manageable: Pittsburgh plays at Cincinnati, the Los Angeles Rams play at Arizona, Minnesota is visiting Green Bay and Buffalo is scheduled to play the Jets in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Police lift evacuation order after bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois
text:
Police lift evacuation order after bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois
An evacuation order that forced hundreds of people from their homes near an industrial site in central Illinois was lifted Saturday after law enforcement agencies completed a search of the area, authorities said.
A bomb was discovered Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. Police said the device had been “rendered safe,” but authorities ordered residents within a 1-mile radius to evacuate while the surrounding area was searched.
State, federal and local law enforcement conducted an extensive search at the facility and “they have found no other items of concern,” the Peoria Police Department said on its Facebook account on Saturday. “Residents are now free to return to their homes in the area that was affected,” the police said, adding that all roads will be opened and the investigation will continue.
FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said his agency was investigating but declined to provide further details.
“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” he said.
No arrests have been made at this time, and no injuries have been reported.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said on Friday that BioUrja is “a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us.” She told reporters late Friday it was a “credible threat,” calling the device a “bomb.”
Local officials determined the device could cause a one-mile blast radius, prompting emergency responders to evacuate more than 5,000 residents and workers as a precaution around the city’s downtown, officials said. Officials established the blast radius due to the material surrounding the device inside the ethanol plant, Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said in a Saturday afternoon news conference.
It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don't result in a credible threat, even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
“This is not the case here,” he said. “We found a credible package there deemed to be a threat… We’re not considering this a hoax," Dixon said.
Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.
“We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said. “We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe.”
Police received the initial report about the threat just after 1 p.m. CT Friday, Dixon said. BioUrja had received an electronic communication about a bomb threat, and it indicated there was more than one package, Ali said.
After officials identified the suspicious package about an hour later, the device was later “rendered safe,” Dixon later said. However, the evacuation order had remained in effect until about 1 p.m. CT Saturday. No injuries were reported.
Officials established shelters at Manual Academy High School in Peoria and EastSide Centre, a sports complex in East Peoria.
Police and other authorities spent hours scouring the large complex for evidence until Dixon on Saturday afternoon said they completed the search, without finding any additional devices.
Overnight, police knocked door-to-door to urge people to get out of the blast radius. At around the same time, bomb teams entered the facility with BioUrja employees to begin searching the facility, he said.
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.
Laura Sharman, Martin Goillandeau and Eduardo Cuevas of CNN contributed.

title: At 25, his Lewiston brewery took the craft beer world by storm. Now he’s helping other local products get noticed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — The heady days of founding and running a regionally distributed beer brand — and the accolades that came with it — will always be a part of Luke Livingston.
In 2011, as the 27-year-old CEO of Baxter Brewing in Lewiston, he was named one of Forbes Magazine’s 30 under 30 entrepreneurs in the food and wine category, selected alongside entertainment and music giants like LeBron James, Lady Gaga, and Taylor Swift.
He was also selected to Uplift L/A 40 under 40 in 2016 and to Maine Magazine’s 50 Mainers charting the state’s future the same year.
Baxter Brewing was a trendsetter. It was the first craft brewery in New England to package its beer in cans instead of bottles, something that is now standard industrywide. Within a decade of operation, it was the third largest craft brewery in the state, producing nearly 20,000 barrels annually.
But Livingston acknowledges there was job burnout, and some boredom, too. “I’d surrounded myself with people that were far more capable than I was. I’d sort of hired myself out of a job,” he said. “And I wasn’t crazy about the direction the beer industry was going as a whole,” calling it less congenial, and less fun than when he started. So, at 34, he decided to retire.
As he parted ways with Baxter, leaving it in the capable hands of his then operations manager Jenn Lever, Livingston said he wanted to do something entirely different.
Livingston recently spoke briefly about what he took away from the Forbes Magazine fame.
“You know, it brought a huge amount of national attention to Baxter, which was great from a notoriety and a sales perspective,” said Livingston, who started the company when he was 25. “But again, I was very young. I probably let it go to my head a bit.”
Life after Baxter
After taking some time off, Livingston reconnected with old friends Jacob Eslinger and Henry Gilbert. Eslinger is a Culinary Institute of America graduate and a former marketing director at Holy Donut.
Together, the trio formed Brickyard Collective, a business consultancy focused on brand development and distribution. Their timing, however, was unfortunate. As they opened for business in March 2020, the world was shutting down as the COVID-19 pandemic took hold.
Livingston says they did some projects, met some people, and added Dylan Veilleux, a former client who is now director of sales, but he admits that Brickyard Collective never truly found success.
The group had an aha moment after hitting a wall with an in-house effort to market a hemp-based fire-starter rope to a large, national campground distributor. There was no communication, Livingston said diplomatically.
Off they went to the New England Made trade show in the spring of 2023, where they kept hearing that, for small companies making local products, distribution was a problem.
Within months, the team decided that was the path forward, and Brickyard Brands was essentially born, focusing on Maine-made and regionally made products, startups and independent entrepreneurs who need help getting to the finish line.
By the end of 2023, Brickyard Brands got its first big break, getting some client products into Hannaford grocery stores through the Shop Local program, which offers products from Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New York and Vermont.
“We got an equity investment in the company, and we were able to expand — buy some vehicles, and additional space at that point. Been off to the races ever since,” Livingston explained.
Breaking through barriers
Getting a seat at the table is one of the most difficult aspects of bringing a new product to market. In the food and beverage world that means knocking on doors, giving out samples, and convincing grocery chains, retail chains and others to carry your product.
Space equals money in retail and every store has a finite amount of it. That’s where Brickyard Brands comes into play.
Among the locally made products that gained traction at Hannaford through Brickyard Brands is Rockland-based Bixby Chocolate. Founder and CEO Kate McAleer described her experience with Brickyard as “fantastic.”
“I think they are hardworking and excited to grow,” she said. “I think they really care about the products.”
That care and attention is what sets Brickyard apart from the mega distributors focused mostly on the dollar, they say. All four partners are hands-on — from stocking products in their modest warehouse, to walking clients through a pitch at Hannaford.
“To have local products in the local section, with a local distributor, I think it’s such a win-win, all around,” McAleer said.
Brickyard Brands is still growing, with nearly 800 products in its portfolio, mostly food and beverages. Livingston said their growth strategy moving forward has changed a bit.
“A commitment we have across the board right now is to go deeper in the stores we’re in currently, and the region we’re in currently,” he said. “I think early on when we launched, we were trying initially to go geographically.”
Brickyard Brands expects to finish out the year with $3 million in sales, but emphasizes that they are just getting started. For now, the focus will remain on food and beverage.
“Food is also constantly changing, and so are consumer habits,” Eslinger said. “So, that’s an ever-evolving thing. I mean, there’s gonna be new products all the time. There’s going to be changes in consumer desires and wants, so you wouldn’t rule it out doing other things other than food down the road.”
What Livingston says he took from his time at Baxter was dealing with brands, how their warehouses operated and how they went to market. Building relationships with retailers is another lesson he learned and that he leverages today with convenience chains Rusty Lantern and Big Apple.
Livingston said he’s learned a lot since those early days at Baxter. One lesson involves work-life balance, family, and quality over quantity, he says, something he attributes to his days as CEO of Baxter.
Another is the critical nature of connection and teamwork.
“I have learned through the importance of partner-to-partner communication,” he said. “I think we, as a founding team, the four of us are tight and work together.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Chris Wheelock can be reached at cwheelock@sunjournal.com

title: Letter: Welcome back Arby’s
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
This letter might seem silly in a world with serious problems. Yet I write in favor of Arby’s, which is returning to Bangor.
Before moving to Maine in 1987, I spent the first 28 years of my life in Colorado where I started going to Arby’s when I was 8. That means I’ve been eating Arby’s sandwiches for nearly 60 years. Sort of mind-boggling.
I’ve always loved Arby’s sandwiches, especially just the basic, classic roast beef sandwich. When she was alive and Arby’s was still open in Bangor, my wife would sit and read in the Arby’s parking lot and when I was leaving from work, she would bring Arby’s home to me.
Arby’s, of course, closed in Bangor in 2015. Per Joni Mitchell, “Don’t it always seem to go/That you don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone.”
I drive to Augusta now and again just for Arby’s. Soon I won’t have to. Getting Arby’s back in Bangor is the best thing that’s happened to me for a long time, among things that are admittedly not terribly important.
I urge people to welcome and support Arby’s. It has the meats!
Brent Singer
Orono

title: Maine is ready to leave the Electoral College. Here’s how it could actually happen.
text:
Maine joined a coalition of states looking to get rid of the Electoral College in 2024. Now, after last week’s midterms, there’s a real possibility the popular vote could decide the next president.
Maine and 18 other states (plus Washington, D.C.) have joined the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact: a group of states pledging to give their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of whether that candidate wins their state.
The agreement only takes effect once there are enough states involved to contribute the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency. As it stands, the states in the compact cumulatively have 222 electoral votes.
In last week’s midterms, Democrats gained trifectas in six new state governments — meaning the party controls majorities in both statehouses and the governorship. One of them, Minnesota, is already in the compact. The remaining states hold 61 electoral votes altogether — enough to flip the Electoral College on its head if they choose to join.
“I don’t have to squint to see a path to 270 electoral votes before 2028,” said Pat Rosenstiel, senior consultant to National Popular Vote, a group advocating for states to join the compact. “We’ve got more than enough states in play. Frankly, I’m looking getting at 286 (votes) and beyond at this point.”
Maine was the 17th state to enter the compact when it joined in 2024 after Gov. Janet Mills allowed a bill to become law without her signature.
Maine’s four Electoral College votes are distributed differently than almost every other state. While most electoral votes are given to the candidate who receives a plurality of votes in each state, Maine uses a system called the congressional district method to apportion its electors.
Two of the state’s votes are given to the winner of the popular vote statewide. The remaining two are split between Maine’s congressional districts and given to the candidate who wins the most votes in each of those districts. Nebraska is the only other state that uses such a method.
That system technically wouldn’t go away under the law passed two years ago. But those electors in each congressional district would become bound to the national popular vote were the compact to take effect.
Maine’s congressional district method was adopted in part as a reaction to the three-way race in the 1968 presidential election between Republican Richard Nixon, Democrat Hubert Humphrey and independent candidate George Wallace. State officials wanted third-party candidates to have the opportunity to receive at least some electoral votes, especially if no candidate received an outright majority.
A similar anxiety is helping propel the national popular vote movement. The Electoral College’s winner-take-all system is a large part of why two parties dominate American politics, according to Nicholas Jacobs, associate professor of American government at Colby College.
“It discourages people from wasting their vote on a third-party candidate,” he said. “If we move to a world of a national interstate vote compact, then it truly is just whomever gets the most votes wins.”
“But if you throw open the doors to lots of minor party candidates,” he added, “it then produces the very real possibility that the national popular vote winner does not get anywhere close to a majority.”
PRINCIPLED OR PARTISAN?
The movement to abandon the Electoral College gained traction after two presidents in the last 25 years — George W. Bush and Donald Trump — won election after losing the popular vote. Democrat Al Gore earned some 540,000 more votes than Bush in 2000, while Hillary Clinton received nearly 3 million more than Trump in 2016.
Nearly all of the states that have joined the compact to this point lean Democratic. And with the party in control of legislatures and executive branches in a number of key states, some newly elected Democrats are openly musing about joining the popular vote compact.
Wisconsin’s new governor, David Crowley, said “We can do away” with the Electoral College, The Associated Press reported. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said on a liberal podcast last week that “the national popular vote makes sense.”
Both states would be crucial to hitting the 270 mark needed for the popular vote compact to take effect, and they’re “well within our reach now,” said Rosenstiel, with National Popular Vote — though he disputed the notion that embracing the popular vote is a partisan idea. A majority of voters (63%, according to a July Pew Research Center poll) support abolishing the Electoral College.
“It has everything to do with putting voters in charge,” he said. “I believe a conservative Second Amendment Republican like me in a blue state like Minnesota should matter as much as a liberal, progressive Democrat in Oklahoma City.”
Though voters widely support adopting the popular vote, the issue remains largely partisan in many state legislatures.
The Electoral College offers more power to smaller and rural states. Each state is guaranteed at least three electoral votes, with more votes distributed based on a state’s population. Voters in small states like Maine and Wyoming, for instance, retain more electoral power than those in populous states like California or Texas as a result.
Whether that’s a good or a bad thing largely depends on your politics, according to Mark Brewer, chair of the University of Maine’s political science department.
Most of those smaller states vote reliably Republican. As a result, the issue has become polarized along party lines in many of the states that have debated joining the compact, Brewer said.
“The system currently benefits Republicans, but it used to benefit Democrats when Democrats controlled the South,” he said. “The reality is, it’s not a principled thing; it’s a partisan advantage thing. And right now, the Electoral College works to benefit Republicans.”
WOULD THE COMPACT LAST?
Given that political push-and-pull, Brewer said it’s not out of the realm of possibility that states could choose to leave the popular vote coalition if political headwinds change in the future.
Some legislatures, including Maine’s, have already debated reneging on their decision to enter the coalition. A bill introduced here to withdraw from the compact narrowly passed the House last year before being defeated in the Senate by a thin margin.
In debating the bill, conservative Maine legislators argued the state’s current system of balancing electoral votes between congressional districts and the in-state popular vote is the best compromise.
Proponents of the compact argue the Electoral College is inherently undemocratic. That votes in some states have more weight than others leads to a level of inequality, they say. And under the current system, they note small states are already largely ignored. Presidential candidates spend most of their time and effort trying to convince voters in swing states.
“Just ask anybody who lives in North Dakota, South Dakota, Alaska — ask anybody in Maine during the last presidential cycle,” Rosenstiel said. “The only way to put small state voters on the map in presidential elections is through a national popular vote.”
Some scholars have warned creating a new way to decide the presidency could undermine trust in American elections and government at a time when many are already skeptical. It may also face legal challenges that would likely reach the Supreme Court.
Though the Constitution leaves it to individual states to administer their elections and decide how to allocate their electoral votes, it also prohibits states from entering compacts without the permission of Congress.
“You could envision lawsuits saying that the interstate compact violates the constitutionally derived principle of one person one vote, right?” Brewer said. “I’m sure the lawsuits are at the ready.”
Brewer has provided testimony to the Maine Legislature in opposition to the popular vote compact. While he agrees that the Electoral College is undemocratic to an extent, he sees potential Constitutional crises that could arise should the compact attain the 270 electoral votes needed to take effect.
“We could find ourselves in a situation where we’ve got a court challenge to who won a presidential election that we can’t figure out before the new president would have to take the oath of office,” Brewer said.
Both opponents and proponents of the popular vote agree ditching the Electoral College would cause a seismic shift in American politics. For better or worse, the way presidential candidates campaign and strategize would be flipped on its head — which may have unintended consequences down the road.
“When you change the rules, you change the dynamics of a democracy,” said Jacobs, the Colby professor. “Every time we change the rules, rarely have we changed them in the way that we anticipated.”

title: NASA's Voyager 1 closes in on a light-day in interstellar space for a new distance record
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to become humanity’s first object to reach one light-day from Earth as it pushes ever deeper into interstellar space.
That’s a mind-blowing distance of more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) for the spacecraft launched 49 years ago.
When Voyager 1 reaches that remarkable milestone on Wednesday, its radio signals will take precisely 24 hours traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth — in other words, one light-day. NASA is looking at another 18,000 years before the spacecraft achieves a full light-year and more than double that before it comes near another star.
Project manager Suzanne Dodd sees Voyager 1 as Earth’s ambassador hurtling between stars while providing a “sense of wonder” on the home front.
“It’s a national treasure,” she told The Associated Press. “Really extraordinary.”
To celebrate this moment, NASA is urging people from all corners to grab their phone or a flashlight to create a wave of golden light after sunset Tuesday, using Morse code to spell the letters V-G-R, Voyager’s call sign, into the night sky.
Despite sporadic problems typical of old age, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 continue to send back science and engineering data as they zoom toward different points in space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph). Although launched two weeks before its sibling in 1977, Voyager 2 won’t reach the one light-day mark until 2035.
Voyager 1 swept past Jupiter and Saturn to scientists’ delight in 1979 and 1980, respectively, before exiting the solar system. It reached what NASA defines as interstellar space — the expansive region between star systems — in 2012. Voyager 2 visited those two planets plus Uranus and Neptune, also sending back stunning photos, before entering interstellar space in 2018.
Almost every day, the Voyagers beam back details about their never-before-explored environment: the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as tidbits about the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays. They’re a bit like weather satellites, according to Dodd, who’s worked with the Voyagers since 1984.
The skeleton flight control team at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, sends commands about once a week. The operation ramps up when spacecraft problems arise, with help sometimes coming from a couple of retirees who once worked on the project.
In September, controllers completed the latest power-conserving effort for the plutonium-powered spacecraft, then in October briefly lost contact with it. They’re still trying to figure out why communication was disrupted.
All this expertise and love have kept Voyager 1 chugging along like “the little engine that could,” according to Dodd, while racking up entries in Guinness World Records. Besides venturing farther than any other human-made object, Voyager 1 in 1990 snapped the most distant picture of Earth: the iconic “Pale Blue Dot” as seen from beyond Neptune.
“On that blue dot, that’s where everyone you know and everyone you ever heard of and every human being who ever lived, lived out their lives. It’s a very small stage in a great cosmic arena,” Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, part of the imaging team, said as he introduced the picture to the world in 1990.
While the majority of people alive today were not yet born when the Voyagers launched, “all of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement. The society was co-founded in 1980 by Sagan, who died in 1996.
The Golden Record also resulted from Sagan’s effort.
Each Voyager carries a 12-inch (30-centimeter) gold-plated phonographic record containing greetings in 55 languages as well as images and diagrams. Sagan included the voice of his son Nick, then 6: “Hello from the children on Planet Earth.” He added a stylus and instructions for any finders-keepers out there.
“It’s a time capsule of life on Earth from 1977,” Dodd said. “I hope something, someone, finds it maybe 1,000 years from now.”
___

title: Maine Celtics suffer first loss of season
text:
Caleb Love scored 21 of his 35 points in the fourth quarter, and the Delaware Blue Coats erased a 10-point deficit Saturday while handing the Maine Celtics their first loss of the NBA G League season, winning 130-119 in Wilmington, Delaware.
Love, a former North Carolina and University of Arizona star who averaged 10 points per game as an NBA rookie for the Portland Trail Blazers last season, helped the Blue Coats outscore Maine 39-18 over the final nine minutes.
Six players reached double figures for the Celtics (3-1), led by Milos Uzan with 22 points. Amari Williams had 19 and Dillon Mitchell finished with 18.

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after hourslong global outage
text:
(AP) - Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X.
Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: National weather radars are not down, federal officials say
text:
Weather radars are not down, National Weather Service says
Nationwide weather radars are not experiencing an outage Friday night.
That is according to the National Weather Service, which put out a statement on social media debunking the fast-moving rumor.
"In case you heard otherwise, there is no radar outage and https://radar.weather.gov is fully operational!" NWS wrote. "Outdated content from isolated webpages stating otherwise has been circulating, but NWS radars are operating normally."
The rumor started soon after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
It's the second time since Sept. 11, 2001, that such an order has been issued. The last was January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Federal officials are investigating what caused the flight system problem and flights remained grounded as of early Friday evening. But rest assured, the weather system is still operational.

title: Husson football finishes up with 65-0 victory over MMA
text:
Brody Gibson threw four touchdown passes as Husson University topped in-state rival Maine Maritime Academy 65-0 at Ritchie Field in Castine in the regular season finale for both teams.
Husson won five of its last six games to finish at 5-5 overall and 5-2 in the Conference of New England. MMA wound up 0-10 and 0-7 and has now lost 46 straight games.
Gibson tossed TD passes of 11 and 14 yards to Jacob Lenz, 17 yards to Dom Rolle and 49 yards to Anthony Santacroce.
Santacroce also scored on a 17 yard run and Daniel Ruiz Cantu scored on runs of 24 and 13 yards.
Chad Monty had a one-yard TD run, Jordan Espo scored on a 15-yard scamper and Ricardo Schulz kicked a 24-yard field goal.
Gibson completed 19 of 24 passes for 260 yards and Lenz had six catches for 110 yards and Caden Crocker had six for 43. Cantu had six carries for 63 yards, DK Koutsoufakis had 11 for 49 and Santacroce had seven for 47.
Noah Snyder’s six tackles and Malik Sow’s five paced the defense.
Harris Stone completed 12 of 27 passes for 118 yards for MMA and Auston Harris had four catches for 62 yards.
MMA’s Lucas Houghton, who came into the game tied for 10th in tackles per game (10.7) among players at 242 Division III schools, had a terrific game with a game-high 21 tackles giving him 117 for the season. Connor Cuba had 18 tackles and Jack Coleman had 16.
In other games involving Maine’s Division III schools, Biddeford’s University of New England beat New England College 56-3 to win the second annual Battle for Route 202. UNE wound up 5-5 overall and a program-best 5-2 in the CNE. It was UNE’s fifth straight win.
Colby beat Bowdoin 19-13 to win the CBB (Colby, Bates, Bowdoin) series. It had edged Bates 21-19 earlier this season.
Hamilton beat Bates 47-17.
Colby finished up at 2-7, Bates at 1-8 and Bowdoin at 0-9.
Bates beat Bowdoin 10-7 previously this fall.

title: Brewer poised to allow data centers that use as much power as a small city
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Brewer is moving to allow data centers that could use as much power as a small city, even as other Greater Bangor towns ban them.
The City Council is weighing zoning changes already approved by the Planning Board that would permit 50-megawatt data centers. They would only be allowed in specific industrial zones. Developers have already looked at a city-owned site behind the Brewer landfill, Assistant City Manager Jason Moffitt said.
The changes wouldn’t approve any specific project, and no one has formally proposed one. But Moffitt said people in the data center industry told city officials that expanded rules would make Brewer a more attractive place to build. While past developers have expressed interest, Moffitt didn’t say when specifically that happened or which companies reached out.
If the changes are approved, Brewer would be the first major municipality in the region to make room for the facilities. Bangor and Old Town have passed bans this year, saying the environmental effects of data centers aren’t yet understood.
The Brewer Planning Board recommended the changes to the city’s land use Monday. Currently, Brewer’s ordinances allow for 20-megawatt or smaller data centers.
In other communities, 50-megawatt centers have taken up roughly a dozen acres. The zones where a center can be built are all in south Brewer, mostly along the city line with Orrington.
During Monday’s meeting, Moffitt and Bill Birney, a member of Gov. Janet Mills’ Maine Data Center Advisory Council, said the changes are needed if a data center were to be built in the city, Planning Board member Joy Sinclair said.
Largely, the discussions at the meeting were “pro data center,” Sinclair, who was the only member to vote against the changes, said. The downsides of a possible center were shared, but not as extensively discussed as potential positives, she said.
Meeting minutes and a recording of the Monday meeting were not available, City Planner Linda Johns said Friday.
Birney did not respond to a request for comment.
A release from City Manager Eric Glidden sent to residents Tuesday echoes what Moffitt and Birney said at the meeting.
“Allowing development up to that limit could, however, provide a significant opportunity to expand Brewer’s tax base and benefit residents and businesses,” Glidden said.
If a 50-megawatt project were developed, the city’s tax base could nearly double, according to the release. That addition could lead to property taxes going down by 25%, the city having funds to repair the city pool or to buy a ladder truck for the fire department, Glidden said in the release.
An informational meeting about the proposed changes will be held on Nov. 24 at 6 p.m. in the Brewer Auditorium.

title: The hunt went great, until the deer stole his rifle
text:
This story was originally published in December 2019.
Spend enough time in the Maine woods and you’re bound to see all kinds of weird stuff. Whether you’re sitting around the campfire or picking up your morning paper, those stories are lots of fun to hear or read.
Today’s odd Maine woods tale comes from reader Chris Greeley, who passed along a story from his dad.
“As an Army veteran who served during the ‘Korean conflict,’ he never hunted, nor would he have anything to do with guns, once back in Maine,” Greeley wrote. “However, he was out with a friend who WAS deer hunting (I guess just accompanying him for companionship), when they came across a nice buck. My dad’s friend, who was armed with a .30-30, took a shot and dropped the mature male deer, which was sporting a nice rack.
“He was so impressed with the number of points on its antlers, that he almost immediately suggested to my dad that he intended to get it mounted. He approached the buck and placed his beloved Winchester rifle onto its antlers in order to envision how it might look as a ‘rifle rack’ on the wall of his living room.
“As the two stepped back to admire my dad’s friends accomplishment, the deer suddenly ‘came to’ and took off … with the gun. Neither the deer or rifle were ever seen again.”
I’ve heard all kinds of odd stories over the years, including one about a rifle-stealing beaver and another that’s remarkably similar to the one that Greeley shares here.
And while we’ll never have concrete proof that the story played out exactly the way it’s told here, it’s interesting enough to share, I figure. File this one: “Well, it could have happened.”

title: Airlines won’t be required to offer passengers additional compensation after ground stop
text:
(AP) - The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could resume Friday after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.
The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that outages of the U.S. air traffic control system were caused by an overload of an old, analog system. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin called for further funding to improve the system.
An FAA computer problem is considered outside the control of the airlines — much like the weather.
So the only thing the airlines are obligated to do is to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers that want to continue to their destinations or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting planes back in the air may take time and that getting air traffic back to normal would be slow.

title: The US cannot rebuild Gaza without Israel
text:
A Nov. 11 op-ed, “A roadmap for Democrats who want peace in Gaza,” places the blame for the conflict in Gaza almost entirely on Hamas. The writer does not mention that the long history of occupation and deprivation that Israel inflicted on Gaza after 1967 led to the rise of Hamas.
As evidence of Israel’s willingness to resolve the current conflict, the writer cites the decision of Ariel Sharon, in 2005, to pull Israeli settlers out of Gaza. Sharon didn’t act out of the goodness of his heart. He realized the cost of protecting the settlers in occupied Gaza was unsustainable and chose to concentrate settlement efforts in the West Bank.
The writer accuses Hamas of scuttling the 2005 Agreement on Movement and Access, but the accord was unraveling before Hamas came to power. The Israelis never fully opened border crossings, did not keep their promise to allow movement between Gaza and the West Bank and dragged their feet on the construction of a needed port.
The writer calls on the international community, led by the United States, to rebuild Gaza, but it is Israel that is responsible for the almost total destruction of Gaza’s infrastructure through a campaign of indiscriminate bombing. Why is it under no obligation to help repair the damage?
The writer wants Democrats to end what he calls their “incendiary campaign rhetoric.” Until Israeli politicians recognize the rights and the fundamental humanity of Palestinians, detailed roadmaps will not lead to a brighter future for Gaza.
Charles Brown
Owls Head

title: Man who went into water after New Orleans cruise ship collision speaks out
text:
'Kept bobbing underneath': Man who went into water after New Orleans cruise ship collision speaks out
A Kansas man who spent 15 to 20 minutes in the water after a tanker crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday is speaking out.
Joe Knab, a Navy veteran from Wichita, Kansas, said he feared he might drown as he bobbed up and down in the water.
"I think that’s pretty much a miracle," Knab said of everyone getting out. Officials there have called it "a miracle on the Mississippi."
He spoke with Hearst Television sister station WDSU about the miracle moment.
"You got dirt still on your jeans. You were on the boat," WDSU Anchor Killion described as he spoke to Knab during his interview.
"OK, well, when the big trader come down there and start blowing the horn. So we knew there was something wrong," Knab said. "And they come alongside and hit us real hard, and it's jammed us up against the pier. And the motor started leaning to the starboard side right off the bat."
Once the boat began to capsize, Knab said that Port Authority crews and "regular old people with boats" helped get passengers out of the water and to safety.
He was taken to a hotel nearby.
"Got a free shirt out of that deal," he quipped. "All my undershirts are at the bottom of the river, so whatever."
