title: Oxford Hills football defeats Windham to claim Class A North title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
PARIS — Keegan and Mason Ridley were middle schoolers playing football in the Gouin Athletic Complex’s south end zone the last time Oxford Hills played in a regional title game in 2022.
“Just like all the little kids do now,” said Mason.
Four years later, the brothers were the ones making plays as the Vikings defeated Windham, 42-33, in the Class A North final Saturday.
Top-seeded Oxford Hills (9-1) will play Bonny Eagle (10-1) in the state championship game next Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland.
“Here we are, going to play for a Gold Ball,” Keegan Ridley said. “It feels amazing.
Keegan rushed 28 times for 161 yards and three touchdowns and also scored on a kick return, while his brother caught four passes for 33 yards and a touchdown, and intercepted a pass.
“Everything was working,” Keegan said. “We just (have) to pound it in and go to work, and that’s all it is.”
Oxford Hills defeated Windham 34-14 in a season opener on Sept. 4. This time around, the Eagles looked more than ready to compete, with a trip to the state final at stake.
Every time Oxford Hills scored in the first half, Windham (7-4) answered. The Eagles’ first touchdown — a 61-yard pass from Patrick Davenport to Landon Wyman — came just 16 seconds after Oxford Hills opened the scoring with a 4-yard TD run from Keegan Ridley.
By halftime, the score was knotted at 21-21.
It wasn’t until the Vikings recovered a fumble in the third quarter that they began to create some separation. Keegan Ridley’s 1-yard touchdown, his fourth of the game, put Oxford Hills ahead, 28-21.
“I’ve been promising them all year that this was going to happen if you put your time in, and it’s paid off, so we’re just extremely happy,” Oxford Hills coach Nate Danforth said.
Windham fumbled again on the kickoff, setting up an 11-yard touchdown pass from Toby Oufiero to Tucker Hilden.
Mason Ridley’s interception on the Eagles’ next possession helped Oxford Hills expand its lead. His 14-yard touchdown reception made it 42-21.
“We turned the ball over three times, and credit to (Oxford Hills), they didn’t turn it over, so that really caught up to us,” Windham coach Matt Perkins said.
The Eagles showed they had a few more scoring plays left in them late in the fourth quarter. Davenport found Ronin Rotaru for a 71-yard reception, then connected with Dre O’Neil for his second score of the game — a 13-yarder — with no time on the clock.
“I was proud of our kids, they kept battling the whole time and didn’t let up,” Perkins said. “So I was very pleased with that, and just the effort.”
Next weekend’s state final is the second matchup of the season between Bonny Eagle and Oxford Hills. The Scots dealt the Vikings their only setback, 45-9, on Oct. 9.

title: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
text:
With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections.
In exchanges with reporters, broadcast interviews and social media posts since Election Day, he's somehow managed to back away from carrying out additional strikes while also backing away from the prospect of additional talks with the Islamic Republic's negotiators on ending the 8-month-old conflict.
The president acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses, while maintaining it was the right thing to do.
Related video above: Falling gas prices aren’t proof gas companies inflated prices to hurt Trump
Then, at the start of this week, he huddled with Qatar's prime minister at the White House and afterward told reporters that he believed it was highly unlikely he'd need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over.”
But by Thursday, he was again raising questions about whether he needed to rush to find an endgame. He declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and brusquely directed Vice President JD Vance — who served as his chief negotiator in earlier peace talks with Iran — to shift his attention to the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democrat-controlled cities and states.
All the while, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate" to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Iran war will shadow Trump during his trip to Asia
Trump's tonal shifts have only added to the uncertainty about what comes next in a war in which America's allies were not consulted before it was started but nonetheless struggle to deal with its economic ramifications.
“President Trump is now acting like an arsonist who has set ablaze our foreign policy,” Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey said in an interview Friday on the sidelines of the Democrats’ postelection gathering in Denver. “And now he just wants to walk away.”
The president's ambiguous positioning on the war is expected to loom large during a visit next week to the Philippines and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
While in Shenzhen, Trump will hold an unprecedented three-way summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump is expected to discuss Iran and the three powers' nuclear stockpiles with Xi and Putin.
The White House declined to comment directly to queries on Trump's postelection rhetoric on Iran. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored that Trump's approach is leading to the Iranian economy collapsing.
“The economic pain that we are inflicting on that regime is so great that there’s no need for military action because we’ve weakened them so much,” Rubio said in a Friday evening speech to the Federalist Society.
Mideast diplomats try to make sense of Trump's position
Chief mediator Qatar continues to try to negotiate an interim agreement that would restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for the flow of oil and natural gas from the Persian Gulf to global markets, while leaving open options for further discussions between the U.S. and Iran.
But those efforts are now clouded by uncertainty following Trump’s shifting — and sometimes contradictory — comments, according to two Middle East diplomats familiar with the process.
The diplomats, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said the situation had appeared to be on the right track earlier this week after Qatar’s prime minister met with Trump.
But Trump's social media post Thursday declaring that the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran and directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign has created a sense of limbo.
One of the diplomats said the post raised questions about why Trump appeared to be sidelining Vance, who was skeptical about launching the war but ultimately supported Trump.
Trump's post came as Vance had been weighing a possible reengagement with senior Iranian negotiators, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The president posted his message calling on Vance to steer away from Iran negotiations the morning after The Wall Street Journal reported Vance was thinking about resuming talks. Trump — who had been aware of Vance's deliberations — believed the Iranians weren't acting in good faith, the person added.
Trump is also increasingly confident that he can credibly declare that he's achieved his military objectives in the war.
But traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains treacherous. The United Nations reports October had the highest number of incidents against commercial ships in the contested waters since February.
Still, Trump believes that with oil shipments through the strait reaching near-prewar levels, he could potentially leave it to Gulf countries to negotiate a deal with the Iranians on governing the critical waterway, the person said.
The other regional diplomat described the push for peace as falling into a holding pattern as people await clarification from the White House on Trump’s intentions.
That diplomat added it was not entirely clear to mediators or the Iranians if Trump’s comments meant he was abandoning a negotiated agreement or was just posturing after the congressional midterm elections that cost his Republican Party control of Congress.
Rubio insists U.S. hasn't given up on mediation efforts
Iran remains unwilling to engage in negotiations over its nuclear program until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.
Differences with Iran over its nuclear activities remain one of the thorniest issues. It's one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.
Tehran's rhetoric has hardly cooled. Iran’s deputy U.N. ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi told the United Nations Security Council on Friday that Iran “has never closed the door to diplomacy.” But he warned that should the U.S. or Israel return to bombing, his country would offer “an immediate and decisive response.”
Rubio earlier this week stressed that the U.S. is not opposed to mediators continuing their efforts.
“If there’s a deal to be done, the president will be the first one to be in favor of it," Rubio said. "But it’s not going to be a stupid deal. It’s not going to be a bad deal.”
Michael Singh, managing director at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said he expects the status quo to persist for some time, with the U.S. and Iran locked in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. continuing its monthslong naval blockade that's curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Singh said the American strategy of squeezing Iran economically is a far more attractive option for Trump than military escalation or making concessions to Tehran.
He also suggested Trump could always reverse his position on Vance engaging with Iranians if the president finds the Iranians are ready to seriously negotiate.
“It’s probably the most sensible path as well to sort of be patient, keep the pressure on, allow the mediators to keep doing their work,” said Singh, who worked on Middle East issues in former President George W. Bush's White House. “And when the time is right, but not before then, is when you want to engage senior officials like the vice president and so forth.”

title: Carbon monoxide toxicity suspected in death of woman, dog in mobile grooming van
text:
BEXAR COUNTY, Texas (KENS) - Two families are mourning the loss of a 10-year-old dog and the groomer who was caring for him.
The Bexar County Medical Examiner’s Office said Friday that carbon monoxide toxicity factored into the deaths.
Deputies find woman and dog unresponsive
Bexar County deputies responded Wednesday night to Dusty Boots Road after receiving a report of an injured adult. When deputies arrived, they found a woman and a dog, both unresponsive, inside a mobile grooming van.
The woman was later pronounced dead. Her identity has not been released.
The dog, Oliver, also did not survive. The dog’s owner said the family is heartbroken after losing their pet of 10 years.
“It’s just so unexpected. You’re just getting your dog groomed and then you don’t have your dog anymore,” Priscilla Coral, owner of Puptown Spa Mobile Grooming, said.
Safety questions in mobile grooming
The deaths are raising questions about safety in the mobile grooming industry.
Coral, who is not related to the deaths, operates several grooming trucks and two storefronts. She said proper ventilation, functioning carbon monoxide detectors and routine maintenance are essential to keeping both pets and workers safe.
“Having a reputable generator person, a reputable mechanic and choosing a reputable company I feel like is really important,” Coral said.
Coral said the deaths have left the mobile grooming community shaken and prompted some business owners to take a closer look at their own safety practices.
“I feel a lot of people worried, but not in a good way, but it’s brought out now people looking at safety,” Coral said.

title: College football scrambles, adjusts kickoffs after FAA groundings
text:
(AP) - College football got a jolt it didn’t expect on the eve of a host of big games Saturday.
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide for several hours Friday, impacting thousands of flights and throwing travel plans into question for scores of college football teams. Most travel the day before Saturday kickoffs.
Many schools — including No. 2 Utah, No. 8 Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — had to scramble to figure things out. The Utes’ game at No. 22 Arizona was pushed back three hours to a 10:30 p.m. Eastern kickoff. Baylor’s game at No. 12 BYU was also moved back by 3 1/2 hours, to a 7 p.m. EST kick.
No. 19 Ole Miss was unable to get out of Starkville, Mississippi, on time and ended up having its game at Oklahoma moved to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST — going head-to-head with early NFL action. The decision also drew the ire of Sooners athletic director Roger Denny.
“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition (Saturday), they were unable to find a solution,” Denny said in a message posted on X. “After multiple conversations with the league office, commissioner (Greg) Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection.
“After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”
Denny said the decision “isn’t fair to our athletes” or fans but “we’ve been given no other choice” after “the wrong outcome was reached.”
Some teams — including the Longhorns (at LSU) and Volunteers (at Texas A&M) — were not expected to travel until late Friday at the earliest, meaning they would suit up for a game on far less sleep than usual. The Big 12 shifted the Arizona State-UCF game from 2:30 p.m. EST to 5:30 p.m., giving the Sun Devils an additional three hours after their flight from Arizona to Florida was delayed.
Other teams went old school, at least for top-tier college football: Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State with the SEC pushing back the Saturday start time by more than four hours to give the Tigers a buffer. Purdue boarded buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.
Top games to watch
Unbeaten Utah can continue its run toward the Big 12 championship game with a late-night win at Arizona (7-2), which puts Noah Fifita up against Devon Dampier in a duel of star quarterbacks.
Texas (7-2) will try to extend its win streak to four games and go 5-0 against Top 25 opponents at No. 24 LSU (6-3), which still has faint playoff hopes.
No. 11 Wake Forest (8-1) visits No. 25 SMU (7-1) in a meeting of Atlantic Coast Conference teams trying to reach the league championship game.
No. 15 Southern California (7-2) will try to build some late-season momentum when it visits No. 6 Indiana (8-1).
Under the radar
Louisville (6-3) visits North Carolina (5-4), where Bill Belichick’s team has played better and needs just one win for bowl eligibility.
The Cardinals have won four straight and are right in the thick of the race for a spot in the ACC championship game. They need some help, though, because second-place Wake Forest is ahead of them by a game in the standings and own the head-to-head tiebreaker.

title: 50 years after iconic film, a gathering of ‘Rocky’ fans in Philadelphia breaks a world record
text:
50 years after iconic film, a gathering of ‘Rocky’ fans in Philadelphia breaks a world record
The story of Rocky Balboa is one that audiences love and know well – of resilience, grit and perseverance despite the odds.
Fans honored his legacy 50 years after the film's release with a Guinness World Record-breaking gathering of people dressed as Rocky on Friday at the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
The uniform? A black beanie, gray sweatpants and sweatshirt, and black high-top Converse sneakers.
Watch above: ‘Rocky’ fans in Philadelphia break a world record
A growing number of Rockys amassed in front of the museum steps Friday afternoon, cheering as stragglers showed up to aid the record-breaking attempt.
“What's your name?” the announcer asked one participant. “Rocky Balboa,” they replied.
A minimum of 250 people needed to be there for the occasion, according to Guinness. The official record was certified with 570 participants, an announcer said.
The city organized a host of events this month to honor its fictional underdog boxer, including a sprint up the stairs that Rocky stormed up in the film, a rededication marking the permanent installation of the Rocky statue, and a meat market challenge where fans can recreate a scene in the film where he trained by punching slabs of frozen meat.
After the world record was confirmed, the group ran up the stairs to pose for a picture in front of the museum.
On Saturday, tourism officials said 45,000 runners from all 50 states and 75 countries will participate in a “Rocky Run” throughout the city.
The 1976 film written by Sylvester Stallone tells the story of a small-time boxer from South Philly who gears up to take on the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed, fighting in the city to celebrate America’s bicentennial. Though he ultimately loses the fight, Rocky proves himself and wins the heart of Adrian, the neighborhood pet store clerk.
The movie was shot for less than $1 million, and Stallone was an unknown actor who had written the script in a desperate bid to land himself work.
The film won the best picture Oscar and became the highest-grossing sports movie at the time. Its numerous spinoffs and sequels have helped it hold the record for most successful sports movie franchise, according to Guinness World Records.
Philadelphia held its inaugural Rocky Day in 2023 with Stallone in attendance, expanding celebrations to a weeklong Rocky Fest the next year. The city kicked off this year’s festivities with the release of Stallone’s memoir, “The Steps,” on Sept. 29.

title: Rescuers make human chain to save 6-year-old from freezing river
text:
TOTOWA, N.J. (WABC) - Officials came to the aid of a 6-year-old boy who had wandered away from his New Jersey home last week.
Police said he was found clinging to a tree in the Passaic River and that a human chain was created to get him to safety. The heroic rescue was captured on body camera video.
“It was super emotional. You know, we are also parents, so we tend to see things a little bit more personal,” Fina Matranga, a Totowa Police Department patrolman, said.
Last Thursday night, Totowa police received emergency calls about a barefoot child knocking on doors and then fleeing.
Crews were dispatched and found the boy’s parents desperately searching for their child, who has autism and is nonverbal.
It’s believed the boy may have escaped from his family’s home through a window.
“Some people were screaming his name,” neighbor Latoya Carswell said. “And some people were just, like, on foot, power walk and some are running.”
The growing search team definitely felt the time pressure when they realized children with autism tend to gravitate toward water.
So, they raced to the Passaic River.
“We quickly widened our resources and called the fire department for extra lighting and more manpower, along with other agencies around town and the sheriff’s department,” Matranga said.
They fortunately found the child before he was swept away by the current. It was reported he was down a dark embankment, half in the freezing river and clinging to a tree.
Because of the steep drop, rescue crews handed the shivering child up a human chain.
“Completely drenched from head to toe, full of mud,” Matranga said. “I sat with him and I was able to comfort him and clean them up a little bit as much as I could … I have some sensory toys in my duty bag for these cases, and I was able to give him some toys.”
Officials believed the child may have been drawn by nearby Christmas lights as well as the water.
Police said the child’s parents will be installing tighter locks on their windows.

title: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit
text:
HONG KONG (AP) — Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence.
The scandal now threatens to intensify that rivalry.
As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week in China, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Congress are seizing on the affair to press for tighter restrictions on technology exports to protect America’s edge.
“The scandal, in many ways, encapsulates the rivalry, where concerns around national security, export control, and foreign policy get intertwined,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at London-based technology research and advisory group Omdia.
At the heart of the competition to build the most advanced artificial intelligence is the race to access the most powerful AI chips. U.S.-led restrictions have barred China from getting the world’s most advanced AI chips, a strategy that has led Beijing to accuse the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly.
Once commanding some 95% of market share in China, Nvidia’s sales to China have plummeted due to the export restrictions, first applied during the Biden administration. After Huang lobbied Washington to loosen the limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Trump earlier this year greenlighted the export of its highly-advanced, though not the most powerful, H200 chips.
Trump has spoken admiringly of Huang — a man at the center of the AI boom Trump has been keen to promote — and the two have talked regularly during his second term, including at least twice this week as the scandal grew around the tech executive.
Supporters of stronger export controls have a new rallying cry
The strategy in Washington has been largely focused on hardware, with officials believing if they controlled where California-based Nvidia’s best chips go, they’d be in control of the race for the most capable AI, said Shaoyu Yuan, an assistant professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs.
That strategy was effective in slowing down Chinese companies, Yuan said, but it assumed the primary threat was the physical hardware, not access to leaders like Huang.
Yuan said what he called “China hawks” in Congress — who have been bullish on oversight and stronger export controls long before this incident — will now have “a story with a name and a face” to support their argument.
“I don’t think anybody in Washington wants to be seen as loosening the controls on chip exports to China right now,” he added.
This week several congressional Democrats wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to ask what officials knew of Huang’s affair with a reported Chinese spy — and to demand an immediate halt to exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Lawmakers from both parties have become more outspoken in their calls for tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. The Senate version of a defense policy bill includes authorizing Congress to review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, authorizing the Commerce Department to track AI chips to ensure they aren’t diverted to unauthorized regions, and compelling U.S. allies to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Beijing has warned the U.S. against using the episode as a reason to impose new restrictions, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning telling reporters on Thursday: “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions.”
China and the US have been pursuing common ground on AI safety
The woman in the relationship with the Nvidia chief is reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to reporting by The New York Times, U.S. officials suspect she was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its cutting-edge chips more available to China.
Beijing has refuted claims she was a Chinese spy and called the allegation “unsubstantiated.”
Trump doe s not plan to confront Xi on the Nvidia issue, according to senior U.S. officials who briefed reporters Friday on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House. The officials also said they do not expect Chinese retaliation if they close loopholes to existing measures that prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips.
Huang has been a frequent visitor to the White House, and in May, he jumped onto Air Force One in Alaska, joining Trump at the last minute for a state visit to Beijing, where he captivated locals by sampling street food. He and his wife, Lori, were seated at the head table with the two leaders when Trump hosted Xi in September in Washington. At a tech summit that month, Huang took a phone call from the president while he was in a live appearance.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and China have committed to the idea of a hotline for AI national security-related incidents.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Brookings Institution, said the Nvidia scandal — and the possibility of new U.S. export control measures — could throw a wrench in the AI talks. “The question is whether Beijing can separate export controls from the AI safety discussion or will view them as connected issues,” Chan said.
The U.S.-China technology race goes on
The U.S. and China have been moving AI technology forward in different ways. U.S. companies are chasing AI frontiers supported by cutting-edge chips and the country’s rapidly expanding data center infrastructure. China is pursuing wider global adoption of its open-source, more affordable models.
Increasingly, experts say, China is emerging as an AI counterweight to the U.S. and closing the gap in its lead on the technology. But advanced chips and other technology from Nvidia are still crucial for many Chinese AI companies and research, analysts say.
Chinese chipmakers, including Huawei, have been making rapid progress to narrow the gap by finding ways to work around the U.S. restrictions, including by clustering large numbers of less advanced domestic chips. But Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips still lead in single-chip capability and outperform Chinese alternatives in training advanced AI models, analysts say.
China’s push for technological self-reliance may have contributed to a reluctance to buy larger amounts of American chips. Despite the U.S. approval to sell some H200 chips to China, Nvidia said earlier this year it had shipped only a small amount to China.
The Huang episode could ultimately add momentum to China’s domestic chip industry, said Rui Ma, founder of Tech Buzz China and a China tech expert.
“For Beijing, the fallout only adds urgency to its efforts to build a domestic semiconductor supply chain. That was already a strategic priority, but if access to Nvidia computing power becomes even more restricted, Chinese companies will have increasingly few alternatives,” Ma said.
___
AP journalists Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles, and Didi Tang, Seung Min Kim and Kevin Freking in Washington contributed.

title: Creole Queen crew rescues nine after Mississippi cruise ship collision
text:
Creole Queen crew rescues nine after Mississippi cruise ship collision
The crew of the Creole Queen paddle-wheeler rescued nine passengers after a tanker collided with the American Heritage cruise ship on the Mississippi River Friday afternoon.
Captain Brian Clesi, who has worked with the Creole Queen for 32 years, and his crew motored a small rescue boat about a quarter-mile to the capsized vessel.
“We rescued about nine people. Only two of the people had life jackets on,” Clesi said.
Among those rescued was a Harbor Police officer who was hanging onto the stern of the capsized boat.
The crew also found a man who appeared to be suffering from a concussion and had blood on his face. He was brought to a fireboat for treatment.
Clesi reflected on the efforts of his team, saying, “Just 24 hours ago, these crew members were saving lives when a tanker crashed into the American Heritage cruise ship.”
Clesi and his crew are now being called heroes, with some referring to him as a “Mississippi Miracle Hero.”

title: Orono football stands tall on final play to win 8-man state title
text:
All season long, Orono football has battled through adversity and stood tall when it mattered most.
It was fitting, then, that their season would come down to a final play, with one stop needed for a state title.
Eli Schaff and Josh Wood were there to make that happen.
The pair of Red Riot defenders combined for a game-saving goal-line tackle as time expired to give Orono a 22-14 win over Orchard Beach, capturing the program’s second 8-Man Small state championship in four years.
“We have a saying around here,” said Orono head coach Bob Sinclair. “Offense wins games. Defense wins championships.”
Orono’s huge defensive stand sealed the win in a game the Red Riots trailed 14-0 at halftime.
“We’ve got such a good group of kids here,” said Sinclair. “To come from behind and then to make that stand in that situation, it’s incredible.”
Orono has knocked off 8-Man Small stalwarts for two weeks in a row. Last Friday, the game script was vastly different, as the Red Riots held on to win an offensive slugfest in the state semifinals at Stearns. This week’s game was a far cry from that, with both defenses largely refusing to budge.
Both Stearns and Old Orchard Beach defeated Orono earlier in the season. Both entered their playoff matchup against the Red Riots undefeated.
Orono never flinched.
“This team has overcome adversity this season and learned a lot of life lessons,” said Sinclair. “In the end, it all worked out.”
The Red Riots will return to town this evening for a parade to celebrate with town residents and the team’s family and friends.

title: Fire department mourns firefighter who died while hiking in park
text:
BOONE COUNTY, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) — The Independence Fire Department is mourning the loss of a firefighter who died while hiking in central Missouri.
The Boone County Sheriff’s Office said it responded to a 911 call at Pinnacles Park, just north of Columbia, at about 10:15 a.m. Tuesday. The caller reported that a person had fallen from a cliff.
Authorities respond to Pinnacles Park
Authorities found Sarah Longest at the scene after she fell about 50 feet from a cliff.
Longest, a HAZMAT technician with the Independence Fire Department, was nonresponsive and was declared dead at the scene, authorities said.
Longest was with an acquaintance at the time of her fall. Authorities said, “there is no reason at this time to believe the female’s fall and subsequent death was anything other than a tragic accident.”
Longest’s role with the department and union
Longest was a member of the Independence Fire Department’s Peer Support Team. She also served as a Good and Welfare Trustee for IAFF Local 781.
Longest had worked for the Independence Fire Department since March 10, 2025.
Department statement
In a statement, the Independence Fire Department said Longest’s commitment to serving others extended beyond responding to emergencies. The department said that through her involvement in the department and union, she demonstrated a dedication to supporting those who served alongside her.
“We extend our deepest condolences to Sarah’s family, friends, fellow firefighters and all who knew and loved her,” the department said. “Her service, compassion and commitment to others will not be forgotten.”
The department added: “Rest in peace, Firefighter Longest. We are grateful for your service to our community.”

title: Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country.
Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor’s office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.
He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited, among other issues, a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.
“If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem-solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.”
Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”
Three former governors, including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father, also endorsed him.
In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.
His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race.
He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy.
Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson’s campaign was not immediately returned.
Many Republicans saw ranking as their party’s best shot of retaining the governor’s seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October.
Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary.
Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state.
The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018.
Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent.

title: US air travel schedule should recover by the end of Sunday, FAA says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the U.S. on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop a day earlier that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world.
The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation’s longest ground stop in 25 years, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Saturday that a contractor had been replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload, leading to Friday’s ground stop that lasted more than four hours. The work caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, according to Trump administration officials.
Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause.
“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said.
The contractor, L3Harris Technologies Inc., did not immediately respond to requests for comment or issue a public statement Saturday.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday’s stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. But many were forced to camp out in airports.
Others got creative. Video in Seattle’s airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were recorded singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.
Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Kona, Hawaii, to Fresno, California, was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego on Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport for a rebooked flight on Saturday.
“There’s nothing you can do,” Russell said, as his wife, Mary, tried to nap on his shoulder.
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent at Dallas Love Field greeted passengers at dawn with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to help keep flights moving.
In Las Vegas, Korean Mexican influencer Sujin Kim, known online as Chingu Amiga, said her Friday flight to Mexico was rescheduled for Saturday morning. Kim said she had never experienced anything like it, though she travels often and “I always lose my suitcase.”
“Many people ended up sleeping at the airport, too, but thank God we managed to find a room,” she said.
At the Newark, N.J., airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when his flights would line up so he could return home to Japan.
“I’m not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home,” said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi’s game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 4,100 flights had been canceled Saturday. Cirium, a similar site, put that number above 3,200 flights.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Trump administration officials also blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding to replace the decades-old technology that helps manage the U.S. air traffic. Duffy said that 70% of the system had been replaced with fiber optic wire but that his agency also needs new air traffic control towers and runways.
The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
“We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace,” Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe. “You won’t get to your destination if we don’t think you can get there safely.”
In a moment that perhaps only further underscored the Transportation Department’s struggling systems, Duffy’s news conference Saturday morning began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps.
Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has largely been quiet on the topic. He has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media, although he commented on other things. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast. That disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line.
Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

title: Microsoft says services are now fully restored after global outage
text:
Microsoft says services are now fully restored after global outage
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company said in an update on X.
Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was "not related to cyber" or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident "was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced" following a recent network change.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
"With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day," said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow's School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, "This problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company's digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem."
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is "no indication" that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed "a recent network change." The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be "unexpectedly unavailable" during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn't send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court's reliance on technology.
The British government said it was "working closely" with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that "robust contingency plans" were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff's office in Colorado's Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
"Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions," a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.

title: It’s time to eradicate the MAHA movement
text:
On Nov. 10, the New York Times reported that measles was once again endemic in the USA — that is, the disease is consistently circulating in our community. In 2000, and for the 26 years since, measles was considered officially “eliminated” in the United States.
To officially have that status revoked, a branch of the World Health Organization must determine that the America “has had uninterrupted transmission of measles” for more than 12 months. At least eight Americans have died of measles this year, including four infants who were too young to receive the vaccine.
That’s the thing about the measles vaccine: infants and people with compromised immune systems can’t get it. They rely on everyone else around them being vaccinated to protect them. Infants can no longer rely on fellow Americans to do that for them. Thank God my son was able to get his first MMR vaccine last month. (I also got another MMR vaccine as a booster last December; no side effects to report and I don’t think it made me any more autistic than I already was.)
Also on Nov. 10, the official newsletter of the Make America Healthy Again Action Inc., a political nonprofit aligned with Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., published a 3,700-word defense of Russell Brand, who was recently convicted in a British court of rape and sexual assault. (By contrast, my weekly columns are between 750-950 words).
If you’ve never heard of Russell Brand, consider yourself lucky. He’s an alleged British comedian (I’ve never actually heard him be funny) who is mostly known for being briefly married to Katy Perry. In recent years, he was involved with the MAHA movement because he’s also an anti-vaccine conspiracist. Brand has made many appearances on the official MAHA podcast, including one where he video called in from a bath.
But Victoria, what does the spread of a deadly childhood illness have to do with an overseas rapist? I was waiting for you to ask. It proves that the Make America Healthy Again movement continues to promote garbage long after it has been proven dangerous. A movement that supports a convicted rapist while attacking vaccines is not a movement that cares about the health or well-being of “America” in general, or really, of anyone but themselves.
The entire concept of “MAHA” isn’t about making the country’s public health any better; MAHA treats health as something strictly personal that can be optimized with the right supplement regimen. It is a selfish movement; it fearmongers about ingredients in vaccines and ignores any responsibility a person might have for the health of others. It’s also a somewhat incoherent movement; adherents are obsessed with supplemental vitamins but encourage parents not to get the newborn vitamin K shot that can prevent catastrophic brain bleeds in children.
With the recent Democratic wave elections in the midterms, and the slow but inevitable curdling of the MAGA movement, the Make America Healthy Again people will probably be trying to reach out to Democrats and liberals to launder their beliefs to remain relevant and accomplish their various goals of making people sicker, selling peptides and providing paid speaking opportunities for various chiropractors.
Remember that even a stopped clock is right twice a day. Occasionally MAHA people support policies backed by actual science that could be helpful; reducing the use of pesticides, for example. I have no doubt they will use those moments of sanity to try to reach across the aisle and worm their way in with Democratic politicians.
A few months ago I wrote about how Rep. Chellie Pingree was proudly engaging with the MAHA movement. The problem is not the individual issues, nor even accepting members’ support and votes. The problem is promoting MAHA as something to be associated with. Its leaders should be driven out of polite society (especially because, given their vaccine stances, they’re probably vectors of disease).
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. should be impeached and removed from office. If a man wants to eat roadkill, fine. This is America and I do believe in personal freedom. I just don’t think he should be in charge of public health policy. I can’t imagine anything more unhealthy for America than a measles epidemic.
Make America Healthy Again is just as much a scam as Make America Great Again was. The only difference is MAGA was invented to sell hats and MAHA was invented to sell supplements.

title: Americans have taken their country back
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
James C. McGuire Jr. lives in Waldoboro and is the author of “The American Crossroads Series” and “A White House for Both Sides.”
The midterm elections should put an end to the comfortable explanation that America is simply divided between Democrats and Republicans.
I see something bigger: We the people pushing back against a Republican leadership that has confused loyalty to Donald Trump with service to the country.
Democrats won control of Congress. Here in Maine, voters chose Troy Jackson over Susan Collins. Those results do not tell us what every voter was thinking. But they give us reason to challenge the idea that this was merely another turn in the usual party rivalry.
My reading is that people want their government back.
They want to afford groceries, heat their homes, see a doctor and grow old without wondering whether everything they worked for will slip away. They want elected officials who answer questions instead of changing the subject. They want someone to remember who pays the bills.
A party label does not fill an oil tank. A campaign slogan does not pay the rent. And telling people how wonderful the economy is does little for someone standing at the checkout counter deciding what to put back.
Here in Maine, we know what it means to work through a long winter and still worry about the next bill. We should not have to compete with wealthy donors for our own government’s attention. A person who cannot afford a campaign contribution still deserves a full voice in the decisions that shape a life.
When Republican leaders defend the president regardless of his conduct, I believe they deserve to be judged for that choice. Holding office comes with an obligation to exercise independent judgment. If your answer to every controversy is to protect the man at the top, who is protecting the people underneath?
That is why I see this election as we the people against the Republicans who have put party loyalty ahead of public responsibility.
Republican voters belong to we the people, too. So do independents, Democrats and people who have stopped trusting either party. Nobody surrenders ownership of this country by registering with a different party. The invitation to demand better is open to everyone.
And Democrats had better understand what that means.
Winning an election is an assignment. It is not a certificate of good character or permission to become comfortable with the same powerful interests voters wanted challenged.
If Democrats turn this moment into a revenge tour, I believe they will waste it. Investigate wrongdoing. Follow the evidence. Apply the law fairly. Then get to work on the problems families face every day. Accountability must have a purpose beyond giving the other side a taste of its own medicine.
The test now is whether the new majority uses its power to make government answer to those people. Hold public hearings. Demand honest answers. Show us where the money goes. Give citizens something they can measure beyond another round of speeches and fundraising emails.
I want a government that can explain whom a decision helps, what it costs and why it serves the public. I want officials willing to challenge their own donors and their own leaders. Those are reasonable expectations in a country that calls itself a democracy.
The Republican leadership should hear a warning in these results. Democrats should hear an obligation.
Neither party owns the people who voted for it. Neither party owns America.
We the people do.
And anyone elected to serve us should remember that we can hire someone else.

title: What are your options, rights after Friday's FAA ground stop?
text:
What are your options, rights after Friday's FAA ground stop?
Flights are a mess right now because of this Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that was just lifted, but you've got somewhere to be, and now you're wondering: what are my rights and options at this point?
If your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to rebook a new flight, you are entitled to a refund. So if you urgently need to get somewhere, it may be worth it for you to take that money and use it toward something like a rental car or a train ticket.
Keep in mind, we might see spillover effects. Everyone is, kind of, thinking the same thing at the same time right now, right?
Now, beyond that, the thing to keep in mind is that this is an FAA issue. This is not within the airline's control. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said as much Friday night, saying that the issues were not caused by the airlines.
Because of that, there's not really much that they can do to help travelers. Now, that said, we are seeing some flexibility. As of Friday night, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines are all allowing passengers to rebook at no additional cost.
The big takeaway is that this is going to take some time to resolve. Travelers will need to be patient and flexible as they navigate this travel issues to come.

title: Clouds move in with an isolated shower
text:
Clouds move in with an isolated shower
Chilly weekend but warming up next week
Clouds move in with an isolated shower
Chilly weekend but warming up next week
A chilly and mostly cloudy Saturday as a low-pressure trough lingers over the region through early Monday. An upper-level disturbance moving south through the area will generate scattered to widespread snow showers in the mountains. Lower elevations across the state will see scattered rain showers and possibly some soft hail, known as graupel.
By Sunday, the weather system will begin to lose its grip on Maine. While skies will stay mostly cloudy and temperatures will remain cool, any lingering shower activity should pull back and stay confined to the higher terrain.
A ridge of high pressure will start nudging into the state at the start of the workweek, kicking off a gradual warming trend. Afternoon highs on Monday will mostly range from the upper 30s to the upper 40s, but temperatures will climb back above normal by midweek. Widespread highs in the upper 40s to upper 50s are expected, with a few spots in southern Maine potentially reaching the lower 60s.

title: Darth Vader’s lightsaber used in ‘I am your father’ duel sells for nearly $5 million
text:
(AP) - A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the “Star Wars” movies “The Empire Strikes Back” and ”Return of the Jedi" sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction.
The lightsaber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City where Vader tells Luke Skywalker “I am your father,” sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any “Star Wars” collectible, according to Heritage Auctions.
The sale also established a new auction record for a screen-used “Star Wars” prop, according to the auction organizer, shooting past their $3.75 million July auction sale of Skywalker’s light saber and severed hand-effects rig from “The Empire Strikes Back.”
Heritage’s Thursday auction also featured material from “Star Wars” Episodes I through IX and additional films and TV shows. In addition to Vader’s lightsaber, 27 other “Star Wars” lightsabers were assembled for public auction, according to Heritage Auctions.

title: Our responsibility to one another doesn’t end with an election
text:
Abdullahi Ahmed, Ed.D., of Portland is a naturalized citizen who came to the U.S. as a refugee from Somalia. He has worked for the Portland Public Schools since 2001.
An election is an important moment in the American collective life, an opportunity to participate in a shared process of decision-making. It allows citizens of diverse backgrounds and views to express their views and listen to different perspectives, to agree or disagree.
Now that the election has passed, citizens have another responsibility: to come together, even when we may have voted differently or hold different views about the outcome.
I recognize that calling upon others to take responsibility must begin with a willingness to accept that responsibility ourselves. I’m starting with this op-ed, not because writing alone will solve the challenges facing our communities, but because I believe we must each find ways to contribute to the conversations and actions that bring people together.
By writing these words, I hope to model the responsibility I’m asking others to embrace: to speak constructively, encourage reflection, promote understanding and remind ourselves of our shared obligations to one another. This is my contribution to a broader conversation and an invitation for each of us to consider what we can do within our own sphere of influence.
Participation in the electoral process requires us to respect the process itself, including the peaceful transition from one chapter to the next. It does not require us to think alike, set aside our convictions or pretend that every concern has been resolved. Rather, it calls on us to remain engaged while treating one another with respect.
In the days and weeks ahead, some conversations may be difficult. Strong feelings are natural, and people may need time to reflect. Make room for those feelings without allowing disagreement to turn into contempt. Ask questions with curiosity, listen without preparing a rebuttal, and speak with care about people whose experiences differ from your own. Respectful discussion does not mean avoiding difficult topics. It means approaching them in ways that preserve the possibility of understanding and cooperation.
Regardless of the outcome, we should work toward a better tomorrow. Our shared lives do not stop at the ballot box. We are neighbors, colleagues, family members, students, educators and community partners. We rely on one another every day in our classrooms, workplaces, local organizations and public spaces. The bonds we build through these everyday connections can help us move forward, even when wider national conversations feel divided.
I recognize that, at times, we may feel that the challenges facing our communities are too big and that the solutions are beyond our control. We may look at the issues around us and wonder what difference one person, one family or one community can make.
Yet, I believe we have more influence than we sometimes realize. We may not be able to change everything, but we can make a difference within our own sphere of influence. We can make our neighborhoods more welcoming, our schools more inclusive, our workplaces more respectful and our communities more supportive.
We can reach out, build relationships, support one another and take responsibility for the spaces we share. Meaningful change does not always begin with those in the highest positions of authority. Often, it begins with ordinary people making deliberate efforts to improve the lives of those around them.
Maine brings together people from different backgrounds, with different ideas, experiences and hopes for the future. When we model respectful disagreement and kindness, we help future generations understand that civic life is not simply about winning an argument or having things go our way. It is also about listening, learning, contributing and finding ways to address the problems we share. These habits matter in every generation.
I call upon my fellow citizens of our city and state to choose unity, create positivity and remain committed to one another. Let us choose words that build rather than diminish. Let us reach out to someone with whom we disagree, not to pressure them to change their mind, but to understand what matters to them.
Let us recognize the good work already happening around us and find practical ways to contribute. A thoughtful conversation, a helping hand, a welcoming gesture or a genuine effort to support a neighbor may seem small, but each has the potential to strengthen the trust our communities need.
We may not have control over every decision or every circumstance, but we all have a role to play in shaping the communities in which we live. Our responsibility to one another does not end with an election. In many ways, it begins again.

title: This gear will help make your time on the trail smooth
text:
George Washington Sears, using the pseudonym “Nessmuk,” wrote in his classic 1891 guide to camping and wilderness life: “We do not go to the green woods and crystal waters to rough it, we go to smooth it. We get it rough enough at home, in towns and cities.” Old Nessmuk was right then and now. So it is that we hikers should carry a few items that make our trail lives easier and more enjoyable. Here are a few little things I recommend.
Proper hydration is essential to good performance on the trail. For years I’ve used a hydration bladder with a drinking tube to stay well-watered on the go. A persistent problem has been that most every time I drop my backpack trailside, the bite valve ends up in the dirt. Yuck! Finally, I found a cover (Platypus, $13) to help protect against muck and debris. It’s a minor extra step each time to drink, but the cleanliness is worth it.
Traveling by airplane with trekking poles in your carry-on? You’re taking a chance because you never know these days whether or not the Transportation Safety Administration agent will confiscate them. My regular trekking poles are expensive carbon-fiber models that I don’t want to risk losing. I looked online and found inexpensive poles (on Amazon, about $17 each) that are sturdy and collapse into three connected sections. So far, so good.
Foam sleeping pads just don’t work well for me and my back, so I’ve become a big fan of air mattresses for a good night’s rest on the trail. The thing is, though, you’ve got to inflate them using lung power at the end of a long, hard day, never my favorite thing to do. Enter the mini pump made by Flextail ($57), a compact unit that weighs just a couple ounces, has a rechargeable lithium battery, and inflates my mattress in under a minute. Voila!
Most times, I like to simply listen to the sounds of nature around me, but sometimes a little company is a welcome thing. I’m very protective of my smart phone battery life, given that it’s my primary navigation tool, so I don’t listen to podcasts or watch videos. Instead, I use a cheap mini FM radio (on Amazon, $16) that’s palm-sized, weighs but a couple ounces and gets me my music, news and sports when I’m in the mood for it.
For too long, I struggled to find a convenient place to carry my smart phone. Pants pocket, belt pack, waistbelt pouch — none were ideal. Finally, I discovered the shoulder strap pocket (there are multiple makers, but mine is by Gossamer Gear, $22) that attaches to my pack strap and makes easy work of grabbing my phone when I need it, which is a lot of the time. The mesh pocket on front is great for lip balm, sunscreen and a snack bar to boot.
Two years ago on the Continental Divide Trail, I found a nice trail umbrella on a long road walk. I tried to find the owner but never could, so now it’s part of my gear inventory. Hikers I know swear by umbrellas for rain and sun protection, but I didn’t use mine because I could never figure out a good method for securing it to my pack strap. The Zpacks Umbrella Holster ($6), with its clip and an adjustable shock cord loop, was an easy game changer.
Photos and videos of your hike are all-important for your own satisfaction and for sharing on social media. That’s why I’ve always carried a small tripod of one sort or another for use as a selfie stick and to capture images with me in them, but they all weigh a little more than I’d like. Recently, I found a super lightweight (two ounces) handle grip tripod that, although it doesn’t extend, is a good compromise for my needs. Ten bucks on Amazon.
Honorable mentions: the IKEA Frakta Storage Bag (2 for $10) is a great duffel for protecting your backpack from aggressive baggage handlers when you travel. Want extra water carrying capacity without taking up a lot of pack space when empty? Get the collapsible, lightweight (two ounces) Nalgene Wide Mouth Cantene ($20).
If you’ve got some cool hiking gear suggestions for me, please do send them along. Thanks!
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Airlines won’t be required to offer passengers additional compensation after ground stop
text:
(AP) - The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could resume Friday after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.
The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that outages of the U.S. air traffic control system were caused by an overload of an old, analog system. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin called for further funding to improve the system.
An FAA computer problem is considered outside the control of the airlines — much like the weather.
So the only thing the airlines are obligated to do is to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers that want to continue to their destinations or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting planes back in the air may take time and that getting air traffic back to normal would be slow.

title: 'The Points Guy' offers advice to those affected by FAA ground stop
text:
'Everybody for themselves': The Points Guy offers advice to those affected by FAA ground stop
Brian Kelly, founder of ThePointsGuy.com, has offered his tips and advice to travelers for nearly two decades. His expertise has helped people save time and money while handling stressful travel moments with ease.
One such situation came up Friday afternoon with the Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop affecting airports nationwide. Thousands of flights and potentially more than a million travelers were affected from coast to coast.
Many were stranded in airports, and some travelers decided against traveling altogether with so much uncertainty in the air.
So many decisions need to be made in a short amount of time and Kelly offered his advice on how to handle this unprecedented event. He has empathy for those who are in a tough position — physically, mentally and financially.
"My thoughts and prayers are with you," Kelly said in an interview Friday with Hearst Television Washington Correspondent Rachel Hirschheimer. "Let this be a reminder that we all need to be proactive. For anyone who doesn't have to travel, call it quits. Take your refund. Airlines do owe you a refund if you decide to cancel. Do not let them give you a voucher. By law, they have to give you a refund if you choose not to take the flight they try to re-accommodate you on."
Kelly said the only thing an airline owes a stranded passenger is a refund if you choose not to get re-accommodated. Other unexpected inconveniences are not their obligation. Purchasing travel insurance in advance is one way to avoid a future headache, he said.
Video below: Airports work to catch up after hourslong ground stop
"Unfortunately, because this is out of their control, they don't owe you any food vouchers or hotel," Kelly said. "Simply put, a situation like this is 'The Hunger Games.' You need to look out for yourself. For those who purchase travel insurance, travel insurance should cover all costs related to this. Travel credit cards may cover some of this; otherwise, it's everybody for themselves. I recommend people act quickly because hotels will get snatched up. I know people are driving instead of flying. You've got to be on the offense here."
Dubbed "The Man Who Turned Credit-Card Points Into an Empire" by The New York Times, Kelly said some credit cards may make a difficult situation like this a little easier, but there are no guarantees.
"If you booked your flight using a credit card that has trip-delay cancellation coverage, generally, an airline cancellation policy would kick in benefits of maybe up to $500 per person to get a hotel or rental car. However, there are exclusions; some credit cards will exclude FAA mass shutdowns," he said. "My best tip is to keep all your receipts. Submit them to your credit card company. Let them decide. Don't try to read the policy and see if you're eligible. Submit it all. Let them decide and hope for the best."
Kelly said to regularly check FAA.gov for updates and download the phone application of the airline. By checking the website and looking up future flights, there is a better chance of finding a potential new flight that could work for a traveler's schedule, as people will be canceling their own flights and seats may open up.
For in-person communication, kindness is key. Focus on making this easier for those who are also in a tough position — especially the workers who are not at fault. Airport workers are generally working hard to create a comfortable atmosphere for those who are in an uncomfortable position. Residual effects from the airport slowdowns will be felt in other sectors of the travel industry — from hotels to concert venues, sports contests and other special events. Many times, tickets and hotel bookings are non-refundable, even in dire situations.
"If you're canceled flight means youre going to miss out on a non-refundable hotel, your best bet is to ask nicely for the hotel to cancel. Some hotels may take pity on you, but understand, it is not their (responsibility)," Kelly said. "They do not owe you a refund. When you're asking for a favor, you should not yell at people. This is where people make mistakes all the time. Your unfortunate flight cancelation is not the problem of a small hotel owner where you are trying to go. This is where you want to be very nice. 'Hey, can I come back again? Can you cancel?' Do not demand it. Frankly, they do not owe it to you."
Travel insurance may make an already expensive vacation cost even more, but Kelly said it will likely be worth it in the end. From his personal experience, it is crucial to get the insurance.
"This is where travel insurance is critical," Kelly said. "I buy a yearly travel insurance policy, even as a travel expert. With these mass travel cancellations happening quite frequently, having travel insurance is key, especially for big-ticket trips like cruises and international trips."
Even as the FAA lifted the ground stop in the 8 p.m. hour Friday night, it will still take a while to get everything back on track. Kelly said it will take weeks for schedules to be back to normal.
"You've got to buckle up," he said. "There's going to be delays. You need to go into this with an attitude of patience. It's going to be a while before airlines are back up and running — easily into next week. You may not be getting out tomorrow, I hate to tell people."
Those who were canceled throughout the afternoon and evening on Friday will not get priority over those who already had travel plans for Saturday.
"If you were on a flight canceled on a Friday, passengers who had booked on Saturday will go out before you," Kelly said. "Airlines don't do it in order of who was supposed to go out first. It's whoever was supposed to be on the flight that's going out. If your flight was rescheduled, it doesn't necessarily mean you're the next passenger to go out. People whose flights were supposed to go out (Friday night), you may not go out until Monday."
As frustrating an experience as this all may be, Kelly again reminds travelers to move forward with peace in their minds and kindness in their hearts.
Of course, that's easier said than done.
Just remember: "It is pointless to yell at airport employees," Kelly said.

title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop for second time since 9/11. What to know
text:
(Gray News) - The recent nationwide ground stop was only the second in the U.S. since the Sept. 11 attacks
The last one happened in 2023, when an outage disrupted the Federal Aviation Administration system that sends safety messages to pilots.
Friday’s ground stop followed “communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that a national security threat caused the outage, though he did not rule out any possible cause, including a cyberattack, CNN reported.
“There is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States,” Mullin told reporters at the White House.
He later repeated that there was “no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us.”
Mullin said all flights were accounted for and that aircraft already in the air were being handled on a “case by case” basis.
Officials have not provided a timeline for resolving the ground stop, as flight cancellations continue to climb.
