title: Ernestine M. Stoddard
text:
Ernestine Marie Stoddard, 81, passed away on Nov. 1, 2026, in Trinity, Florida, after a long-fought battle with Alzheimer's disease.
Born in Augusta, Maine, on March 28, 1945, she was the daughter of Woodrow and Laura Gagnon. On April 6, 1963, she married the love of her life, Ronald Stoddard, beginning a partnership that spanned 63 years.
Ernestine and Ronald lived in Augusta, where they worked side by side running businesses together for over 50 years. She was best known for operating J&M Camper Sales alongside Ronald and their son, Jeff. Later, Ernestine and Ronald moved to Boothbay Harbor, where they operated McSeagull's Restaurant with Jeff before retiring and relocating to Florida full-time.
Ernestine will be remembered for her quiet strength, tireless work ethic, and unwavering devotion to her family. When she wasn't working, she loved being near the ocean and spent her free time boating and traveling.
She is survived by her beloved husband, Ronald; her two sons, Jeff and Michael and his wife, Melissa; her granddaughters, Jessica Douin and her husband, Adam, and Mykel Stoddard; her grandson, Logan Stoddard and his fiancée, Sofie; and her great-granddaughter, Hailey Douin. She is also survived by her sister, Marie Joy of Augusta. She was predeceased by her parents, two brothers, and four sisters.
A private cremation has taken place to honor Ernestine, and per her wishes, no formal service will be held. In lieu of flowers, donations in honor of the excellent care provided to Ernestine may be sent to Gulfside Hospice (2061 Collier Pkwy.Land O' Lakes, FL 34639).

title: 20-year-old patient leaves hospital after 184 days on life support
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (WEAR) — A Florida woman is leaving the hospital after spending half a year on an advanced life-support system.
Akira Griffin, 20, is moving from Baptist Hospital in Pensacola to inpatient rehab.
Griffin suffered an illness that caused lung failure.
About 100 doctors, nurses, therapists and support staff cared for her during her hospitalization. Many of her caregivers lined the halls Wednesday to show support as she begins the next phase of her recovery.
A cardiologist said that, at one point, it seemed Griffin would never recover enough lung tissue and function to come off a ventilator, but she has.
Her mother said she hopes to bring her home by Christmas.
The average length of treatment with the advanced life-support system is about 11 days.

title: Deputy working security at South Carolina gun show fatally shoots customer who shot him
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — A deputy working security at a gun show in South Carolina fatally shot someone who fired on him Saturday, authorities said.
The Lexington County deputy was taken into surgery and was in stable condition, the sheriff’s office said in a statement.
The sheriff’s office did not release any additional information about the shooting at the Jamil Temple, where the South Carolina Arms Collector Association was holding the gun and knife show. The group did not immediately respond to an email and phone call seeking comment.
According to the rules for the gun show, posted on its website, loaded weapons are banned except for on-duty police officers, and all weapons must have their actions secured.
The Jamil Temple is owned by the Shriners and is frequently rented out for gun shows, jewelry expos, roller derbies and other events.

title: The Electoral College was not about democracy
text:
A recent letter (“States like Maine need the Electoral College,” Nov. 10) overlooks important historical context.
The Electoral College wasn’t designed as a model of democracy. It was created in 1787 through compromises that boosted the political power of slaveholding states, using the Three-Fifths Compromise to count enslaved people who couldn’t even vote.
The argument that California and Texas would dominate elections is not valid because states don’t vote, people do. A Republican in California or a Democrat in Texas should have the exact same voice as a voter here in Maine.
We have a chance right now to fix this problem by having states approve the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It would not require a constitutional amendment. Maine joined in 2024. Participating states currently hold 222 electoral votes — just 48 short of the 270 needed to activate it.
The Electoral College is a system built on 18th-century compromises. Maine voters deserve a voice, but so does every American. Every vote should count equally, regardless of state lines.
Donald Cailler
Gardiner

title: Restaurateur plans to convert Rockland office building to apartments
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND — The owner of the High Tide restaurant in Rockland has submitted plans to convert the Heritage Office Building into apartments.
Thomas Shanos, through Penobscot Rentals, LLC, submitted the application Nov. 12 with the Rockland code enforcement office for the Heritage project at 30 School St.
Shanos purchased at an auction in October 2020 the restaurant at 275 Main St. that he opened in 2023 as High Tide.
Penobscot Rentals purchased the Heritage building in December 2025 for $800,000.
The proposal calls for creating 14 one-bedroom apartments that will be between 400 and 570 square feet. The name of the development will be School Street Apartments.
The project is scheduled to be completed by October 2029, according to the application.
Shanos said the current commercial tenants in the building have leases and he has given them enough time to find other commercial spaces before the project is underway. He pointed out that there are a lot of vacant commercial spaces in downtown Rockland.
He said the residential project will be done well and be a nice addition to downtown Rockland.
The project has no dedicated parking spaces but the application states that the developer wants to lease spaces from the city.
The Heritage Building was constructed in 1981. Linda Bean owned the building for many years. The Rockland area school district leased space in the building for administrative offices in the late 1980s and into the early 1990s.
The Rockland Planning Board will review the proposal at its Tuesday, Nov. 17 meeting that will start at 5:15 p.m.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Marshwood football outlasts Kennebunk in overtime to win B South title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH BERWICK — Once again, Parker Ferrer had potentially saved the championship hopes of the Marshwood football team. Greg Castoras made sure his teammate’s effort was rewarded.
Castoras scored the winning touchdown in overtime after Ferrer’s interception on the previous possession, and top-seeded Marshwood took down No. 2 Kennebunk 14-8 in the Class B South final on Saturday.
Castoras’ plunge from 3 yards out sent the Hawks (9-1) to the state final for the first time since 2021, when Marshwood won its sixth Class B title in seven seasons.
“(There are) a lot of emotions; it felt great, just the thought of how much work we put into this season,” said Castoras, who ran 29 times for 152 yards and a pair of touchdowns. “It just all really came together in those final moments.”
Marshwood will face North champion Cony next Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland.
The big news surrounding Marshwood before this season was the departure of Alex Rotsko, who had coached at the South Berwick school since 2012 and led the Hawks on their dominant run. In his first season leading the program, Andrew Elwell brough it back to its familiar heights.
“I’m obviously overwhelmed,” he said. “It’s everything. I don’t say this lightly; in June, we had 21 guys signed up for football. This senior class saved Marshwood football.”
And they saved the day on Saturday. Marshwood took an 8-0 lead on its first possession, but Kennebunk (7-3) stiffened from there and pulled even in the third quarter on Ethan White’s 18-yard run.
The score remained 8-8 through four quarters, and the teams headed to overtime to decide the regional championship.
On Kennebunk’s first possession, Sam Therrien — one of those seniors — brought pressure up the middle and got a hand on Giovanni D’Elia’s throw, forcing the pass intended for Charlie Pentland to fall short. Ferrer, another senior, was ready on the goal line to make the grab.
“I knew my boys were going to hype me up after that, so I had to make a play,” said Ferrer, who also had a key red-zone interception in the fourth quarter. “(But) I had to let my boys know the job’s not finished. We’ve got to get the score. We’ve got to win the game.”
Castoras, another senior, took it from there. On third-and-goal from the 3, he received a handoff, saw an opening to the right and slipped through Kennebunk tacklers for the winning score.
“I saw the hole,” said Castoras, whose collar and turtleneck were bloodied from a first-half cut to his chin. “And I knew, as soon as I see it, I’ve just got to hit it. I’ve just got to go. And nobody’s bringing me down from there.”
Early on, it looked like Castoras and the Marshwood rushing attack would be too much for the Rams. Marshwood had the ball for 16 of the first 17 and a half minutes and took the lead when Castoras scored on a 2-yard run and Jon Buttrick ran in for the 2-point conversion with 5:51 left in the first quarter.
Kennebunk, however, held Castoras and Noah Goodwin to 66 yards in the second half after allowing 120 in the first.
“The kids were resilient,” Rams coach Keith Noel said. “We did a couple of adjustments, but it came down to making our correct reads and doing what they’re taught to do. They’re a fast team. You’ve got to adjust to the speed of the game.”
The Rams pulled even with 5:04 to go in the third when White (13 carries, 73 yards) started up the gut before bouncing left and running 18 yards for a score, then D’Elia found Peter Landenberger for the conversion.
Kennebunk was zeroing in on the lead, with the ball at the Marshwood 8 before a sack by Malachi Garrett. Ferrer, who had had an interception erased by a pass interference call four plays earlier, picked off a pass intended for Bradley Farrell to end the threat with 7:29 to play.
“We had chances,” Noel said. “That’s a rough one. … We were on the short end of the straw this time.”

title: TSA agents find live snakes in traveler’s suitcase, pausing security screenings at airport
text:
ONTARIO, Calif. (CNN) — Airport security screening was paused at Ontario International Airport in Southern California after Transportation Security Administration agents found two live snakes inside a traveler’s suitcase last month.
What agents found
TSA agents saw what appeared to be ropes on an X-ray scan of the suitcase. The items were two live snakes confined in a pillowcase.
The traveler told agents he had flown with the snakes before.
Screenings halted
Screenings stopped while officials determined the snakes were not venomous.
The traveler was able to give the snakes, which he called his pets, to a relative who was not traveling.
Agents say travelers should check with their airline to confirm whether they can travel with pets.

title: Flight disruptions continue a day after nationwide ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Flight disruptions continued Saturday, one day after the nation’s longest ground stop in 25 years, as officials work to explain what led to the pause in flying.
A nationwide ground stop began Friday just before 4 p.m. E.T., and lasted more than four hours, halting flights across the U.S. Officials said the cause was an equipment outage.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on an effort to update old technology. He said new equipment overloaded old routers, causing communications and radar gaps.
“At least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber,” Duffy said. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router.”
Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford addressed travelers affected by the ground stop.
“I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons,” he said.
The ground stop left hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded and disrupted travel plans for 1.5 million fliers. It also caused thousands of flight delays and cancellations.
Questions arose over whether the outage was a cyber attack. The FAA said it does not believe that was the case.
Former Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood commented on the effect on air travel.
“It’s a national calamity, there’s no question about it,” LaHood said. “This is something that no one wishes would ever happen, but when you have old equipment, this is what happens.”
LaHood, a former Republican Congressman from Illinois, served as Transportation Secretary in the Obama administration from 2009-2013.
Duffy has asked Congress to approve more funding to replace old systems. He used Friday’s ground stop to renew that request.
Air traffic control operations are slowly resuming. The FAA expects about 5,000 flight cancellations Saturday as airlines adjust their schedules. Most operations are expected to be back on track by Sunday night.

title: 37-year-old elected governor in Alaska
text:
Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm election wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country.
Video above: Alaska voters react to national and state election results in US
Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.
He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited, among other issues a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.
Video below: Republicans, Democrats select next leaders for new Congress
“If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem-solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.”
Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”
Three former governors — Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father — also endorsed him.
In a statement, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.
He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy.
The Associated Press called the race for Kreiss-Tomkins on Friday.
Video below: Marjorie Taylor Greene slams GOP after House blocks vote on Hegseth impeachment
Many Republicans saw ranking as the party’s best shot of retaining the governor's seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October.
Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary.
Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state.
The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018.
Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent.

title: LCCT announces auditions for 'The Spitfire Grill'
text:
The Lincoln County Community Theater (LCCT), the resident theater company of Damariscotta’s Lincoln Theater, announces auditions for its upcoming production of The Spitfire Grill, a heartwarming musical that lifts up the beauty in second chances and the transformative nature of friendship.

title: Whitefield Library Finishes Building Renovations
text:
Almost five years since reopening its doors to the public, the Whitefield Library has finished its major renovations. Now, the goal is to keep it running as a year-round facility.
In late October, the final renovations to the exterior library, located at 1 Arlington Lane in Whitefield, were completed. The western clapboards were scraped and sanded or replaced. Deteriorating window trim was replaced and rejuvenated with green paint.
According to Whitefield Library Board of Directors President Cheryle Joslyn, completing the exterior work was only one of many steps of renovation the library has taken since acquiring the almost 140-year-old building in 2019.
“We think that pretty much takes care of the renovation of the building,” Joslyn said.
Other than books, the Whitefield Library hosts numerous community events, such as reading groups and educational programs. It serves the communities of Whitefield, Somerville, Jefferson, Alna, Pittson, and Windsor for free. Joslyn said renovations allow for more space and opportunities, and that the library has changed tremendously since it opened full time in 2022.
There is not an exact date on when the building was constructed, but Joslyn said the estimate is around 1884, making it 137 years old. According to a Sun Journal article from that year, the building was intended to be used as a school, library, and gathering center. In 1889, other records show the building was used for women’s sewing groups and community dinners.
Starting in 1917 and for the next 102 years, the building was owned and operated by Whitefield Arlington Grange Post No. 528.
Flash-forward 100 years, in 2016, a 9-year-old attending Whitefield Elementary School wrote a letter to the Whitefield Select Board about how there wasn’t a library open in the summer. In his letter, Quinn Conroy said there were not many activities for children to do over the summer and that even when not in the class, they like to read.
“I think that we should have a public library in Whitefield because on summer vacation there is nothing to do other than take a two hour trip to the beach and kids like to read in the summer and grown-ups like reading to,” Conroy said in the letter.
Conroy also pushed for the space to have computers.
In response to the letter, Whitefield Select Board member Sue McKeen approached the school to see if the school library could be run by volunteers during the summer, but Joslyn said plans never materialized.
In 2017, the Arlington Grange allowed volunteers to create a summer library on the first floor of the building. The first election of officers for a building acquisition committee came around early the following year, with McKeen sworn in as president and Joslyn as vice president.
For two summers before moving into the building, Joslyn said a “summer library” was hosted on the main floor with a table full of donated books.
In July 2018, the Whitefield Library Association was granted a nonprofit 501(c)(3) designation. Throughout the year, the committee worked and created design concepts for the Grange building, later dissolving once the work was finished the nonprofit designation was given.
In September 2018, the Whitefield Library Association submitted an $8,000 bid to Maine State Grange for the purchase of the property. The first bid was denied, and a second one was later submitted for $25,000.
On Jan. 3, 2019, the Maine State Grange accepted the bid, which led to the committee tasked with the acquisition to begin fundraising efforts.
“We didn’t know how we were going to raise $25,000 to buy this building,” Joslyn said.
It was in March 2019 when Kennebec Saving Bank donated the total amount needed for the purchase to the library after getting wind of the committee’s efforts through a Kennebec Journal article by George Smith titled “There’s Nothing Like a Library.”
“We got a call from Kennebec Savings Bank and they said ‘We’d like to come out and meet with you,’” Joslyn said. “We thought they were coming out to make us a proposal for borrowing the money from their bank. They came out with a check for $25,000.”
Now with the building and no money left in their account, the committee started brainstorming ways to raise money to start renovations, Joslyn said. Throughout the rest of 2019, the library hosted fundraising efforts such as a dodgeball tournament, art nights, and other events. As work started to roll, the library continued to be operated in the summer, but the building was not ready for year-round use yet.
The first renovation done in the building once it was in the hands of the library association was the removal of a faulty furnace. For the next two years, the building went through a transformation.
In March 2020, as the library paused operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, the committee kept on working, installing new heaters and adding additional support beams, among other tasks.
Joslyn referred to herself and the group of volunteers who did most of the work as “the geezers,” because they were all retired. She said the group was very fortunate to find so many craftsmen around the area to help.
Most of the money for renovations was raised through grants, according to Joslyn, including the Stephen and Tabitha King Grant Award. The David Family Foundation Award, and a Bangor Saving Grant Award.
“We renovated no more than what we had the money granted to us and it wasn’t all grants,” Joslyn said. “We had some very, very good donors from our community who stepped up with some big checks to help.”
In January 2022, the newly renovated Whitefield Library opened to the public. Only the first floor was complete at this point, with a new main room, office, hallway, storage closet, bathroom, and kitchenette.
At Whitefield’s annual town meeting in March 2023, $15,000 was approved to help fund the salaries of the library administrator and the children’s program coordinator, as well as an additional $10,000 for parking lot repairs.
In May 2023, the association received the building permit to begin second floor renovations. Joslyn said the library faced the problem of figuring out how to fund the project until a community member donated $200,000 while advocating for a larger children’s space.
According to Joslyn, many people stopped by when the association was working on the major renovations before opening. One of those people, Niki Janus, offered to fund the remaining renovations.
For the next three years, renovations continued. The second floor received the required permitting to host people in February 2025 and an appreciation celebration was held in September of that year.
With years of hard work, renovations, and hoops to jump through, the Whitefield Library is now a community center used for everything from checking out books, after-school programs, author visits, music groups, and more.
Even with the bigger projects done, Joslyn said the goal is to now prioritize preventative maintenance. She said she also would like to find a way to either install a chair lift or other accessibility tool to help get everyone upstairs.
“We’re thrilled to have such wonderful facilities,” Joslyn said.
For more information about the Whitefield Library, call 549-0170 or go to whitefieldlibrary.org.

title: Wild video shows the moment a tanker struck a docked cruise ship in New Orleans
text:
Watch the moment a tanker struck a cruise ship in New Orleans, prompting rescues

title: Thousands of flights canceled as airlines work to dig out from nationwide ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — More than 2,000 flights were canceled Saturday as airlines across the U.S. worked to dig out from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, which stranded passengers and forced professional and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.
Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours.
A limited number of domestic flights departed after the stop was lifted around 8:15 p.m. ET. But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were traveling to surprise her daughter’s best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she’s planned this whole weekend,” Brown said. “Now we’re not sure when we’re gonna be able to go.”
Ruth Coles was stuck on her plane for more than five hours after landing at Los Angeles International Airport from Newark, New Jersey. She said the passengers were told they were waiting for a gate to open.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said.
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports across the U.S., passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations. Some passed the time by breaking out in song.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses.
Auburn University’s football team opted to take a bus to Mississippi State and the Saturday start time was pushed from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. Other universities affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and No. 19 Ole Miss, which did not plan to fly until Saturday morning for its game against Oklahoma.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy encouraged NCAA football teams to reach out to the FAA so the agency can prioritize flights for Saturday games.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Corbyn Wascher’s flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. Everyone was cordial on the American Airlines plane as they talked and stretched their legs and the flight attendants handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, he said.
“The stewardesses were amazing. You could tell that they were pretty stressed out,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher, who took a $100 uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find new flights. He was scheduled for a Saturday afternoon flight to Chicago O’Hare International Airport.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed Friday.
Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to Friday’s failure.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
Friday’s ground stop also was different from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska, and Golden from Seattle. Associated Press journalists Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed to this report.

title: 17-year-old surfer saves person who jumped from Golden Gate Bridge
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) - It was a dramatic rescue in the shadow of the Golden Gate Bridge.
A group of surfers helped save a person who jumped from the bridge Tuesday afternoon, reaching him before a U.S. Coast Guard boat arrived.
Voices coming from the top of the Golden Gate Bridge alerted a group of surfers that something was wrong.
“I yelled to my dad, like, call someone. Everyone was yelling to the beach to call someone. And then he ended up just jumping off,” 17-year-old Colby Ralls said. “There were guys up there, like, telling him not to, and he just jumped off. And just right as we saw that happen, me and a couple of other guys that were out there just started paddling to go get him.”
Ralls of San Rafael was in the water with two other surfers and knew they had just seconds to get to him.
“He was yelling, ‘Help,’ as we were paddling towards him. You know, he’s still alive,” Ralls said.
The three strangers grabbed the man they believe was in his 20s.
“We’re all kind of just helping, like stabilizing the board and just keeping him afloat because he couldn’t really swim. And, you know, the guys were talking to him like, ‘hey, it’s OK. It’s OK. We’re getting help,’” Ralls said.
Within minutes, a Coast Guard rescue boat made it to them.
“They’re going fast. You know, they’re like, ‘We need to go. We need to go. We need to,’ because it was just such a miracle that he even survived that drop. You know, it’s kind of crazy,” Ralls said.
U.S. Coast Guard Lieutenant John Thompson was part of the watch team Tuesday afternoon.
“Hitting that water at that speed, and you can experience shock very quickly. So those surfers being there, to be able to pull the person onto a surfboard, provided those vital seconds in order to be able to save the person,” Thompson said.
Ralls and the two other surfers went back to shore, still processing what happened.
“I think people … there should be easier ways to get help for people like that, you know. I just, I just really hope he’s OK,” Ralls said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the man was in stable condition when he was transferred to an ambulance.

title: Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country.
Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor’s office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.
He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited, among other issues, a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.
“If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem-solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.”
Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”
Three former governors, including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father, also endorsed him.
In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.
His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race.
He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy.
Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson’s campaign was not immediately returned.
Many Republicans saw ranking as their party’s best shot of retaining the governor’s seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October.
Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary.
Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state.
The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018.
Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent.

title: Port of New Orleans sues tanker owners following ship collision on Mississippi River
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - The Port of New Orleans has filed a $1 million federal lawsuit against the owners of the tanker vessel that struck and sank a New Orleans riverboat on Friday.
The lawsuit was filed Friday evening in the Eastern District of Louisiana and names the Atlantic Asphalt MV, Nave Shipping SA, and Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd. as defendants.
It alleges the maritime mishap caused at least $1 million in damage to the Thalia Street Terminal where the paddlewheel cruise ship American Heritage was docked.
An arrest warrant was also issued, directing federal marshals to seize and hold the marine vessel Atlantic Asphalt, a 525-foot ship that on Friday afternoon appeared to lose control as it passed beneath the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to court documents.
The tanker veered to the right, striking the docked river cruise ship American Heritage, causing it to capsize and partially sink.
The riverboat had 192 passengers aboard, but authorities said all were rescued safely, with 32 requiring hospital treatment.
“As a result of the Atlantic Asphalt’s allision with the American Heritage and the incident, the Board’s Thalia Street Terminal was significantly damaged,” the lawsuit noted. “The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed $1 million with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated.”
The lawsuit identifies Nave Shipping SA as a corporation registered in the country of Liberia.
“According to publicly available information, Nave Shipping is the registered owner and ship manager and commercial manager of the Atlantic Asphalt,” the suit said.
Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd. is identified in the suit as a private limited company based in Singapore.
According to the lawsuit, Thome is the Atlantic Asphalt’s ISM manager, “responsible for the effective implementation of the ‘International Safety Management’ code aboard the tanker.
The lawsuit said the Port of New Orleans board has “incurred and will continue to incur additional damages and expenses including ... cleanup, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs, resulting in a maritime lien against the Atlantic Asphalt.”
The claim cites “negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness of the Atlantic Asphalt” as the cause of the allision, a term referring to a moving vessel striking one that is securely moored.
“As a result, ... the Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping, Thome (and potentially other parties not yet identified with responsibility for the operation, condition, crewing and seaworthiness of the Atlantic Asphalt) are solidarily liable for all damages sustained by The Board,” the lawsuit said.
Plaintiffs in the lawsuit listed are the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, represented by attorneys Christopher Hannan, Sara Kuebel, and Abigail Weiland of the high-powered New Orleans law firm Jones Walker.
Court records show the initial case assignment allotted to federal magistrate Karen Wells Roby and to U.S. District Judge Wendy Vitter, chief judge at the federal courthouse in New Orleans.

title: Westbrook gym hosts weightlifting competition to benefit Make-A-Wish Maine
text:
Westbrook gym hosts weightlifting competition to benefit Make-A-Wish Maine
Saturday was the 9th annual Operation Change deadlifting competition hosted by Iron Legion to benefit Make-A-Wish Maine.
For months, members at Iron Legion in Westbrook and Scarborough had been training to lift as much as they could Saturday morning, all while raising funds for kids in Maine to get their wishes.
"So that is the heart of it. That is like the most important part," said lifter Rebecca Laaser. "If I get up there and don't lift my weights, but I still raise money for Make-A-Wish, like I'm so proud of that."
What began in the gym nearly a decade ago with around 20 lifters and just more than $2,000 has grown incredibly.
"We break decibel warnings here, the energy from the crowd, because of what we're doing," added volunteer Jodi Benvie. "Both because there are people that you would walk by on the street, you would never know that they could pick up 300 pounds and they're getting on the stage, like in front of all these people. And that's a pretty brave thing to do."
On Saturday, nearly 80 lifters set the goal of $100,000, enough for ten wishes for Maine kids. Before the event started, the group was just a few thousand away from reaching the goal.
"All of this is amazing," said lead administrator Kaleigh Leighton. "The lifters are amazing, the training is amazing, this whole event is amazing. But when you actually see a kid get their wish granted and it completely changes their life, in the midst of going through something so intense and scary and it gives them this moment with their family, this moment of elation and joy and peace."

PORTLAND — Mann Law, an award-winning, female-led personal injury law firm serving clients across Maine, has welcomed five new team members, strengthening its legal team, daily operations and support for people navigating life after an injury.
The additions include Associate Attorney Liam Morrissey, Practice Manager Alexis Fowlie, Legal Coordinator Cindy Rogers, Legal Intern Liv Neuhauser and Front Office Assistant Zaina Maist.
“When someone comes to us after an injury, they need to know they have a team that will listen, guide them and stand up for them,” Chrissy Mann, founder and principal attorney of Mann Law, said. “Each of our new team members brings valuable experience and a shared commitment to ensuring that every client feels heard, valued, informed and supported throughout the process. As we grow, we’re building on what has always mattered most to us: personal attention, strong advocacy and helping our clients move forward.”
Liam Morrissey, associate attorney
A 2026 graduate of the University of Maine School of Law, Morrissey brings experience in private practice and public service. He clerked at a general practice law firm in Portland, externed with the Maine District Court in Augusta and interned with the Maine Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Standards.
Alexis Fowlie, practice manager
Fowlie oversees Mann Law’s daily operations, human resources and staff development. She previously built a career in healthcare leadership, including serving as a director of human resources, gaining extensive experience in employee relations, operations and team management.
Cindy Rogers, legal coordinator
Rogers brings a background in executive-level support, with experience coordinating day-to-day responsibilities in fast-paced professional environments. Her organizational and communication skills support the firm’s work on behalf of its clients.
Liv Neuhauser, legal intern
A second-year student at the University of Maine School of Law, Neuhauser first joined Mann Law as an intern in 2023. Before attending law school, she studied history and secondary education.
Zaina Maist, front office assistant

Founded by Mann in 2018, the firm combines personal injury advocacy with an understanding of how insurance companies handle claims. The proposed development would include a 125-seat restaurant and four two-bedroom apartments on a property across from Lobster in the Rough
A new restaurant and apartment building could be coming to Route 1 in York.
Plans submitted to the town call for a two-story mixed-use building at 985 and 995 U.S. Route 1, directly across from Lobster in the Rough.
The proposed development would include a 5,000-square-foot restaurant with seating for 125 people on the first floor and four two-bedroom apartments on the second floor.
The applicant is associated with Green Leaves Chinese Restaurant, an existing Chinese and Japanese restaurant in York that has operated for decades. The proposal does not specify whether Green Leaves would relocate or expand into the new building.
According to the application, the building would have a footprint of approximately 6,352 square feet and would be constructed on three lots totaling about 6.5 acres. The property is currently undeveloped and consists mainly of woodland.
The project would also include storage space for the residential units and access to public water, with plans for a private septic system.
The applicant requested waivers for a traffic impact analysis and a high-intensity soil survey.
The proposal is listed in materials for the York Planning Board's Nov. 19 meeting.
The project requires town approval before moving forward.

title: Evacuation order issued in Peoria, Illinois
text:
Evacuation order issued in Peoria, Illinois
Evacuation order issued in Peoria, Illinois
Officials have issued a mandatory evacuation order for Peoria and East Peoria in central Illinois, as they investigate a bomb threat at an ethanol and alcohol production plant.
A suspicious package found at the BioUrja Renewables plant in Peoria Friday afternoon prompted the evacuation order. The evacuation order affected all workers in the plant, as well as all residents living within a mile radius of the facility.
"The evacuation recommendation is being issued out of an abundance of caution while officers and emergency personnel investigate the threat," Peoria police said in a post on Facebook. "Officers are currently on scene conducting a thorough investigation and search of the facility to determine the credibility of the threat and ensure public safety."
At 11 p.m. Friday, Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said, “A device has been identified. We know it’s a credible threat. We know it’s a bomb. We don’t know whether there are other devices.”
If people don’t have a way to get out of the area, the mayor urged people to call 911 or the local chapter of the American Red Cross, saying public safety mattered. Those traveling in the area may run into backups and delays as a portion of Interstate 74, a major highway covering most of the Midwest, is shut down in central Illinois.
"We are assisting Peoria PD with this threat. Please stay away from downtown Peoria and the riverfront area of East Peoria. I-74 is shut down both ways through the city of Peoria. Use 474 to bypass," Peoria County Sheriff Chris Watkins said on Facebook.
The evacuation order remains in place overnight, as the city said, "The BioUrja bomb threat in Peoria, Illinois is an ongoing threat. All evacuations will remain in place and another update will come no later than 0900. Public safety personnel in East Peoria remain in constant contact to provide updates and relevant information as available."
BioUrja Renewables runs the former ADM ethanol plant in Peoria, which is focused on beverage-grade and industrial alcohol. The BioUrja Group company operates 19 other plants around the U.S., and has a global presence with facilities in Mexico, Singapore, Indian, United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.

title: LISTEN: Student pilot seeks help from air traffic control during nationwide ground stop
text:
RADIO TRAFFIC RECORDING: Student pilot seeks help during nationwide ground stop
A student pilot turned to air traffic control for guidance during his first solo cross-country flight as an unusual nationwide ground stop unfolded.
In a recording of the radio traffic, the pilot explains that he was traveling from Hicks Airfield, which is in Fort Worth, Texas.
Traffic controller: There is a ground stop nationwide. I advise you land your aircraft. Where would you like to land?
Pilot: Ma'am, I'm a student pilot. Honestly, this is my first time doing solo cross-country, and I don't know what do.
Traffic controller: Where did you come from?
Pilot: I came from Hicks.
Traffic controller: Landing at Hicks, I advise you land the airplane. There is multiple traffic in the vicinity of Hicks… both helicopters.
Pilot: So am I clear to land at Hicks then?
Traffic controller: You can change to advisory frequency at Hicks; I cannot give you clearance to that airport. Would you like to talk to approach?
Pilot: No, I just changed frequencies, speak to them, and there's nothing wrong with the airport itself? It's just like nationwide?
Traffic controller: Affirmative, nothing wrong with Hicks Airport itself. You can change to advisory frequencies; just suggest you land the airplane.
Pilot: Will do, thank you so much, I'll switch to Hicks now.

title: TSA agents find live snakes in traveler’s suitcase, pausing security screenings at airport
text:
ONTARIO, Calif. (CNN) — Airport security screening was paused at Ontario International Airport in Southern California after Transportation Security Administration agents found two live snakes inside a traveler’s suitcase last month.
What agents found
TSA agents saw what appeared to be ropes on an X-ray scan of the suitcase. The items were two live snakes confined in a pillowcase.
The traveler told agents he had flown with the snakes before.
Screenings halted
Screenings stopped while officials determined the snakes were not venomous.
The traveler was able to give the snakes, which he called his pets, to a relative who was not traveling.
Agents say travelers should check with their airline to confirm whether they can travel with pets.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: A Few Snow Showers Possible This Weekend Before Sunshine And Warmer Temperatures Return Next Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday! We’re heading into a fairly quiet weekend across the region, despite the potential for a few rounds of light rain and snow showers. The good news for those of you with weekend plans is that we’re not expecting anything significant in the way of snowfall for most locations. Temperatures will remain fairly consistent throughout the upcoming weekend, with highs in the upper 30s and lower 40s. Looking ahead to the new work week, sunshine makes a return to the region, along with a gradual warming trend that will bring temperatures back above average for this time of year.
Heading into the overnight hours tonight, we’ll continue to see mostly cloudy skies across the region, with the potential for a few flurries to develop, especially across northern and western portions of Aroostook County. Temperatures won’t cool off quite as much as what we saw last night, with lows for most locations falling back into the mid to upper 20s, and a few lower 30 degree readings across the St. John Valley. I don’t anticipate much, if anything, in the way of accumulating snowfall overnight tonight.
As we head into the start of the upcoming weekend, an area of low pressure in the upper levels of the atmosphere will be making its way through the region, allowing for some scattered snow showers to develop. Some of the better chances for seeing these snow showers will be during the morning hours, especially across northern and western portions of The County. As temperatures warm up a little heading into the afternoon hours, we could see a few rain showers begin to mix in with the snow shower activity. High temperatures tomorrow look to top off in the mid to upper 30s for most locations, with lower 40 degree readings possible across southern portions of the region. Those of you in southern Aroostook County will likely see a fairly quiet day overall.
Taking a look at the latest snowfall potential from our NextGen model, we continue to see some of the better chances for accumulating snowfall across the higher elevations of northern and western Aroostook County. For the majority of us along the Route 1 corridor, I don’t anticipate much in the way of accumulating snowfall, with most locations seeing little to nothing. Across the higher elevations, we could see a light coating of snow develop over the course of the weekend. There is still the potential for some of the heavier snow showers, especially during the day Sunday, to produce a quick inch of snowfall in a few isolated locations. Those traveling along and west of Route 11 north of Ashland will want to keep an eye out for the potential of some slick spots if those heavier snow showers develop. Again, this isn’t looking like a widespread accumulating snowfall event for The County.
More cloud coverage looks to stick around as we head into the second half of the weekend, with temperatures remaining very similar to what we’re expecting during the day tomorrow. While I anticipate a good portion of the day Sunday remaining quiet, another disturbance making its way through the region could allow for a few additional rain and snow showers to develop. Some of the better chances for seeing this shower activity will once again be across northern portions of the region, though we could see some of these showers extend into eastern Aroostook County as well. High temperatures Sunday look to range from the mid to upper 30s across northern locations to the lower 40s across southern locations. It’ll feel a little chillier at times given a northwesterly breeze, with occasional gusts around 20 mph.
The good news as we head into the new work week is that we’re finally looking at a return to more sunshine across the region. High pressure will begin to build into the region Monday, helping to clear out some of the cloud coverage we’ve been dealing with over the weekend. Temperatures Monday will still be fairly chilly despite the return of sunshine, with highs in the mid to upper 30s and lower 40s. However, this looks to be the start of a gradual warming trend that will continue through much of the upcoming work week.
Looking further ahead into next week, high pressure looks to remain in control of our weather pattern for much of the week, keeping things fairly quiet across Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick. Temperatures look to rebound into the mid to upper 40s Tuesday and Wednesday, with some locations potentially making a run at 50 degrees by Thursday. While the return of sunshine and warmer temperatures will certainly be welcomed by many of us, the unfortunate part of this forecast is that we’re not looking at much in the way of additional precipitation to help with our ongoing drought situation. Groundwater levels remain well below where they should be for this time of year, with record low groundwater levels being reported at both Clayton Lake and Millinocket. The rainfall we saw earlier this month was certainly welcomed, but we still have a long way to go in making up for our precipitation deficits. For more details on what to expect heading into the upcoming weekend and the new work week, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening and a wonderful weekend!

title: Travelers around the country react after rare FAA nationwide ground stop
text:
'People in tears': Travelers around the country react after rare FAA nationwide ground stop
While the ground stop only lasted for about four hours on Friday, air travel will likely not return to normal for a few days.
'People in tears': Travelers around the country react after rare FAA nationwide ground stop
While the ground stop only lasted for about four hours on Friday, air travel will likely not return to normal for a few days.
While flights have resumed after the Federal Aviation Administration's rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, thousands of travelers around the country were left scrambling to make hotel accommodations or find other ways to get to their destinations.
Video above: 'I don't know what to do': Travelers stuck amid nationwide ground stop
While the ground stop only lasted for about four hours on Friday, air travel will likely not return to normal for a few days.
It was the FAA's first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
'People in tears'
Hearst Television sister station WPTZ reported from the Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Burlington, Vermont, where lines formed at the check-in counters as people waited for answers.
Two people who spoke to the station said they were on their flight when the pilot broke the news that their flights and thousands of others across the U.S. would not be taking off.
"I saw a couple of people in tears," said Chad Brightbill, from Colorado.
Friday's ground stop lasted a few hours, but during the chaos, some travelers say it brought back memories of 9/11 when no flights took off for two days.
"Everybody's sort of looking at each other and trying to figure out what's going on. It was a little scary. I was around for 9/11, so it kind of felt like that," Brightbill said. "I was just getting ready to get on a plane that day. It was concerning."
He said he plans on using the unexpected delay to explore Burlington, booking a hotel for the weekend before his rescheduled flight on Sunday.
The unexpected hiccup, while inconvenient, is part of the price of travel, said Dan Leonardi, who travels from Burlington, Vermont, to New York City every week.
"I travel a lot, like every week, so it's part of the deal. I feel bad for people who I think there was a family that had a cruise tomorrow. They might miss that. I feel bad for people that have real plans," said Leonardi. "I have plans to go see my family, but unfortunately, when you travel as much as I do, it's part of the deal."
'We were baffled'
Meanwhile, Hearst Television sister station KOAT reported from the Albuquerque International Sunport.
A track and field team from Wyoming that was in New Mexico was looking for ways to get back home.
"We're thinking about driving back because it's about. It's just a little bit longer to drive back. Just an inconvenience to get cars and stuff," a team member said.
Two travelers heading to Nashville for a weekend getaway shared their reaction to the situation.
"We were baffled, mostly because our flight was initially delayed right before the ground stop had even occurred," one of the travelers said.
Another passenger, who had been sitting on a plane at Sunport, described the sudden change in plans.
"They pulled us back into the gate, held us there for about 15 minutes, and then pulled the jet bridge up, and we deplane. Yeah. Big, big, big inconvenience for you. Oh. Very much. My son's birthday is tomorrow," the passenger said.
'We're just trying to figure it out'
Hearst Television sister station KHBS in Arkansas spoke with travelers at Northwest Arkansas National Airport waiting to return to Indiana and a Fayetteville man grounded in Dallas.
Matthew Hoover and Caroline Newitt, who were visiting Northwest Arkansas from Upland, Indiana, said their American Airlines flights had been changed three times as they tried to get home.
"We’ve been, you know, headed to Charlotte and then said, headed to Dallas and all these things. O’Hare, Chicago," Hoover said. "So, we’re just trying to figure out. They’ve been, you know, delayed by an hour, delayed by two hours, delayed by three hours. We’re ready to fly. We’ll see what happens."
Noel Sosa, of Fayetteville, was aboard an American Airlines flight from Dallas to Northwest Arkansas when the ground stop took effect. He said the situation began developing while the plane was in the air.
"Apparently, man, all this developed while we were up in the air. They made an announcement that something was going on. But we’d be fine," Sosa said. "But once we got here, and, you know, you’re able to get out of airplane mode, we started getting all the news that, you know, nothing’s going anywhere."
After the plane landed in Dallas, Sosa said, passengers learned their flight would not be taking off again. The aircraft sat on the tarmac for about an hour as they waited for a gate.
"We’re all just here on the runway, waiting our turn, I guess," Sosa said.
He and his coworkers tried to figure out how to get home, possibly by passenger van.
"If not, man, I was just going to tell my wife, ‘Hey, get in that Jeep and come get me,'" Sosa said.
Sosa said he was supposed to be back in Northwest Arkansas around 7:30 p.m. Friday, with a full day of work ahead of him Saturday.
"I was ready to get back to it, get back to work, get back to my beautiful wife, get back to my life," Sosa said. "And apparently all that’s on pause right now."
Travelers were advised to check with their airlines for updated flight information.
Hearst Television stations WPTZ, KOAT and KHBS contributed to this report.

title: VIDEO: Man saves senior whose walker gets stuck on train tracks as Brightline approaches
text:
VIDEO: Man saves senior whose walker gets stuck on train tracks as Brightline approaches
For Nico Edwards, Sept. 27 was a special day for two reasons.
Not only was his family celebrating his son’s 11th birthday, but shortly after, the Riviera Beach man saved somebody’s life — a senior who was about to be struck by a Brightline train.
"I was doing what I can to help him because he was panicking," said Edwards.
Watch above: Man saves senior whose walker gets stuck on train tracks as Brightline approaches
That day, Edwards’ son wanted to start off his 11th birthday at Singer Island with his puppy.
"He wanted to go bring the dog to the beach, and that’s what we did," Edwards said.
However, Edwards says a lifeguard asked them to leave because 8-month-old Nova was not allowed on the beach.
"Us leaving at that time, I felt like that was God, you know?" Edwards said.
Edwards said that as they were in their car approaching the Blue Heron Boulevard and President Barack Obama Highway intersection, he heard people blowing their horns and saw the man crossing, attempting to cross the train tracks.
"I see the guy; his walker is kind of stuck inside the track, and the train is coming," Edwards said.
Edwards ran out of his car toward him. You can see in the video he’s barefoot because he ran so fast that his shoes flew off.
Edwards said he found the man tired and panicking, worried that he couldn’t get his walker unstuck in time and that he was being blocked by the crossing arms.
"If you zoom in on the video, you can see where he was going down," Edwards said. "That was one of his concerns: He wasn’t going to be able to get up. And I told him, 'Just bend and I got you.'"
You can hear the train conductor blaring the horn as the Brightline approaches and Edwards guides the gentleman under the gate arms, just in the nick of time.
Asked if he knew the man’s name, Edwards said, "No."
"He started to talk, but the light was — I wanted to catch the light, and he was saying thank you," Edwards said. "He said thank you. Like, 'Man, I was tired. I was out of breath. I didn’t think I was going to make it.'"
Easing the man back onto his walker and giving him a pat on the back for reassurance, Edwards ran back to his car before the traffic light turned green.
"That’s somebody’s grandfather," Edwards said. "If the shoe was on the other feet, I would want them to help me, too."
Edwards said he didn’t even realize the gravity of what he did until he watched the video and heard his son Mari’s reaction in the background.
"He just saved that man," said Mari.
As for Mari, it made his birthday celebration that much more special.
"I was thinking he was a superhero," said Mari.
Edwards said the biggest takeaway he wants people to have with this story is that people don’t have to know each other to help each other.
When asked if there was one thing he could say to the older man, Edwards said he would thank him. "God bless you," he said. "I appreciate him for allowing me to see God work in me."

title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
text:
Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker.
Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.
Lawsuit leads to warrant to get control of tanker
The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.
The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.
The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said.
Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.
The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.
Survivor recalls harrowing minutes in the river
The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV.
The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66-degree Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius).
Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
“It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.
Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him.
“They taught us not to drown,” Knab said.
Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.
Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.
“Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.
Tanker owner is subsidiary of Chinese company
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.
The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.
Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment.
The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

title: Charted: Here's how FAA ground stop compares to other flight cancellations, delays this year
text:
Charted: Here's how FAA ground stop compares to other flight cancellations, delays this year
The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop — which lasted about four hours on Friday — caused the second-highest number of flight cancellations this year, according to a Get the Facts Data Team analysis of FlightAware data.
It was surpassed by the major winter storm earlier this year that led to more than 11,500 canceled flights on Jan. 25.
FlightAware data as of 9 a.m. EST on Saturday shows more than 9,100 flights canceled within, into, or out of the U.S. on Nov. 13. More than 7,200 flights were delayed, although some were delayed prior to the FAA ground stop, and that's not an abnormal number of delays.
The cancellations have spilled into Saturday. More than 3,700 flights within, into, or out of the U.S. are canceled as of 9 a.m. EST.

title: ‘I’d do it a million times’: Man sentenced for killing father of 5 shows no remorse in court
text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) – A man sentenced for killing a California father showed no regret in the courtroom.
Damien Murphy was sentenced Thursday to 32 years in prison for the October 2023 shooting death of William Carney, a Fresno father.
Carney’s family had waited more than three years for sentencing. Loved ones filled the courtroom.
Plea and sentence
Murphy shot Carney in central Fresno in October 2023. Two months ago, he pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter. The plea avoided a first-degree murder conviction and resulted in a lower sentence.
Murphy did not express remorse when the judge gave him the chance to address the court.
Family speaks in court
Carney left behind five children. His family said he was less than one month shy of his 40th birthday.
More than a dozen friends and family members attended the hearing. Five of them addressed the court, including Carney’s mother and his 16-year-old daughter.
Among those who spoke, one family member said: “He could never walk me down the aisle on my wedding day and cry seeing how much I’ve grown.”
Another said: “My life simply no longer holds the happiness it once had. The joy that used to come naturally has been replaced by grief.”
One of Carney’s childhood friends spoke directly to Murphy.
“I can’t hate you because I know you’re suffering more than he is, and that brings me peace of mind,” the friend said.
Judge and defendant
Murphy showed no reaction during more than 20 minutes of statements from Carney’s family, including as the judge described the weight of the crime.
“I hope every second of your 32 years you think about William and his family, and the damage you’ve caused,” the judge said.
The judge then offered Murphy a chance to address the court and Carney’s family.
“I would apologize, but I’m not going to apologize for protecting my family, sir. I’d do it a million times,” Murphy said.
The judge responded: “I hope you change your mind and have some remorse for your actions, and don’t be disrespectful to people you’ve murdered and hurt their family.”
What’s next
Murphy will return to court next month for a restitution hearing. He will not have a chance at probation.

title: Officer resuscitates infant who stopped breathing
text:
NORTH PORT, Fla. (Gray News) - A police officer in Florida is being hailed as a hero after resuscitating an infant who had stopped breathing.
The North Port Police Department shared footage from the officer’s body camera of the rescue on Facebook Thursday.
“Not every call ends in an arrest or involves a crime. Sometimes, it’s an officer rushing to help an infant who isn’t breathing, relying on his training until he hears that first cry,” the police department said in the caption.
In the video, dated Nov. 7, the officer is seen working to resuscitate the baby. His efforts don’t stop until he hears the baby begin to cry, a sign that the infant is breathing again.
“You good?” the officer asks as the baby begins to cry. “That’s good.”
The police department said in the video’s caption that “police work is about more than enforcing the law.”
“It’s about protecting life,” the department said. “And sometimes, a baby’s first cry is the greatest reward of all.”
