title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
text:
What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
Normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
Normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday. He said airlines "will still have delays and cancellations" Saturday but promised that the "worst is behind us."
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here's what to know.
Flights have resumed, but disruption continues
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could resume late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday, and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport on Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe's aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
The reason for the grounding
New technology being hooked up to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
"We didn't think we would have this kind of outage. We did," he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
The Microsoft outage and cyberattacks were unrelated to the stoppage
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
"There was never any lives at risk," Mullin added. "There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted "out of an abundance of caution," he said.

title: Why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues
text:
Regional U.S. air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that’s “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country,” and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.
Here’s a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues:
Top official cites ‘instability’ in communication system
New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that somehow resulted in the system overload. Duffy said officials were probing whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
Planes flying at the time of the ground stop were able to land safely using “well-known procedures” in place for such circumstances, Duffy said Friday.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines, while old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports. But the work is far from complete, and Duffy used the news conference on Friday and Saturday to urge Congress to provide more funding.
Regional air control centers play a key role in high-altitude flights
The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday due to issues at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The U.S. operates 22 regional air traffic control centers, managed by the FAA, oversees long-distance aircraft operating between departure and arrival airports. according to McCormick, associate professor and program coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. McCormick estimates these control centers take over flights at altitudes over 10,000 feet.
These centers, which operate in such places as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis, are one of the three layers that guide pilots. The airport towers direct pilots at the takeoffs at the 500-plus airports that have towers. Then, the so-called Terminal Radar Approach Control centers take over and guide pilots as they get further away from the airport. And then the regional control centers take over. When descending, the reverse happens, experts say.
Experts say that the controllers at the regional centers are sitting at radar displays and are responsible for only that airspace.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” said Stephen Creamer, president of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
Pilots use radio frequency to communicate
McCormick said the country’s regional, high-altitude air traffic control centers need to be connected to remote radio transmitter or receiver sites. That’s to allow for radio frequency coverage to communicate with the aircraft.
Those transmitter sites are connected to the centers via telecommunications systems, the likes of which are in the process of moving from copper wires to fiber optic lines. The two-way communication is important to ensure — among other things — that planes maintain safe spacing, he said.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it’s unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
But he and other aviation experts said that the FAA is now transitioning to what’s known as controller pilot data link — a digital, text-based messaging system that allows controllers and pilots to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through the data link instead of voice radio.
A problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
In September, Newark Liberty International Airport temporarily lost radar communications with aircraft, after a backup fiber optic line was inadvertently cut by railroad construction workers. That forced the FAA to immediately cancel hundreds of flights going in and out of the airport.
But airline experts say that scenario was different from what occurred on Friday. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday that intermittent frequency instability affected as many as 17 of the 22 U.S. regional air control centers.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” he said. “It propagated around the country.”
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the “knock-on” effect is incredible.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Even with a complete outage, pilots can still communicate
Aviation experts say that pilots can still communicate with aircraft even during intermittent communications disruptions, noting as an example that many planes have satellite phone systems.
John Hansman, aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation, said that pilots can still talk directly to other pilots in airplanes around them via radio. And there’s also equipment on the airplane that tells pilots if there are airplanes around them, he said.
If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high intensity light beams, which send signals to pilots to alert whether it’s safe to descend, he said.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” said Hansman.

title: ‘Thank God for her’: Head Start director’s quick action saves choking child
text:
WAYNESBORO, Ga. (WRDW/Gray News) - The director of a Head Start program in Georgia is being hailed as a hero after stepping in to save a choking child during a family event.
The emergency unfolded Thursday during the Burke County school’s annual fall family meal, when more than 140 families came to eat with their children and do activities in the classroom.
Director Yolanda Willis said that upon leaving, the child was given a piece of candy, and it got lodged in his throat.
Surveillance video from the center showed little Jo Freeman in the hallway in obvious distress as a guardian nearby tried to help.
Willis, about 20 feet away, looked over and realized something was wrong.
“When I looked, the child was blue in the face, and I just took action from there, from everything I’ve been trained to do,” Willis said. “You never know when you’ll be able to use it – and yesterday was the day.”
Willis rushed over and began the Heimlich maneuver, performing several abdominal thrusts until the candy came loose and 2-year-old Jo could breathe again.
Jo’s mother, Felicia Freeman, said she had stepped into the hallway as the commotion started.
“My baby was choking on a piece of candy that he had put in his mouth, and it lodged in his throat,” she said. “When I stepped out into the hallway, I realized that he was choking. Miss Willis immediately started doing the maneuver on him and got it out.”
The mother said she tried to stay calm even as she was terrified.
“It was very frightening and very scary,” Freeman said. “I know it was best that I did not panic at a moment like that, or he could have died if I panicked. So I had to stay calm, but I was in a state of shock right there.”
Freeman, who appeared in the video wearing a red hat, said her son has been thriving in the program.
For her, watching Willis jump in was overwhelming.
“I thank God she had that training, because if she had not been there, I just don’t know.”
Willis said she relied on years of training in education and child care.
“Over my 25-plus years of being in education, I’ve had to perform CPR on a child, the Heimlich once before,” she said. “You just have to be prepared and ready if something like this occurs.”
Willis also recently had surgery and was supposed to be under lifting restrictions.
“But all of that was out the door, and adrenaline rushed in, and it was go time,” she said.
Freeman noted that learning that detail afterward brought her to tears.
“She’s an angel to us,” Freeman said. “There were a lot of tears behind it, and I thank God for her.”
Willis says Jo was able to continue his day after the scare.
The team said they hope the viral video and the attention it’s getting will inspire more parents and caregivers to get trained in CPR and first aid.
“A parent with toddlers, it is No. 1 priority,” Willis said. “That’s our goal, that we would bring awareness to this and that we could get our parents trained in these types of life-saving measures.”
Freeman agrees and said she’s just thankful her son’s story ended differently than others she’s seen.
“I thank God for everybody that was involved and how everybody reacted,” she said. “No one panicked. He’s doing better, and I just thank God she was there.”

title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, White House says
text:
Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, White House says
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.
Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" on nuclear disarmament "that can be productive going forward," said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.
But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to "step up ... to the adult table" on a matter of international importance.
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
"I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
"You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism," he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as "dear friend."
Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a "no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.
"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
___
Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow.

title: New Hampshire driver killed in Saco crash, police say
text:
Maine State Police were investigating a fatal crash Saturday on northbound Interstate 95 in Saco.
According to a preliminary probe by the department, the incident occurred early Saturday when Felix Melo, 36, of Manchester, New Hampshire, operating a Hyundai Santa Fe, rear-ended a Ford Explorer traveling in the center lane.
“After the initial collision, the Ford spun and came to rest on the roadway, while the Hyundai left the roadway, entered a wooded area, and rolled onto its side,” Maine State Police said in a news release.
Melo was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
The driver of the Ford Explorer, Yara Schneider, 42, and passenger Ana Dos Santos Augusto, 24, both of Lowell, Massachusetts, were treated and released on scene.

title: Congress must resume military aid to Ukraine to end Russian atrocities
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Brian Milakovsky lives in Bath. From 2015 to 2022 he lived in Siverskodonetsk, Ukraine, where he worked on economic recovery programs funded by the United States.
Just hours before Americans went to the polls on Nov. 3 to decide the character of our country, Russia made it blindingly clear what kind of country it is by butchering 55 civilians and first responders in a small town in eastern Ukraine.
Our new Congress should understand just what happened in Komyshuvakha, and what must be done.
Before the war the 5,000 residents of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region grew sunflowers and wheat, worked on the railroad or at the grain elevator and a few small factories. This is working class Ukraine, struggling but decent. Today, all but about 200 residents have fled, and on Nov. 2 Russian forces bombed the town’s humanitarian aid distribution center. First responders rushed residents into the basement bomb shelter, only for Russia to drop more bombs that collapsed the entire structure. Five days later, 55 bodies have been pulled from the rubble and dozens more people are unaccounted for.
As it always does, Russia immediately claimed that the hub was a legitimate military target. It flooded the internet with fakes to back up this ghoulish lie. But Ukraine released body cam footage from one of the fallen policemen, which showed only a panicked crowd of civilians rushing into the basement that would become their tomb.
There is nothing new or unexpected in any of Russia’s actions. Since my wife and I fled her hometown with our newborn baby in 2022, we have watched the cities and villages of eastern Ukraine become a geography of Russian atrocity: cluster bombing of cities and villages, imprisonment, torture and execution of loyal Ukrainians, indoctrination of their children. Popasna, Izium, Bakhmut, Mariinka, and Mariupol, jewel of the Azov Sea, surrounded now by mass graves.
Since 2022, Americans have watched Russia’s actions in places like Komyshuvakha and they have supported U.S. military aid to Ukraine. This fact seems to have kept President Donald Trump from forcing Ukraine into a deal that would leave it disarmed and exposed to Russia’s next invasion. But he has dialed back military aid to near zero, declined to impose crushing sanctions that Congress has authorized and legalized import of Russian diesel. His family and closest advisors socialize and talk business with Russian oligarchs and with Vladimir Putin’s slick team of negotiators.
But this new Congress can make a course correction, and every member of Maine’s delegation can contribute. In the lame duck session that stretches through the rest of 2026, Congress must pass the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) and Sen. Angus King, a veteran member of the Armed Services Committee, can push for amendments to provide rocket interceptors, intelligence support and Starlink access to Ukraine’s army.
Once the new Congress is sworn in a priority should be amending the “Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act,” passed this year to narrow the president’s discretion on whether or not to impose them on Russia. Support for such amendments would be particularly meaningful from Rep.-elect Paul LePage, a longtime ally of the president. The representative’s counsel could help influence President Donald Trump’s thinking on the 2027 NDAA and the resumption of military aid packages to Ukraine.
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, the first rank and file union member in the Senate, and Rep. Chellie Pingree, a member of the House Committee on Agriculture, can shape the restoration of humanitarian aid to the beleaguered Ukrainian people. They should focus on the real economy: the steelworkers, shipbuilders and dockworkers working under Russian bombardment and maritime blockade, the family farmers tilling mined fields and dodging murderous drones.
Supporting Ukraine with arms and financial assistance is not about prolonging the war. The path to a lasting peace is to build Ukraine’s arsenal of deterrence and make further aggression too costly for Russia to bear. Only then will we see the end of atrocities like the one at Komyshuvakha.

title: Deb Haaland breaks political barriers as Native women in her home community face hurdles
text:
PARAJE, N.M. (AP) — On the morning of a Laguna Pueblo village’s annual Feast Day, Ashley Sarracino knelt in her family home holding clothespins between her teeth. She straightened her niece’s black cotton manta, a traditional one-shouldered dress, and tied a sash around her waist.
On these days, Sarracino is a caretaker, dressing relatives for the harvest dance and helping feed up to 150 guests. And as a former member of the pueblo council, she knows how to balance those traditional responsibilities with official duties.
“To me, those things aren’t in conflict at all,” she said.
Yet even as another Laguna Pueblo woman, former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, is set to become the first Native American woman state governor, women with leadership aspirations such as Sarracino say they are swimming upstream in their Pueblo communities. Sarracino said she was forced off the council after alleging she was paid less because she was a woman, a claim pueblo officials deny.
In some of the 19 pueblos in New Mexico, including Laguna, tribal law and customs do not allow women to hold top government positions.
Haaland told The Associated she was once nominated to serve on her pueblo council but did not make it past a primary. She quipped it was “easier to raise $1 million and run for Congress” than succeed in Pueblo politics.
“It’s still a man’s world in a lot of Pueblo communities, and certainly in mine,” she said.
A pay disparity became a fight over women’s place in tribal leadership
Sarracino was offered a road map familiar to ambitious young Native people: Leave the reservation to get an education, then return home to serve your community.
She built a career in nonprofit work and political organizing, including as chair of her county’s Democratic Party.
In 2022, Sarracino was nominated by a pueblo elder to run for council secretary. She finished second, but was appointed to the post after a resignation.
“Finally I had an opportunity to use my skills to help my own community,” she said.
While reviewing budget documents, Sarracino discovered she was being paid $14,000 less than her male predecessor. She asked the pueblo governor for an explanation, sparking a bitter dispute that would end her tenure on council.
The council says Sarracino was paid less because she lacked experience and that she abandoned her post.
But Sarracino insists she was ousted and that the pay discrepancy reflects sexist attitudes embedded in tribal law. Since 1996, the pueblo’s election code has allowed women to run for council treasurer and secretary, but it does not explicitly allow them to serve as governor or lieutenant governor.
Its constitution, last amended in 2012, refers to the governor as “he” and “him.”
Sarracino’s dispute landed in tribal court but was dismissed this year on sovereign immunity grounds and she’s exhausted her appeals. The case took a toll on her mental health. She said it’s been bittersweet to watch Haaland make political history.
“We all know she would never have the same opportunity here,” she said.
Yet Haaland’s ascent could help change attitudes at home. Emily Hunt, who became Laguna Pueblo’s first female elected official in the late ’90s with legal help from Haaland, believes the pueblo will someday nominate a woman governor.
“Whether I’ll see it in my lifetime, I don’t know,” Hunt said.
Pueblo governance is varied and complex
Some pueblos retain traditional theocracies, with government roles appointed by ceremonial elders and reserved for men.
Charlotte Little, a citizen of San Felipe Pueblo, said women in those communities hold esteemed roles of their own. A New Mexico state representative, Little never aspired to lead at home.
“It’s about respecting the culture that I come from,” she said.
Other pueblos, under federal pressure in the 1930s, adopted secular constitutions and elections. That includes Isleta Pueblo, where in 1986 Verna Teller overcame a contentious legal battle to become its first and only woman governor.
Council incumbents attempted unsuccessfully to strike Teller’s name from the ballot, arguing a woman could not hold office under Isleta law. She won in a landslide.
Now in her 70s, Teller blames colonization for the patriarchy that she says persists in traditionally matrilineal Pueblo communities.
“When the Spaniards and the Catholics came here, they didn’t want to deal with the clan mothers. They threw women in the back seat,” Teller said. “That has turned into this paternalistic attitude that men have to be in charge.”
That’s not the case at every pueblo. At Pojoaque Pueblo, where council positions are open to all and candidates don’t need to be nominated, women have held all four executive positions since 2021.
Planning with the next generation in mind
Haaland is the most prominent among a wave of Pueblo women who have found success in mainstream politics, from school boards to state government and U.S. Congress. She encouraged Pueblo women to look beyond their home communities for opportunities.
“We need more Native women everywhere,” she told The AP.
Sarracino has not ruled out a future pueblo council run and, after attending Haaland’s election night celebration, now sees a potential path in state politics.
On Feast Day, as her family home sprang to life with visitors, Sarracino greeted friends and relatives with hugs, refilled their iced teas and later made sure they went home with oven bread and fruit pie.
She watched with pride as her nieces giggled over plates of enchiladas, their hands white with ceremonial clay from the morning’s dances. She is planning her next move with those girls in mind.
“That’s the reason I couldn’t just let it go,” she said. “Because I know they’re coming up behind me.”
___
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Dunkin’ location operating without doughnuts for nearly 4 months after opening
text:
FARGO, N.D. (KVLY/Gray News) - A Dunkin’ store inside a Fargo-area Walmart isn’t selling doughnuts nearly four months after opening.
The location opened July 17 without doughnuts available, with the doughnut case remaining empty during a return visit this week.
A Dunkin’ worker confirmed the sweet treats were still not being sold.
The worker said the location is looking into using Walmart’s bakery to make doughnuts in the morning. However, it remained unclear when the items would become available.
The Dunkin’ location continues to offer drinks, including coffee and energy drinks.

title: Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
text:
Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump's ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president's far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an "invasion." The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.
Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.
At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.
Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.
"Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. The executive order has been the "single most important factor in the President's success at the border," the Homeland Security Department's general counsel, James Percival, said in a social media post.
Attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.
They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to "invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.
The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn't allow the administration to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.
"The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban," said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. "Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum."
The ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear the case in the spring and hand down a decision by the end of June.
It's the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.
The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a "metering" policy that has been used to turn back immigrants at the border in years past.

title: Why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues
text:
(AP) - Regional U.S. air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that’s “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country,” and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.
Here’s a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away, among other issues:
Top official cites ‘intermittent’ gaps in communication system
The nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.
A contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
Planes flying at the time of the ground stop were able to land safely using “well-known procedures” in place for such circumstances, Duffy said Friday.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines, while old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports. But the work is far from complete, and Duffy used the news conference on Friday and Saturday to urge Congress to provide more funding.
Regional air control centers play a key role in high-altitude flights
The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday due to issues at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The U.S. operates 22 regional air traffic control centers, managed by the FAA, and they oversee long-distance aircraft operating between departure and arrival airports, according to McCormick, associate professor and program coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. McCormick estimates these control centers take over flights at altitudes over 10,000 feet.
These centers, which operate in such places as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis, are one of the three layers that guide pilots. The airport towers direct pilots during takeoffs at the 500-plus airports that have towers. Then, the so-called Terminal Radar Approach Control centers take over and guide pilots as they get further away from the airport. And then the regional control centers take over. When descending, the reverse happens, experts say.
Experts say that the controllers at the regional centers are sitting at radar displays and are responsible for only that airspace.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” said Stephen Creamer, president of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
Pilots use radio frequency to communicate
McCormick said the country’s regional, high-altitude air traffic control centers need to be connected to remote radio transmitter or receiver sites. That’s to allow for radio frequency coverage to communicate with the aircraft.
Those transmitter sites are connected to the centers via telecommunications systems, the likes of which are in the process of moving from copper wires to fiber optic lines. The two-way communication is important to ensure — among other things — that planes maintain safe spacing, he said.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it’s unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
But he and other aviation experts said that the FAA is now transitioning to what’s known as controller pilot data link — a digital, text-based messaging system that allows controllers and pilots to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through the data link instead of voice radio.
A problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
In September, Newark Liberty International Airport temporarily lost radar communications with aircraft, after a backup fiber optic line was inadvertently cut by railroad construction workers. That forced the FAA to immediately cancel hundreds of flights going in and out of the airport.
But airline experts say that scenario was different from what occurred on Friday. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday that intermittent frequency instability affected as many as 17 of the 22 U.S. regional air control centers.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” said John Hansman, an aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation. “It propagated around the country.”
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the “knock-on” effect is incredible.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves on to C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Even with a complete outage, pilots can still communicate
Aviation experts say that pilots can still communicate with aircraft even during intermittent communications disruptions, noting as an example that many planes have satellite phone systems.
Hansman said pilots can still talk directly to other pilots in airplanes around them via radio. There is also equipment on board that tells pilots if airplanes are around them, he added.
If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high intensity light beams, which send signals to pilots to alert whether it’s safe to descend, Hansman said.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” he said.

title: Bucksport man arrested after driving the wrong way on I-95
text:
A Bucksport man was arrested early Saturday morning after reportedly driving the wrong way on I-95 in Argyle Township.
Maine State Police received reports that a vehicle was traveling southbound in the northbound lane at about 2:28 a.m., according to Maine State Police spokesperson Aaron Turcotte.
Troopers located the vehicle, a 2005 Ram pickup, and arrested Tyler Hawksley, 24.
He was taken to Penobscot County Jail and charged with operating under the influence, driving to endanger, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon and unlawful possession of schedule W drugs.
No injuries were reported.

title: Yarmouth football’s explosive offense starts with the three guys up front
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — In eight-man football, an offensive line is a power trio instead of a quintet. As he celebrated his team’s state championship Saturday afternoon, Yarmouth quarterback Iggy McGrath knew the three guys charged with keeping him upright all season did it better than any trio in the Large School division, from mid-August when practices started through Saturday, when the Clippers capped an undefeated season with a 72-26 win over Old Town at Edward Little High School.
“I don’t have to look over my back shoulder or anything,” McGrath said. “Without them, we are crumbling. They are the base and heart of our team.”
They are junior center Teo Davis and senior guards Lucas Tebbenhoff and William Wignall, and they did the dirty work that allowed the Clippers to churn up yards and points at an absurd rate.
Saturday’s win was the third time in 11 games that Yarmouth scored at least 70 points. The Clippers averaged 63 points and were held under 50 just twice, in the first two games of the season. Their 44 points in the season opener was the lowest total. They rolled up 559 yards on Saturday — 294 in the first half when the game was still somewhat in doubt, before running time took hold midway through the third quarter.
When did the three linemen know they could be the battery for this high-powered scoring machine?
“First practice,” Davis said without any hesitation.
Line play was a point of emphasis for the Clippers in the offseason, coach Nick Orsi said. When the 2025 season came to an end, Orsi and his assistant coaches asked themselves, how will we become a more physical team on both sides of the ball?
“We lost in the first round last year, and we really got manhandled up front,” Orsi said.
The addition of running back Stephen Connolly, a student at North Yarmouth Academy, gave the Clippers a dangerous new weapon. McGrath and a slew of receivers could get the ball downfield. The development of Davis, Tebbenhoff and Wignall as a cohesive pancake-blocking unit was the final piece.
“Our offense, that’s the best group of athletes I’ve seen in my life. We’re just along for the ride,” Tebbenhoff said.
Neither Wignall nor Tebbenhoff are anchored to a certain side of the line. One play, Wignall may line up to the left of Davis. On the next, he and Tebbenhoff could switch. The formations are designed to play up to their individual strengths, Orsi said.
The Clippers ran a lot of outside zone blocking schemes to one side, and power and gap schemes to the other. Flip the two guards from side to side, and teams still can’t decipher what Yarmouth was doing, Orsi said.
“William is big and strong, and he’s really good on down blocking. Then Lucas is fast and can move a little better, so we can put him on the side we run zone schemes to,” Orsi said. “Obviously, we have really good skill guys, but those guys up front killed it all season for us on both sides of the ball.”
Need a couple inches, like Yarmouth did late in the second quarter at the Coyotes 2-yard line? Davis, Tebbenhoff and Wignall will put the defense on its heels with an impressive push off the snap. Connolly scored easily on that play, through a hole Wignall created.
Last season, the Clippers averaged around 4.5 yards per carry, Orsi said. This season, they averaged more than 12 yards.
Need to give McGrath a little extra time to find an open receiver downfield? They did that, too, over and over again as the days became shorter and colder. Keep Iggy clean, Wignall said.
From September until Saturday, Yarmouth’s offense was an unstoppable force in the eight-man football ranks. The skill position players ended up in the highlight videos, but Davis, Tebbenhoff and Wignall were the power trio. They kept the chains moving, and now they have the Gold Ball to prove it.

title: ‘Thank God for her’: Head Start director’s quick action saves choking child
text:
WAYNESBORO, Ga. (WRDW/Gray News) - The director of a Head Start program in Georgia is being hailed as a hero after stepping in to save a choking child during a family event.
The emergency unfolded Thursday during the Burke County school’s annual fall family meal, when more than 140 families came to eat with their children and do activities in the classroom.
Director Yolanda Willis said that upon leaving, the child was given a piece of candy, and it got lodged in his throat.
Surveillance video from the center showed little Jo Freeman in the hallway in obvious distress as a guardian nearby tried to help.
Willis, about 20 feet away, looked over and realized something was wrong.
“When I looked, the child was blue in the face, and I just took action from there, from everything I’ve been trained to do,” Willis said. “You never know when you’ll be able to use it – and yesterday was the day.”
Willis rushed over and began the Heimlich maneuver, performing several abdominal thrusts until the candy came loose and 2-year-old Jo could breathe again.
Jo’s mother, Felicia Freeman, said she had stepped into the hallway as the commotion started.
“My baby was choking on a piece of candy that he had put in his mouth, and it lodged in his throat,” she said. “When I stepped out into the hallway, I realized that he was choking. Miss Willis immediately started doing the maneuver on him and got it out.”
The mother said she tried to stay calm even as she was terrified.
“It was very frightening and very scary,” Freeman said. “I know it was best that I did not panic at a moment like that, or he could have died if I panicked. So I had to stay calm, but I was in a state of shock right there.”
Freeman, who appeared in the video wearing a red hat, said her son has been thriving in the program.
For her, watching Willis jump in was overwhelming.
“I thank God she had that training, because if she had not been there, I just don’t know.”
Willis said she relied on years of training in education and child care.
“Over my 25-plus years of being in education, I’ve had to perform CPR on a child, the Heimlich once before,” she said. “You just have to be prepared and ready if something like this occurs.”
Willis also recently had surgery and was supposed to be under lifting restrictions.
“But all of that was out the door, and adrenaline rushed in, and it was go time,” she said.
Freeman noted that learning that detail afterward brought her to tears.
“She’s an angel to us,” Freeman said. “There were a lot of tears behind it, and I thank God for her.”
Willis says Jo was able to continue his day after the scare.
The team said they hope the viral video and the attention it’s getting will inspire more parents and caregivers to get trained in CPR and first aid.
“A parent with toddlers, it is No. 1 priority,” Willis said. “That’s our goal, that we would bring awareness to this and that we could get our parents trained in these types of life-saving measures.”
Freeman agrees and said she’s just thankful her son’s story ended differently than others she’s seen.
“I thank God for everybody that was involved and how everybody reacted,” she said. “No one panicked. He’s doing better, and I just thank God she was there.”

title: Drone activity over US base in Britain prompts security response
text:
Drone activity over US base in Britain prompts security response
Unauthorized drone activity prompted a security response at an American base in Britain, but the situation has been “resolved,” U.S. and U.K. defense officials said Friday.
Security forces at Royal Air Force Base Lakenheath in eastern England responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity, but no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, the U.S. Air Force in Europe said in a statement.
“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the statement said.
Related video above: Transportation leaders give update after rare FAA nationwide ground stop
A spokesperson for the British Ministry of Defense said the incident has been “resolved.” U.S. Air Force security personnel had responded to the reports, and the U.K. ministry is working closely with the Americans to determine what happened, according to the spokesperson, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters.
The drone incident means that three U.S. bases in the United Kingdom have been affected by threats in recent weeks. Friday's security response at RAF Lakenheath comes just days after the U.S. moved more than a dozen aircraft from a different base just miles away in eastern England — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat.
During the plane exodus, RAF Mildenhall also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second-highest level, which is used when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely.
A U.S. official said at the time that the decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive.
Several weeks ago, a group of men was detained after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford, roughly 150 miles (240 kilometers) west of Mildenhall and Lakenheath. British authorities linked the plot to Iran, and the U.S. withdrew its bombers that had been stationed there.
The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war. Other arrests followed, and at least three men have been charged with plotting to attack RAF Fairford.
Also this week, a U.S. Army officer assigned to a NATO unit at a military base near Gloucester, England, was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with the suspected terror plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford, also near Gloucester.

title: Wells mobile home residents battling for clean water
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WELLS — When Lindy Rowe turns on his bathtub faucet, the water comes out cloudy.
“Just give it a second,” he says.
As the water fills the tub, it’s no longer just cloudy — it’s brown.
And it’s not just water. It’s also imbued with debris, and as the water drains away, dirt particles remain behind.
Lindy, 69, has lived with his wife, Sylvia, 74, their dog, Diesel, and their cat, Spike, at their manufactured home in Blueberry Ridge Mobile Village for 12 years.
They spend a little over $40 a month on bottled water. They can’t rely on the cleanliness of their well water, and they’re not alone.
Other residents at Blueberry Ridge have said water issues have been a park-wide problem for 25 years. They’re fresh off the approval of a new mobile home lot rent stabilization ordinance that passed on Election Day, and many of them are now focused on working to fix their next problem: water quality.
The rent stabilization ordinance came about in response to rent increases that mobile home park residents say are pricing them out of one of the only affordable housing options available to them.
While the water quality and rent increases have some overlap, the community at Blueberry Ridge stresses that the water is a separate issue that predates rent increases.
Lynzy Kosmes, 48, manages medical offices and has lived at the park for 15 years. She said she’s been fortunate enough to invest in a filtration system for her faucets, but some of her neighbors can’t afford to spend the money.
Diane Whiteside, 79, still has to work because she can’t afford to live on just her Social Security. Her neighbor Dave Coulson, 66, also had to return to work after retirement to afford park rent increases until a work-sustained injury took him back out of commission.
Kosmes said it feels like little progress has been made to address water quality, which has spanned several owners of the mobile home park. The discoloration has even impacted their laundry. Sylvia said she can’t own white blouses anymore, because they turn yellow when she washes them.
“It turns my hair yellow,” said Patty Coulson, Dave’s wife.
Residents say they feel their higher rent isn’t being put toward resolving issues like the dirty water.
Blueberry Ridge has two wells split between about 60 homes, residents say. Amy Lachance, director of the Drinking Water Program for the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, said iron and manganese cause discoloration in water, which has occurred in hundreds of water systems in the state.
“The main issue is that it’s just a naturally occurring phenomenon,” she said. She said while there’s no health concerns, “I certainly do understand. It’s nasty looking.”
In October, a group of residents, including Kosmes and Whiteside, met with representatives from Gov. Janet Mills’ office, the Maine Office of Community Affairs and Maine’s Drinking Water Program.
Lachance said an inspector tested the water after a complaint was filed in summer 2025.
Kosmes said they were told that inspections at the park indicated the water hadn’t reached high enough bacteria levels to be considered a risk, and that the discoloration doesn’t count as a contaminant. Because the water didn’t meet the risk threshold for bacteria or contaminants, the state has no authority to force the owner to do anything to improve the water quality.
“He has taken samples for iron and manganese and determined that there’s no health based standards that are being exceeded,” Lachance said.
Lachance said state officials began working with park owners and operators to act on the concerns regardless.
In a statement attributed to Blueberry Park Management, officials for the mobile home park said they were working with the town and the state to alleviate the water issues, which they said predated Phillips International’s ownership.
Park officials added, “(s)ince acquiring the property, we have made maintaining a properly functioning water system and addressing any issues a priority.”
This included hiring Aquamen Water Solutions to take over management of the system. Park management said Aquamen recommended “that more extensive replacement of parts was required.”
“In addition, it was discovered that before the water treatment improvements could move forward, a separate septic system design was required by the state,” they said. “The septic system design has now been approved by the town and is with the state for review. Once that part of the project is complete, the next step is to begin work on the water filtration system.”
Lachance said some of the initial work has begun and permit applications have been filed. The state may approve final permits soon so work can begin before the ground freezes.
Until the repairs are finished, Lindy Rowe’s dog Diesel drinks his water from a pre-packaged gallon jug, Sylvia Rowe refuses to wash her last white blouse and Patty Coulson works to keep her hair as white as she can.
“What’s the matter?” Diane Whiteside asks her, jokingly. “Don’t you want to be a blonde?”

title: Rescuers make human chain to save 6-year-old from freezing river
text:
TOTOWA, N.J. (WABC) - Officials came to the aid of a 6-year-old boy who had wandered away from his New Jersey home last week.
Police said he was found clinging to a tree in the Passaic River and that a human chain was created to get him to safety. The heroic rescue was captured on body camera video.
“It was super emotional. You know, we are also parents, so we tend to see things a little bit more personal,” Fina Matranga, a Totowa Police Department patrolman, said.
Last Thursday night, Totowa police received emergency calls about a barefoot child knocking on doors and then fleeing.
Crews were dispatched and found the boy’s parents desperately searching for their child, who has autism and is nonverbal.
It’s believed the boy may have escaped from his family’s home through a window.
“Some people were screaming his name,” neighbor Latoya Carswell said. “And some people were just, like, on foot, power walk and some are running.”
The growing search team definitely felt the time pressure when they realized children with autism tend to gravitate toward water.
So, they raced to the Passaic River.
“We quickly widened our resources and called the fire department for extra lighting and more manpower, along with other agencies around town and the sheriff’s department,” Matranga said.
They fortunately found the child before he was swept away by the current. It was reported he was down a dark embankment, half in the freezing river and clinging to a tree.
Because of the steep drop, rescue crews handed the shivering child up a human chain.
“Completely drenched from head to toe, full of mud,” Matranga said. “I sat with him and I was able to comfort him and clean them up a little bit as much as I could … I have some sensory toys in my duty bag for these cases, and I was able to give him some toys.”
Officials believed the child may have been drawn by nearby Christmas lights as well as the water.
Police said the child’s parents will be installing tighter locks on their windows.

title: Darth Vader's lightsaber used in ‘I am your father’ duel sells for nearly $5 million
text:
Darth Vader's lightsaber used in ‘I am your father’ duel sells for nearly $5 million
From a galaxy far, far away to a Dallas auction house — a lightsaber wielded by Darth Vader before he delivered the famous line “I am your father” sold for over $4.87 million on Thursday.
Described by Heritage Auctions as the character’s “primary dueling lightsaber,” it is the most expensive item of “Star Wars” memorabilia ever to go under the hammer.
The prop was used by actor David Prowse and his stunt double, the Olympic fencer Bob Anderson, in several fight scenes. It was most famously brandished in the Cloud City duel with Luke Skywalker, in 1980’s “The Empire Strikes Back,” which sees Darth Vader severing his son’s hand before making the shock reveal.
Related video above: Darth Vader lightsaber sold at auction
Three years later, in “Return of the Jedi,” the same prop featured in the pair’s confrontation in Emperor Palpatine’s throne room. In its sale catalog, the auction house said it was unable to confirm whether the lightsaber was also used in the original movie, 1977’s “A New Hope,” while adding that it was “possible.”
The $4.87 million price tag surpassed the auction record for a “Star Wars” prop, previously held by the other lightsaber from the Cloud City fight. Luke Skywalker’s weapon, which was sold with a special effect rig of an amputated hand (created by makeup artist Stuart Freeborn using a mold from actor Mark Hamill), fetched $3.75 million, also at Heritage Auctions, in July.
Rather than being custom-made, many of the original trilogy’s lightsabers were in fact repurposed flash holders from vintage cameras. Those used in fight scenes were modified to support prop blades (none of which featured in the auction) and withstand the stresses of combat. The weapons’ iconic glow was later animated by artists, frame by frame, in post-production.
Darth Vader’s lightsaber displayed damage “consistent with usage as a working dueling prop,” the auction catalog said, including scratches, a crack, a missing portion of the upper shroud and a partially broken grip.
Heritage Auctions’ “Ultimate Star Wars” sale featured almost 200 props and artworks related to the “Star Wars” franchise, as well as spin-offs like “The Mandalorian.” Top lots included other props from “The Empire Strikes Back,” including a rifle used by Boba Fett (sold for $375,000) and a miniature model of a Snowspeeder that was used during filming and was once owned by Princess Leia actor Carrie Fisher (sold for $200,000).
The auction also featured 27 other lightsabers, including ones used by Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi and Daisy Ridley’s character Rey Skywalker. Darth Vader’s record-breaker aside, the highest lightsaber prices were achieved by those used by Ray Park’s Darth Maul and Hayden Christensen’s Anakin Skywalker in "The Phantom Menace" and “Revenge of the Sith,” respectively. Both fetched $162,500.
Other screen-used “Star Wars” props to attract multi-million-dollar bids include a miniature Red Leader X-wing Starfighter, which sold for over $3.13 million in 2023, and a complete R2-D2 unit that fetched $2.75 million in 2017.

title: Evacuation order lifted after bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant
text:
PEORIA (25News Now/Gray News) - An evacuation order was lifted after bomb teams found a bomb Friday night and rendered it safe at an ethanol plant in South Peoria, Illinois.
Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon made the announcement shortly after 1 p.m. Saturday. Officials ordered the evacuation of a one-mile blast radius of the plant shortly after 7 p.m. Friday.
The police department released the following statement:
“State, Federal, and Local Law Enforcement have done an extensive search of the BioUrja facility. They have found no other items of concern at this time. The evacuation order will no longer be in effect. The street barricades will be removed, and all roads will be opened.
Residents are now free to return to their homes in the area that was affected by this order.
Law Enforcement will continue their investigation into this incident and updates will be provided.
The Peoria Police Department thanks the community for their cooperation during this incident."
Earlier, Dixon said authorities were looking for explosives at the plant, equivalent to 44 1/2 football fields.
Dixon declined to reveal the type of device discovered Friday, only to say the package that was “rendered safe” was a “credible threat. Peoria Mayor Rita Ali confirmed for reporters late Friday night that the device was a bomb.
Dixon also did not provide details of what he said was an extensive criminal investigation. Also participating the news conference were representatives of the FBI, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the U.S. Coast Guard, and the Peoria Fire Department.
Dixon said about 60 to 80 people were housed at the evacuation shelter at Manual High School.
No one sought shelter at EastSide Centre, East Peoria officials said.
East Peoria’s government released the following statement:
“As of 1:00 p.m., the 1-mile evacuation zone has been lifted and our residents can return to their homes and all businesses can resume normal operations. Once again, thank you to the East Peoria community for their continued patience and understanding during this situation. We are proud of our staff’s dedication to public safety and their actions to keep this community safe.”

title: Why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues
text:
(AP) - Regional U.S. air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that’s “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country,” and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.
Here’s a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away, among other issues:
Top official cites ‘intermittent’ gaps in communication system
The nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.
A contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
Planes flying at the time of the ground stop were able to land safely using “well-known procedures” in place for such circumstances, Duffy said Friday.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines, while old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports. But the work is far from complete, and Duffy used the news conference on Friday and Saturday to urge Congress to provide more funding.
Regional air control centers play a key role in high-altitude flights
The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday due to issues at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The U.S. operates 22 regional air traffic control centers, managed by the FAA, and they oversee long-distance aircraft operating between departure and arrival airports, according to McCormick, associate professor and program coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. McCormick estimates these control centers take over flights at altitudes over 10,000 feet.
These centers, which operate in such places as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis, are one of the three layers that guide pilots. The airport towers direct pilots during takeoffs at the 500-plus airports that have towers. Then, the so-called Terminal Radar Approach Control centers take over and guide pilots as they get further away from the airport. And then the regional control centers take over. When descending, the reverse happens, experts say.
Experts say that the controllers at the regional centers are sitting at radar displays and are responsible for only that airspace.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” said Stephen Creamer, president of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
Pilots use radio frequency to communicate
McCormick said the country’s regional, high-altitude air traffic control centers need to be connected to remote radio transmitter or receiver sites. That’s to allow for radio frequency coverage to communicate with the aircraft.
Those transmitter sites are connected to the centers via telecommunications systems, the likes of which are in the process of moving from copper wires to fiber optic lines. The two-way communication is important to ensure — among other things — that planes maintain safe spacing, he said.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it’s unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
But he and other aviation experts said that the FAA is now transitioning to what’s known as controller pilot data link — a digital, text-based messaging system that allows controllers and pilots to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through the data link instead of voice radio.
A problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
In September, Newark Liberty International Airport temporarily lost radar communications with aircraft, after a backup fiber optic line was inadvertently cut by railroad construction workers. That forced the FAA to immediately cancel hundreds of flights going in and out of the airport.
But airline experts say that scenario was different from what occurred on Friday. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday that intermittent frequency instability affected as many as 17 of the 22 U.S. regional air control centers.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” said John Hansman, an aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation. “It propagated around the country.”
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the “knock-on” effect is incredible.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves on to C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Even with a complete outage, pilots can still communicate
Aviation experts say that pilots can still communicate with aircraft even during intermittent communications disruptions, noting as an example that many planes have satellite phone systems.
Hansman said pilots can still talk directly to other pilots in airplanes around them via radio. There is also equipment on board that tells pilots if airplanes are around them, he added.
If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high intensity light beams, which send signals to pilots to alert whether it’s safe to descend, Hansman said.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” he said.

title: Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins says his successful gubernatorial campaign 'covered every corner' of Alaska
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said Saturday that being the first Democrat elected governor in Alaska in nearly 30 years holds special meaning for him and he credits his win to an ambitious campaign that “covered every corner of the state.”
Winning as a Democrat on a statewide level in Alaska can be like “working against gravity,” he said in an interview with The Associated Press. The 37-year-old former state representative, who often goes by JKT, also said he was proud of the “big-tent base of support” he received from Alaskans of all political backgrounds.
Kreiss-Tomkins traveled more than 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) within the vast state to pitch himself to voters, including hundreds of miles (kilometers) by snow machine and by boat to visit rural villages, according to his campaign. Most communities in Alaska are not connected to the main road system and often are only accessible by air or water. The campaign said it had more than 10,000 individual donors.
Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans in the Nov. 3 general election, including Bernadette Wilson. Wilson was endorsed by President Donald Trump, who carried the state in each of his presidential races. Trump announced the endorsement while in Alaska last month for a rally in support of GOP candidates including U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Messages seeking comment were left with Wilson’s campaign Friday and Saturday. The two other Republicans in the race — Dave Bronson, a former mayor of Anchorage, and Treg Taylor, a former state attorney general — wished Kreiss-Tomkins success.
His victory means Democrats will control governor’s offices in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control.
Kreiss-Tomkins succeeds Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred by term limits from seeking a third consecutive stint in office. Kreiss-Tomkins said he ran into Dunleavy on Saturday at a state office building in Anchorage, and the two spoke in Dunleavy’s office.
“I appreciated the conversation. It was gracious. He’s been very open and wanting to be helpful,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Kreiss-Tomkins said during the campaign that over the last eight years, Alaska became “broken” and experienced a “loss of optimism.” He emphasized a willingness to compromise and work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents. He focused on issues including affordability and advocated for full funding of K-12 public schools.
Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski was among those who endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, as did former governors including her father, Republican Frank Murkowski; Bill Walker, an independent; and Tony Knowles, the state’s last Democratic governor, who left office in 2002 after two terms.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he is still working on assembling his team. He will be sworn in Dec. 7 along with his lieutenant governor, Zac Johnson, an independent.
Kreiss-Tomkins said his decade-long experience in the Legislature will be an asset in his new role. One of the first issues he hopes to tackle during the legislative session beginning in January is passage of an education budget that he wants to see happen quickly.
Legislative leaders have outlined plans to organize bipartisan coalitions in both the House and Senate.

title: Mother and daughter found dead in home; suspect shot hours later, police say
text:
LONG BEACH, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) - Two women were found dead inside a Mississippi home Friday, and a suspect was later shot by deputies in Florida, authorities said.
The women were identified as Doris Crimmins, 84, and her daughter, Kimberly Hernandez, 63, both of Long Beach. Crimmins’ death appeared to be natural, while Hernandez’s death is being investigated as a homicide, Switzer said.
Long Beach police responded to the home around 10:15 a.m. after a reported shooting and found both women dead inside.
Switzer said Crimmins owned the home and was receiving hospice care for cardiac issues. Hernandez lived there with her mother.
Investigators named Richard Timothy Ward, Crimmins’ son and Hernandez’s brother, as a suspect, according to Long Beach Police Chief Billy Seal.
Police identified a vehicle involved in the incident and later found Ward and the vehicle in Pensacola, Florida, Seal said.
Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in a video posted to Facebook that deputies and highway patrol officers learned around 2:15 p.m. that a homicide suspect was staying at a nearby motel.
Deputies made contact with Ward, who pulled out a gun, Simmons said. After deputies gave him several commands to put the weapon away, Ward fired at them, the sheriff said.
Three deputies returned fire and struck Ward, Simmons said. He was taken to a hospital for treatment.
