title: Microsoft says services fully restored after hourslong global outage
text:
(AP) - Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X.
Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: 'Almost magic': SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 makes history
text:
'Almost magic': SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 makes history, catching upper stage from orbit
SpaceX on Friday launched the 15th flight test of its Starship rocket from Starbase in Texas and, on Saturday, successfully caught the upper stage of the launch vehicle.
Starship rockets are designed with sections that can be reused after being caught with large "chopsticks" back on Earth. Friday's flight test sought to recover both the upper stage and booster from the launch vehicle, yet the booster ultimately landed in the ocean instead of returning to Starbase.
Video above: SpaceX's Starship landed back on Earth after entering orbit
The upper stage went on to orbit the Earth 14 times before returning after about 22 hours for what would become a history-making, successful maneuver.
The mission marked the second time Starship's upper stage has made it to orbit, and the first time SpaceX has caught it.
Starship late Friday otherwise delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit to expand the network's capacity and user speeds, SpaceX said.
In a statement, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX and its CEO, Elon Musk, on a mission that "was almost magic."
More: What is Starship?
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
When is Starship going to Florida?
While test flights of SpaceX's Starship continue in Texas, construction is well underway at Kennedy Space Center to house the mega rocket.
Each test flight marks a step toward future missions to the moon and Mars.
Engineers are currently focused on refining Starship's launch reliability, improving its heat shield, and perfecting booster recovery. SpaceX is also continuing construction of its massive Gigabay at Kennedy Space Center, where the rocket will eventually move to support NASA's Artemis missions.
Isaacman shared his enthusiasm for space exploration.
"What has me excited about space exploration and NASA goes to the heart of it," he said. "We're pursuing the secrets of the universe. I can't imagine a more exciting endeavor."
He also explained how SpaceX and competitor Blue Origin's focus on reusability will help reduce the cost of space travel, which will be key to supporting regular missions.
Before Starship can achieve its ambitious goals, it must prove it can fly safely, reliably, and repeatedly.
SpaceX has acknowledged that several test flights have ended in anomalies or explosions, which it says are a normal and necessary part of the rocket's development process.
For now, in Texas and eventually in Florida, the future of space travel continues to unfold one launch at a time.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

“I wish a couple more would have went in for sure, but that’s definitely not all that went into it. So, I’ve just got to remember that as well, but not to put too much pressure on myself. title: Son of former CIA Director John Brennan arrested on child sexual abuse images charge
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was arrested Friday on a federal charge related to child sexual abuse images, according to authorities.
The case against Kyle Owen Brennan brought in federal court in Virginia stems from an investigation by local authorities that was referred to the FBI earlier this year, according to court papers.
An attorney for Kyle Brennan did not immediately return a phone call seeking comment.
Local authorities began investigating after the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received a tip in 2024 about suspected child sexual abuse material uploaded to his Adobe account, according to an affidavit filed in court.
His cellphone was seized that year as part of the local investigation before the case was referred to the FBI in October, the court papers say. An FBI review of data from the phone uncovered child sexual abuse images, according to the affidavit.
John Brennan, who served as CIA director under President Barack Obama, has been under scrutiny by President Donald Trump’s Justice Department over allegations that he lied to Congress during 2023 testimony.
John Brennan has vigorously denied those allegations, which relate to the intelligence community assessment that Russia had launched an influence campaign during the 2016 U.S. presidential election with a goal of boosting the Republican over Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton.
Prosecutors have not filed charges despite warning his lawyers that he is a target of their probe. Brennan has also been entangled in a broader conspiracy investigation in Florida scrutinizing Trump adversaries, but that inquiry has shown signs of floundering.

title: Students return to class for first time since deadly Oregon school shooting
text:
BEND Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - While cars and buses still moved through the drop-off lines, Justinna Rosett said most Silver Rail parents took a different approach to the start of school Thursday.
“Everybody walked their kids. Everybody talked to one another. The sense of community was really nice,” she said.
It was the first day back for families since a shooting last month at the Bend school left three students and a teacher dead.
“It was pretty hard for me as a mom,” parent Nicole Ybarrondo said. “I mean, I held it together to the best of my ability.”
Rosett said she felt mixed emotions. She has a fourth-grader.
“He wants to go back,” she said. “Kids are so resilient. I think it affects me more than him, to be honest.”
Leaders of Bend-La Pine Schools said going back to school is the best thing for most students. However, everyone needs to return in their own way and at their own speed.
“Returning to routine and predictable schedules and experiences are really good for kids as they navigate this trauma,” said Karen Rush, executive director of elementary schools.
Rush said they tried to make the day feel as normal as possible while still acknowledging the tragedy and offering support to those who needed it.
To help with the transition, Thursday was an early release day. Teachers started off by reading grade-appropriate scripts to their class about what happened.
There were counselors on site for all students and staff who needed extra support, as well as a new school resource officer who came out of retirement to work at Silver Rail full-time.
“I’m really grateful that we have one,” Rosett said. “I feel for all the schools that don’t.”
The district also replaced damaged doors and locks, added privacy screens to certain windows, and blocked off the area where the shooting happened.
Before coming back officially, parents had the chance to bring their kids for a walk-through. Ybarrondo said it was tougher than expected.
“I don’t think I was even prepared for my daughter’s reaction,” she said. “It turned into a trauma tour of sorts. ‘Mom, let me show you where I was running to find a place to hide. Let me show you the closet that I hid in. Let me show you where I was when it started.’”
The district said more than 90% of the students came back to school Thursday. The rest may have requested transfers to other schools within the district. Others might have withdrawn entirely and are now homeschooling or exploring other options.

title: Fire department mourns firefighter who died while hiking in park
text:
BOONE COUNTY, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) — The Independence Fire Department is mourning the loss of a firefighter who died while hiking in central Missouri.
The Boone County Sheriff’s Office said it responded to a 911 call at Pinnacles Park, just north of Columbia, at about 10:15 a.m. Tuesday. The caller reported that a person had fallen from a cliff.
Authorities respond to Pinnacles Park
Authorities found Sarah Longest at the scene after she fell about 50 feet from a cliff.
Longest, a HAZMAT technician with the Independence Fire Department, was nonresponsive and was declared dead at the scene, authorities said.
Longest was with an acquaintance at the time of her fall. Authorities said, “there is no reason at this time to believe the female’s fall and subsequent death was anything other than a tragic accident.”
Longest’s role with the department and union
Longest was a member of the Independence Fire Department’s Peer Support Team. She also served as a Good and Welfare Trustee for IAFF Local 781.
Longest had worked for the Independence Fire Department since March 10, 2025.
Department statement
In a statement, the Independence Fire Department said Longest’s commitment to serving others extended beyond responding to emergencies. The department said that through her involvement in the department and union, she demonstrated a dedication to supporting those who served alongside her.
“We extend our deepest condolences to Sarah’s family, friends, fellow firefighters and all who knew and loved her,” the department said. “Her service, compassion and commitment to others will not be forgotten.”
The department added: “Rest in peace, Firefighter Longest. We are grateful for your service to our community.”

title: Flight disruptions continue a day after nationwide ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Flight disruptions continued Saturday, one day after the nation’s longest ground stop in 25 years, as officials work to explain what led to the pause in flying.
A nationwide ground stop began Friday just before 4 p.m. E.T., and lasted more than four hours, halting flights across the U.S. Officials said the cause was an equipment outage.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on an effort to update old technology. He said new equipment overloaded old routers, causing communications and radar gaps.
“At least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber,” Duffy said. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router.”
Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford addressed travelers affected by the ground stop.
“I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons,” he said.
The ground stop left hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded and disrupted travel plans for 1.5 million fliers. It also caused thousands of flight delays and cancellations.
Questions arose over whether the outage was a cyber attack. The FAA said it does not believe that was the case.
Former Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood commented on the effect on air travel.
“It’s a national calamity, there’s no question about it,” LaHood said. “This is something that no one wishes would ever happen, but when you have old equipment, this is what happens.”
LaHood, a former Republican Congressman from Illinois, served as Transportation Secretary in the Obama administration from 2009-2013.
Duffy has asked Congress to approve more funding to replace old systems. He used Friday’s ground stop to renew that request.
Air traffic control operations are slowly resuming. The FAA expects about 5,000 flight cancellations Saturday as airlines adjust their schedules. Most operations are expected to be back on track by Sunday night.

title: Trailblazing film producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler make Governors Awards history
text:
Killer Films co-founders Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler are making history Sunday at the Governors Awards. The two women, who have spent their careers bringing bold, independent cinema into the world — from “Boys Don’t Cry” to “Safe” — are being honored with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.
That honorary Oscar has been given to some of the biggest names in Hollywood, from Walt Disney to Steven Spielberg. But Vachon and Koffler are the first female producing team and the first independent producers to receive it.
“It really feels so bound up in our longevity in New York City and in the independent film community in New York,” Koffler said in an interview with The Associated Press. “We do all know each other and, over the years, those of us who are still doing it really feel like an extended community that has supported each other, because opportunities are a little bit fewer, the movies are a little bit tougher, and it really feels like an acknowledgment of this space that we’re the ones who are being honored.”
Vachon chimed in: “A producer said to me … ‘I know it’s not my award, but it feels like it does belong to all of us.’”
Vachon and Koffler met in the 1990s in New York
It was a vibrant moment in independent cinema in New York when Vachon met Koffler in the early 1990s.
Vachon had already made a name for herself with her own films, and as the producer of Todd Haynes’ first feature “Poison” — someone who, despite all odds, was getting quality queer-themed films made. Koffler was bouncing around on indie film sets doing dozens of different jobs when Vachon asked if she wanted to supervise postproduction on “Postcards From America.” Koffler didn’t know what that entailed, but it hardly mattered: It was a great time to just dive in and figure things out.
“We met at the right time where it was like we could take these risks,” Vachon said. “We had some luck, because a lot of it is luck. But we also had really good taste.”
It was also the beginning of a beautiful partnership: In the past 30 years, Koffler and Vachon have produced over 100 films, and some television too, with their company Killer Films: “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” “One Hour Photo,” “Velvet Goldmine,” “Far from Heaven,” “I’m Not There,” “Carol” and “Past Lives,” for which they received their first best picture nomination. It is a body of work that speaks for itself, with provocative and imaginative art house films, landmarks of New Queer Cinema and many, many cult classics finding second lives and fandoms.
‘Our company, our rules’
“We were so inventing a wheel in a way that we didn’t even really know how crazy and ambitious it was to do it,” Koffler said.
They didn’t set out to make an “all-female company,” Vachon said, but they were grateful to be their own bosses. Indie film in New York in the 1990s was very male, not to mention the time of Miramax and Harvey Weinstein. And it was the kind of environment where Vachon, instead of telling New Line that she couldn’t come to a Todd Solondz set one day because her 1-year-old was very sick, said that she had to tend to another movie that was falling apart.
With Koffler, however, Vachon didn’t have to lie about family responsibilities. When Koffler was in the same boat with a newborn and stressing about missing an early screening of “One Hour Photo,” Vachon said, gently, “Just bring the baby.”
“It was a hundred percent our company,” Vachon said. “Our company, our rules.”
Audiences are rediscovering their films
Koffler and Vachon have loved seeing some of their films get rediscovered over the years, especially the ones that weren’t greeted with much fanfare when they came out. Recently they have noticed people talking about Mary Harron’s Valerie Solanas film “I Shot Andy Warhol” and Tim Blake Nelson’s war drama “The Grey Zone.”
“It’s fun, but it’s also not why we do it,” Vachon said. “Because if it was why we did it, we’d be really dumb because it doesn’t happen that often.”
Even “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” Vachon said, is “so iconic now, but people forget it didn’t make any money.”
“Hedwig,” she pointed out, is part of Mike De Luca’s filmmaking legacy. De Luca, who has recently been in the headlines for his work and recent departure from Warner Bros. under their new ownership, “really pushed to make it happen and make it happen on our terms,” Vachon said. “We really got to make the movie that John Cameron Mitchell wanted to make.”
Staying optimistic amid industry changes
They have been in the industry long enough to have seen sky-is-falling crises come and go every few years, but they are “eternal optimists,” Koffler said.
“We still get great material. We are managing to get things made,” Koffler, 60, said. “Would we like the budgets to be bigger? Yeah.”
Vachon, 63, chimed in: “Would you like our fees to be bigger? Yeah, I mean, we’d like to retire eventually.”
Sometimes they amuse one another by quoting lines from their projects, like “He’s got me all tied up with that greasy contract” (from “I Shot Andy Warhol”). But in this case, “You gotta live on what you earn, Mildred” (from “Mildred Pierce”) seems most apt.
And they are still hard at work, excited by new scripts and filmmakers and challenges. They have a new Haynes movie coming up, the romantic drama “De Noche” starring Pedro Pascal and Danny Ramirez that they rescued from ruin after Joaquin Phoenix abruptly dropped out days before filming was set to start. And there are always other projects in the works.
In fact, when the film academy’s president Lynette Howell Taylor, also a producer, was trying to get Vachon and Koffler on the phone to tell them about the Thalberg Award, they assumed that she was calling with her producer’s cap on to tell them that one of their movies was falling apart. (It later did.)
“The thing is it’s so hard to get these movies made and we’re lucky we’ve done it over a hundred times,” Vachon said. “I always do make this joke that every time I show up, I’m like, ‘Oh right, I forgot, I hate this.’ But, that said, there is something, there is this sort of magic of it all coming together that never really gets old. I mean, I think if it did, we would have stopped a long time ago.”

Savannah Guthrie renews NBC contract after 15 years
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.
The move by one of morning television’s most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.
The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.
In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.
Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”
The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
“The world goes on, things appear ‘normal,’ ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”
“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”
Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC’s election coverage, most recently for last week’s midterm elections.

title: Darth Vader’s lightsaber used in ‘I am your father’ duel sells for nearly $5 million
text:
(AP) - A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the “Star Wars” movies “The Empire Strikes Back” and ”Return of the Jedi" sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction.
The lightsaber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City where Vader tells Luke Skywalker “I am your father,” sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any “Star Wars” collectible, according to Heritage Auctions.
The sale also established a new auction record for a screen-used “Star Wars” prop, according to the auction organizer, shooting past their $3.75 million July auction sale of Skywalker’s light saber and severed hand-effects rig from “The Empire Strikes Back.”
Heritage’s Thursday auction also featured material from “Star Wars” Episodes I through IX and additional films and TV shows. In addition to Vader’s lightsaber, 27 other “Star Wars” lightsabers were assembled for public auction, according to Heritage Auctions.

title: Bonny Eagle football shocks Thornton to win A South title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SACO — The Bonny Eagle football team knew it needed to do a lot differently than it had three weeks ago if it was going to come to Hill Stadium and upset Thornton Academy.
The Scots did just that, improving defensively, offensively and especially on special teams to beat Thornton, 35-28, in the Class A South regional final Saturday.
“It feels better than what I expected it to feel like, honestly,” said Lucas Klehn, Bonny Eagle’s senior quarterback who rushed for two touchdowns and threw for two more. “I told Drew (Gervais) during the week that it’s going to be a feeling like we’ve never felt before, and it’s beyond that.”
Compared to a regular-season 49-14 Week 8 loss in Saco, Bonny Eagle turned the tables on Thornton in the special teams department. In the loss, Bonny Eagle gave up a kickoff return touchdown and were stopped on a fake punt that set up another score.
On Saturday, Bonny Eagle’s Ben Havu blocked a punt to set up a first-half touchdown and Gervais had a 90-yard kick return touchdown.
Bonny Eagle snapped its seven-game losing streak against Thornton, dating to the Scots’ win in the 2019 Class A championship. That year, too, Bonny Eagle had lost by a big margin in the regular season.
“We have examples from Bonny Eagle football history of our team losing to these guys in the regular season and coming back at the end of the year and winning a game,” Cooper said. “There’s proof, and our guys this year accepted that. These guys (from the past) did it, we can do it, too.”
Bonny Eagle (10-1) will face face North champion Oxford Hills (9-1) in the Class A championship next Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland. Bonny Eagle handed Oxford Hills its only loss, 45-6, in Standish o Oct. 9.
“They’re big, they’re physical. They’re going to be the team trying to shock the world, just like we were today,” Klehn said.
Defending state champion Thornton Academy finishes 10-1, one win shy of reaching its eighth consecutive state final.
Bonny Eagle led 21-7 at the half, scoring three consecutive touchdowns after Thornton had struck first on a 26-yard touchdown pass from Noah Fullerton to Brennan Tabor.
Klehn’s 1-yard score to tie the game was set up by a Wes Pinkham quarterback sack and forced fumble, which was recovered by Finn Leavitt. Later, Klehn hit Pinkham on a 40-yard post pattern to make it 14-7. Then it was Klehn to Ben Noe for a 19-yard touchdown one play after Havu’s punt block.
“We were terrible on special teams. We just gave up a lot of big plays that we don’t normally do,” said Thornton coach Kevin Kezal. “Then they kind of leaned on us, too. They were physical. They deserved to win.”
In the second half, fourth-down touchdown passes by Fullerton to Logan O’Keefe and Aiden Morin and a 35-yard scoring run by Chase Paquette trimmed Bonny Eagle’s lead to one touchdown.
The Scots responded, though, with Gervais’ kick return touchdown and a 42-yard scoring run by Klehn (set up by a long kick return by Pinkham).
Gervais used his New England 100-meter champion speed and great blocking on his kick return touchdown that made it 28-14. He caught Fullerton’s kick near the left sideline and then angled toward the middle.
“I saw our blockers blocking the right people, and I (saw) a massive hole — you could drive a semi-truck through that hole right down the middle,” Gervais said.
Thornton played without junior wide receiver Logan LeBlanc, who scored four touchdowns in the regular-season win against Bonny Eagle. Asked why LeBlanc did not play (he had been at practice on Tuesday), Kezal said he would “talk about kids on the field. No comment.”
STATISTICS
• Bonny Eagle: Lucas Klehn (18 carries, 141 yards, 2 TDs; 5 for 9 passing, 79 yards, 2 TDs); Ben Noe (6 carries, 16 yards; 1 receptions, 19 yards, 1 TD); Wes Pinkham (2 carries, 12 yards; 1 reception, 40 yards; 2 TFLs); Drew Gervais (90-yard kickoff return touchdown).
• Thornton: Noah Fullerton (13 carries, 60 yards; 13 for 20 passing, 143 yards, 3 TDs); Brennan Tabor (14 carries, 58 yards; 4 receptions, 28 yards, 1 TD); Logan O’Keefe (5 receptions, 52 yards, 1 TD); Aiden Morin (3 receptions, 54 yards, 1 TD).

title: Are the Microsoft Outlook outage and FAA ground stop connected?
text:
Are the Microsoft Outlook outage and FAA ground stop connected?
The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued a rare nationwide ground stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
It's the second time since Sept. 11, 2001, that the FAA has issued such an order. The last was January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
The world-stopping news comes just a day after a massive Microsoft outage left thousands of users without access to Outlook, the company's email platform.
According to Downdetector, reports peaked at 130,000 users impacted, though other estimates say it was closer to millions.
These two events, both stemming from apparently complicated technological issues, happening so close to each other have left many wondering whether they are connected.
However, Microsoft and the federal government have denied any connection.
Hours after the ground stop was put in place, Microsoft released a statement on social media.
"We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company wrote.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also rejected the link.
Responding to questions Friday afternoon outside the White House, Mullin said they are "separate issues," and that he didn't see “any reason to connect those two at all.”

title: NFL referee to officiate two games Sunday
text:
NFL referee Don Willard to officiate two games Sunday
NFL referee Don Willard will make history Sunday. He will officiate two games in the same day, becoming the first NFL referee to do so.
Video above: Boston researchers share new estimate of CTE in ex-NFL players
Willard will begin his day in Indianapolis, Indiana, to referee the Miami Dolphins game against the Indianapolis Colts. That game kicks off at 1 p.m.
He will then drive 109 miles to Cincinnati for the Sunday Night Football game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Cincinnati Bengals.
The marathon day is happening because of Friday's Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that halted flights nationwide. Thousands of flights were affected by the nearly five-hour ground stop, leaving passengers stranded.
In a statement, the NFL said, “Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns. The changes will necessitate that three back up referees – umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard – will work as referees in the following games: Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt: Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson: Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati: Don Willard. Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise.”
According to Bleacher Report, Willard will arrive at Lucas Oil Stadium at 10 a.m. By 4 p.m., the Dolphins-Colts game should be complete. He is slated to leave central Indiana by 5:30 p.m. to get on the road to southern Ohio. He will arrive at Paycor Stadium by 7:20 p.m. for the 8:20 p.m. kickoff between the Bengals and Steelers.
That game should be over by 11:30 p.m., and he should leave the stadium around 12:15 a.m.
Willard has been an NFL official for nine seasons.

title: New Orleans cruise ship collision: Dispatch audio gives a glimpse into initial chaotic moments
text:
New Orleans cruise ship collision: Dispatch audio gives a glimpse into initial chaotic moments
New dispatch audio gives a glimpse into the chaotic moment a cruise ship was struck by a tanker in the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday.
Broadcastify captured the dispatch calls between emergency officials as first responders mobilized to help with search and rescue efforts.
"Watercraft in distress, 1384 New Orleans Place," said an automated voice on the dispatch call.
A dispatch operator then could be heard calling for assistance from New Orleans officials.
"There is a green vessel; we have three tugboats en route and ships around it," the operator said. "It's under the Crescent City Connection behind the Convention Center."
Another first responder could be heard naming the impacted cruise ship, the American Heritage.
"It's a river cruiser named the American Heritage. It's definitely taking on water," the first responder said.
All passengers aboard the American Heritage have been accounted for after a tanker struck the docked cruise ship on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, in what officials called "A Miracle on the Mississippi."
About 129 passengers, along with crew members, were aboard when the Atlantic Asphalt struck the ship at about 12:30 p.m., according to Port NOLA. LCMC Health is treating 32 injured passengers.
Others who were not hospitalized were given hotel rooms by Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser.

title: Bowdoin men’s soccer ousts Thomas in NCAA tournament
text:
Patrick Brady and Stefan Zehnacker scored second-half goals to lead Bowdoin to a 3-1 win over Thomas in the first round of the NCAA Division III men’s soccer tournament Saturday in Brunswick.
Aiden Mehta scored in the first half for Bowdoin (9-3-5), which advances to face St. Lawrence at 1 p.m. Sunday in Brunswick.
Max Cook had two assists and Patrick Ritter added one. Bowdoin keeper Oliver King stopped one shot.
T’Syi Showers scored with an assist from David Ivarsson in the second half for Thomas (12-4-1).
MIDDLEBURY 2, ST. JOSEPH’S 1: Dylan Payne scored the go-ahead goal midway through the second half, lifting the Panthers (11-2-3) over the Monks (9-3-8) in an NCAA Division III first-round game in Middlebury, Vermont.
Cole Bishop tied the game for St. Joseph’s with an unassisted goal 18:59 into the first half, just over three minutes after Middlebury’s Will Sawin converted a penalty kick.
WOMEN’S SOCCER
TUFTS 2, HUSSON 0: Emily Nicholas and Audrey Cromett scored as the Jumbos (14-1-3) beat the Eagles (9-6-2) in the first round of the NCAA Division III tournament in Poughkeepsie, New York.
Waverly Sumner added an assist. Gigi Edwards made two saves for Tufts.
Gabrielle Smith stopped seven shots for Husson.
COLBY 2, MARY WASHINGTON 1: Grace Missett’s goal late in the first half lifted the Mules (10-4-3) to a win over the Eagles (12-3-4) in the first round of the NCAA Division III tournament in Ewing, New Jersey.
Colby fell behind early when Emma Braxton scored for Mary Washington, but an own goal just a few minutes later tied the game.
The Mules will play the College of New Jersey on Sunday.
FIELD HOCKEY
AMHERST 1, BOWDOIN 0: Genevieve Caruso scored in the fourth quarter and the Mammoths (11-7) beat the Polar Bears (13-5) in the second round of the NCAA Division III tournament in Brunswick.
Cate LaFreniere assisted on the goal.
Eva Filipponi stopped four shots for Bowdoin.
CROSS COUNTRY
NCAA DIVISION III EAST REGIONAL: Bates College freshman Charlotte Crum won the women’s race and Colby junior Stephen White won the men’s race at Wainwright Complex in South Portland.
Crum finished the 6K race in 21:08.19. Liv Girand of MIT was second (21:15.78), followed by Lily Simmonds of Tufts (21:23.06), Sofia Mokuaddem of Suffolk (21:23.42) and Zui Chinchalkar of Tufts (21:25.73). Also from Bates, Leah White finished sixth and Zoe McCullough was 10th.
Bowdoin’s Laura White finished ninth in 21:36 and Colby’s Ada Grant was 11th in 21:37.67.
Bates finished third in the team standings, followed by Bowdoin (fourth), Colby (fifth) and UNE (sixth). Tufts won the team title.
White finished the 8K men’s race in 24:00.20, less than a second in front of Dylan Fiegener of MIT (24:01.03). Johan Reisner of Tufts was third, followed by MIT teammates Nate Martinez and Owen Sondag. Also for Colby, Curtis Leachman was seventh, Eli Ziegler ninth and Henry Reichle 10th.
Colby was second in the men’s standings, while Bates was fourth and Bowdoin was eight. MIT won the team title.

title: Man accused of handcuffing 2 children to bedframe, court records say
text:
VANCE, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A Tuscaloosa County man is charged with child abuse, torture and aggravated child abuse.
According to court records, David Philips handcuffed a boy and a girl to a bed frame and whipped at least one of the children after she told law enforcement about the handcuffing.
The sheriff’s office began investigating after Philips failed to enroll the two children in school. Deputies who visited the home said they found one child with handcuffs still attached to his leg, chains on one child’s bed frame and pills under the bed.
According to court records, the children are in the care of the Department of Human Resources. Philips is being held without bond.

title: FBI part of investigation into credible bomb threat at Illinois ethanol plant
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (WEEK/Gray News) - The mass evacuation of neighborhoods within a one-mile radius of an Illinois ethanol plant continued Saturday after police said a suspicious package was determined to be a credible bomb threat.
While the package found at BioUrja Renewables was “rendered safe,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said a search was being conducted at the South Peoria plant.
Search of the facility continues
Dixon said the company notified police of the threat at 1:08 p.m. He said bomb technicians rendered the package safe just over seven hours later.
At a news conference at 12:40 a.m. Saturday, Dixon asked for the public’s patience as investigators search the large facility for other explosive devices.
Ryan Presley, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Springfield office, declined to provide additional details. He said investigators will work “tirelessly” to find whoever is responsible and “bring them to justice.”
Mayor confirms device
About two hours earlier, Peoria Mayor Rita Ali addressed reporters at Manual Academy on South Griswold Street, which was being used as an evacuation shelter.
“A device has been identified. We know it’s a credible threat. We know it’s a bomb,” Ali said.
She was the first to confirm a bomb was found.
“We don’t know if there are other devices,” Ali said.
Evacuation order and shelters
The evacuation order went into effect at 7:02 p.m. Peoria police released a statement saying the department was investigating a reported bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables, formerly the ADM plant, at 1 Edmund Street.
The statement urged anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to evacuate homes and businesses until further notice.
Police asked people to avoid the one-mile area around the facility until further notice. The statement said most streets in the area have been closed.
According to the statement, officers were on scene conducting an investigation and search of the facility to determine the credibility of the threat and ensure public safety.
Dixon said early Saturday that about 70 people were housed in the shelter at Manual. City officials said EastSide Centre is the designated shelter for East Peoria.
Late Friday night, East Peoria’s government reported the evacuations would remain in effect. Another update on the evacuations will come no later than 9 a.m. Saturday. Peoria police planned another briefing at noon Saturday.
Employers respond
Caterpillar told employees not to report for third shift Friday night.
“Due to guidance from local officials on the safety situation in downtown Peoria, employees should not report for third shift. Please follow local law enforcement guidance on this developing situation,” the company said.
OSF HealthCare St. Francis Medical Center, downtown Peoria’s largest employer, released a statement saying it was taking “all appropriate precautions.”
“The safety and well-being of our patients, visitors and Mission Partners remain our top priority. We are taking all appropriate precautions in response to the situation in downtown Peoria and are working closely with local authorities. We will continue to monitor the situation and take any additional steps necessary to maintain a safe environment for those we serve and those who work at our facilities,” the hospital said.
OSF Life Flight also released a statement saying its emergency medical helicopters and their radio communications have not been affected.
“It is not business as usual tonight, it is business as trained. Emergency medical helicopters and their radio communications have not been affected, and we will continue to provide only safe transportation. We always have a policy that ensures everyone arrives safely, and will continue offering support to our hospitals, agencies and other partners as needed,” OSF Life Flight said.

title: What passengers can expect now that nationwide ground stop has lifted
text:
What passengers can expect now that nationwide ground stop has lifted
The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday ordered the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
United States Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said this was a telecommunications outage and not linked to a cyberattack.
The ground stop was lifted just after 8:30 p.m. ET.
Although the ground stop lasted just over four hours, federal authorities said it could take time to untangle the travel mess.
Boston's Massport said that passengers can expect a lot of delays similar to what happens during a major storm.
Massport's former director, Tom Kinton, said this won't be a quick fix.
"This is going to take days," he said. "You're going to have canceled flights, you're going to have crews out of position, which means it's going to take a long time to unravel, unfortunately."
Kinton also said that crew hours will become a factor as the ground stoppage continues.
"The vast majority of flights are stuck on the ground, which means eventually crews are going to time out, which means flights are going to be canceled and now passengers are going to be scrambling to get on other flights leading into some of the busiest travel time this country experiences on an annual basis - before Thanksgiving and then, obviously, Thanksgiving week," Kinton said.

title: FAA ground stop raises questions after rollout of new AI air-traffic system
text:
FAA ground stop raises questions after rollout of new AI air-traffic system
A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop Friday prompted questions online about a new artificial intelligence tool recently introduced across the country. The system is the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, also known as SMART, and it's designed to analyze weather, flight paths, air traffic and controller staffing to help predict congestion and recommend more efficient routes.
The FAA expanded SMART to all 22 air traffic control centers on Nov. 10, after first using it in the Washington, D.C., area in September.
The ground stop began Friday afternoon after communications problems affected air traffic control centers around the country. In audio from Atlanta air traffic control, a controller told pilots, "I've been told ground stop everything."
Another transmission said the only information passed along was "frequency issues in multiple centers."
As speculation spread online that SMART may have contributed to the outage, Air Space Intelligence, the company awarded the FAA's $875 million, 12-year contract for the system, said in a post on X that the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage involved aging air traffic control infrastructure, including an old TDM analog system. He said outdated switches, routers and copper lines were overwhelmed with data.
Duffy also called on Congress to allocate $50 billion to upgrade the system, pointing to administration initiatives including the Modern Skies Act.
The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocated $5 billion to air traffic control, with that money beginning to roll out in 2022. More recently, the One Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion to fix and modernize air traffic control systems.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials were still investigating whether a cyberattack or artificial intelligence played a role. He said there was no indication of a malicious attack, but he would not rule out possibilities while the investigation continued.
The FAA lifted the ground stop Friday night. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the agency's Notice to Air Missions system failed, and the second since the Sept. 11 attacks.

title: UMaine football can’t halt losing streak
text:
Kai Colón passed for two touchdowns and ran for another, and Albany extended Maine’s losing streak to nine games with a 37-3 victory Saturday in Coastal Athletic Association football game in Albany, New York.
The Black Bears (1-9, 1-6 CAA) were held to 162 yards overall and just 42 yards passing. Starting quarterback Michael McMaugh was 9 of 20 for 36 yards, with an interception. Rashawn Marshall accounted for the bulk of Maine’s offense with 74 yards on 14 carries.
Maine’s only points came on a 42-yard field goal by Omar Aboutoui in the second quarter.
Albany improved to 7-4 overall and 5-2 in the CAA.
UNE 56, NEW ENGLAND COLLEGE 3: Damien Jones rushed for 206 yards and two touchdowns, and the Nor’easters (5-5, 5-2 CNE) ended their season with a five-game winning streak as they rolled past the Pilgrims (2-8, 1-6) in Henniker, New Hampshire.
Nathan Delgado also had a pair of TD runs, Chris Lang tossed two touchdown passes despite throwing the ball only seven times, and Cole McLaughlin returned a fumble for a touchdown. Javin Willis gained 101 yards and scored the final touchdown.
HUSSON 65, MAINE MARITIME 0: Brody Gibson was 19 of 24 for 260 yards and four touchdowns, all in the first half, as the Eagles (5-5, 5-2 CNE) ended their regular season by routing the Mariners (0-10, 0-7) in Castine.
Anthony Santacroce opened the scoring with a 12-yard run, then caught a pass from Gibson for a 49-yard touchdown that made it 13-0.
After adding a field goal late in the first quarter, the Eagles pulled away with five touchdowns in the second quarter. Gibson connected with Dom Rolle for a 17-yard TD and tossed a pair of touchdown passes to Jacob Lenz (11 and 24 yards). Daniel Ruiz Cantu had two TD runs — 24 and 13 yards.
Husson outgained MMA by nearly 500 yards, 608-112.
COLBY 19, BOWDOIN 13: Jagger Matera rushed for a touchdown and passed for a TD in a span of 53 seconds early in the second half, and the Mules (2-7) won the CBB title by holding off the Polar Bears (0-9) in Brunswick.
After a scoreless first half, Colby opened the second half with a six-play, 75-yard drive, capped by Matera’s 2-yard run. Avi Gotshalk missed the extra point, but the Mules got the ball right back when Santanna Cardoso picked off a pass by Soren Hummel. Matera connected with Alex Clapp on the next play for a 31-yard score.
Gotshalk made it 16-0 with a 34-yard field goal on Colby’s next possession, after the Mules recovered a Bowdoin fumble.
A pair of Colby fumbles sparked Bowdoin’s comeback bid in the fourth quarter.
First, Angus Leary recovered a fumble by Matera in the end zone. The Polar Bears attempted a 2-point conversion but failed. Then, another fumble set up a 4-yard touchdown pass from Hummel to Conrad Babka.
Following another Gotshalk field goal, Bowdoin had two chances to take the lead in the closing minutes, but both drives ended with turnovers.
Hummel was 31 of 50 for 285 yards. Matera finished with 227 yards on 14-for-21 passing.
HAMILTON 47, BATES 17: Luke Kurzum passed for 310 yards and four touchdowns, and the Continentals (3-6) scored 30 unanswered points in the second half to beat the Bobcats (1-8) in a season finale in Clinton, New York.
Kurzum’s chief target was Matthew Kearns, who caught 15 passes for 201 yards and three touchdowns.
Zachary Hurd and Tyler Walcott each had a rushing touchdown for Bates in the first half. Jeff Vidou caught seven passes for 131 yards.

title: US air travel schedule should recover from ground stop by the end of Sunday, FAA says
text:
US air travel schedule should recover from ground stop by the end of Sunday, FAA says
During a press conference on Saturday, White House officials gave an update after a rare Federal Aviation Administration nationwide ground stop on Friday.
In a moment that perhaps only further underscored the Transportation Department’s struggling systems, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's news conference Saturday morning began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps.
U.S. air travel should be fully recovered from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years by the end of Sunday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
Bedford said the flights “will still have delays and cancellations” on Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
His comments came as airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from a ground stoppage that lasted four hours, stranding hundreds of thousands of passengers.
New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said.
“At least at one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire and bringing it to over to fiber,” Duffy said. “What we are working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error — installer error from L3Harris — or did they install a faulty router.”
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many were forced to camp out in airports.
Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers participated in a cornhole tournament at the Lexington, Kentucky, airport. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.
Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Kona, Hawaii, to Fresno, California, was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego on Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport for a rebooked flight.
“There’s nothing you can do,” Russell said.
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent at Dallas Love Field greeted passengers at dawn with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to help keep flights moving.
At the Newark, N.J., airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when his flights would line up so he could return home to Japan.
“I’m not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home,” said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi’s game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 6,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Trump administration officials also blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding to replace the decades-old technology that helps manage the U.S. air traffic. Duffy said that 70% of the system had been replaced with fiber optic wire but that his agency also needs new air traffic control towers and runways.
The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
“We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace,” Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe. “You won’t get to your destination if we don’t think you can get there safely.”
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said.
Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has largely been quiet on the topic. He has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media, although he commented on other things. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast. That disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line.
Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

title: Mother and daughter found dead in home; suspect shot hours later, police say
text:
LONG BEACH, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) - Two women were found dead inside a Mississippi home Friday, and a suspect was later shot by deputies in Florida, authorities said.
The women were identified as Doris Crimmins, 84, and her daughter, Kimberly Hernandez, 63, both of Long Beach. Crimmins’ death appeared to be natural, while Hernandez’s death is being investigated as a homicide, Switzer said.
Long Beach police responded to the home around 10:15 a.m. after a reported shooting and found both women dead inside.
Switzer said Crimmins owned the home and was receiving hospice care for cardiac issues. Hernandez lived there with her mother.
Investigators named Richard Timothy Ward, Crimmins’ son and Hernandez’s brother, as a suspect, according to Long Beach Police Chief Billy Seal.
Police identified a vehicle involved in the incident and later found Ward and the vehicle in Pensacola, Florida, Seal said.
Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in a video posted to Facebook that deputies and highway patrol officers learned around 2:15 p.m. that a homicide suspect was staying at a nearby motel.
Deputies made contact with Ward, who pulled out a gun, Simmons said. After deputies gave him several commands to put the weapon away, Ward fired at them, the sheriff said.
Three deputies returned fire and struck Ward, Simmons said. He was taken to a hospital for treatment.

title: 20-year-old patient leaves hospital after 184 days on life support
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (WEAR) — A Florida woman is leaving the hospital after spending half a year on an advanced life-support system.
Akira Griffin, 20, is moving from Baptist Hospital in Pensacola to inpatient rehab.
Griffin suffered an illness that caused lung failure.
About 100 doctors, nurses, therapists and support staff cared for her during her hospitalization. Many of her caregivers lined the halls Wednesday to show support as she begins the next phase of her recovery.
A cardiologist said that, at one point, it seemed Griffin would never recover enough lung tissue and function to come off a ventilator, but she has.
Her mother said she hopes to bring her home by Christmas.
The average length of treatment with the advanced life-support system is about 11 days.

title: College football scrambles, adjusts kickoffs after FAA groundings
text:
(AP) - College football got a jolt it didn’t expect on the eve of a host of big games Saturday.
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide for several hours Friday, impacting thousands of flights and throwing travel plans into question for scores of college football teams. Most travel the day before Saturday kickoffs.
Many schools — including No. 2 Utah, No. 8 Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — had to scramble to figure things out. The Utes’ game at No. 22 Arizona was pushed back three hours to a 10:30 p.m. Eastern kickoff. Baylor’s game at No. 12 BYU was also moved back by 3 1/2 hours, to a 7 p.m. EST kick.
No. 19 Ole Miss was unable to get out of Starkville, Mississippi, on time and ended up having its game at Oklahoma moved to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST — going head-to-head with early NFL action. The decision also drew the ire of Sooners athletic director Roger Denny.
“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition (Saturday), they were unable to find a solution,” Denny said in a message posted on X. “After multiple conversations with the league office, commissioner (Greg) Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection.
“After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”
Denny said the decision “isn’t fair to our athletes” or fans but “we’ve been given no other choice” after “the wrong outcome was reached.”
Some teams — including the Longhorns (at LSU) and Volunteers (at Texas A&M) — were not expected to travel until late Friday at the earliest, meaning they would suit up for a game on far less sleep than usual. The Big 12 shifted the Arizona State-UCF game from 2:30 p.m. EST to 5:30 p.m., giving the Sun Devils an additional three hours after their flight from Arizona to Florida was delayed.
Other teams went old school, at least for top-tier college football: Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State with the SEC pushing back the Saturday start time by more than four hours to give the Tigers a buffer. Purdue boarded buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.
Top games to watch
Unbeaten Utah can continue its run toward the Big 12 championship game with a late-night win at Arizona (7-2), which puts Noah Fifita up against Devon Dampier in a duel of star quarterbacks.
Texas (7-2) will try to extend its win streak to four games and go 5-0 against Top 25 opponents at No. 24 LSU (6-3), which still has faint playoff hopes.
No. 11 Wake Forest (8-1) visits No. 25 SMU (7-1) in a meeting of Atlantic Coast Conference teams trying to reach the league championship game.
No. 15 Southern California (7-2) will try to build some late-season momentum when it visits No. 6 Indiana (8-1).
Under the radar
Louisville (6-3) visits North Carolina (5-4), where Bill Belichick’s team has played better and needs just one win for bowl eligibility.
The Cardinals have won four straight and are right in the thick of the race for a spot in the ACC championship game. They need some help, though, because second-place Wake Forest is ahead of them by a game in the standings and own the head-to-head tiebreaker.

title: Maine men’s hockey shuts down Vermont
text:
Jaden Lipinski scored the go-ahead goal on a backhand wraparound early in the third period, lifting Maine to a 3-1 win over Vermont in a Hockey East game Saturday in Burlington, Vermont.
The Black Bears (6-5-1, 2-3-1 Hockey East) grabbed a 1-0 lead 5:08 into the game when Dante Siciliano scored his first college goal. Vermont (5-4-2, 4-2-2) tied it just 1:03 later on a power-play goal by Ethan Burroughs.
After Lipinski put the Black Bears back in front 2:29 into the third period, Owen Fowler’s empty-net goal with 13 seconds remaining clinched the victory.
Albin Boija made 22 saves for Maine, which has a three-game unbeaten streak. The Black Bears and Catamounts played to a 0-0 tie on Friday night.

title: Officer resuscitates infant who stopped breathing
text:
NORTH PORT, Fla. (Gray News) - A police officer in Florida is being hailed as a hero after resuscitating an infant who had stopped breathing.
The North Port Police Department shared footage from the officer’s body camera of the rescue on Facebook Thursday.
“Not every call ends in an arrest or involves a crime. Sometimes, it’s an officer rushing to help an infant who isn’t breathing, relying on his training until he hears that first cry,” the police department said in the caption.
In the video, dated Nov. 7, the officer is seen working to resuscitate the baby. His efforts don’t stop until he hears the baby begin to cry, a sign that the infant is breathing again.
“You good?” the officer asks as the baby begins to cry. “That’s good.”
The police department said in the video’s caption that “police work is about more than enforcing the law.”
“It’s about protecting life,” the department said. “And sometimes, a baby’s first cry is the greatest reward of all.”
