title: Republican deja vu is in full swing
text:
In the 1880s, Republicans instituted tariffs to protect American industry. The result? Higher prices for consumers. Then, in 1883, the “spoils system,” whereby victorious politicians could reward their supporters with government jobs, was replaced with the Pendleton Civil Service Act, which promoted a merit-based bureaucracy.
Later, in 1919-20, we had the red scare and the Palmer raids, whereby thousands of “radicals,” many of whom were immigrants, were summarily deported with little or no regard for their constitutional rights. That perceived “threat” from immigrants gave rise to the Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the National Origins Act of 1924.
Religious fundamentalism was also a leading cause of confrontation. The era spawned the birth of the KKK, and its goal of making the country “100% American.” Many of its tactics remind one of present-day ICE activities.
Then there was the Great Depression. And now we have MAGA, its love of tariffs, its perceived threats from immigrants, its religious fundamentalism and the goal of making our country “100% American.”
Talk about deja vu.
Carl Morin
Topsham

title: Whitefield Library finishes building renovations
text:
Almost five years since reopening its doors to the public, the Whitefield Library has finished its major renovations. Now, the goal is to keep it running as a year-round facility.
In late October, the final renovations to the exterior library, located at 1 Arlington Lane in Whitefield, were completed. The western clapboards were scraped and sanded or replaced. Deteriorating window trim was replaced and rejuvenated with green paint.
According to Whitefield Library Board of Directors President Cheryle Joslyn, completing the exterior work was only one of many steps of renovation the library has taken since acquiring the almost 140-year-old building in 2019.
“We think that pretty much takes care of the renovation of the building,” Joslyn said.
Other than books, the Whitefield Library hosts numerous community events, such as reading groups and educational programs. It serves the communities of Whitefield, Somerville, Jefferson, Alna, Pittson, and Windsor for free. Joslyn said renovations allow for more space and opportunities, and that the library has changed tremendously since it opened full time in 2022.
There is not an exact date on when the building was constructed, but Joslyn said the estimate is around 1884, making it 137 years old. According to a Sun Journal article from that year, the building was intended to be used as a school, library, and gathering center. In 1889, other records show the building was used for women’s sewing groups and community dinners.
Starting in 1917 and for the next 102 years, the building was owned and operated by Whitefield Arlington Grange Post No. 528.
Flash-forward 100 years, in 2016, a 9-year-old attending Whitefield Elementary School wrote a letter to the Whitefield Select Board about how there wasn’t a library open in the summer. In his letter, Quinn Conroy said there were not many activities for children to do over the summer and that even when not in the class, they like to read.
“I think that we should have a public library in Whitefield because on summer vacation there is nothing to do other than take a two hour trip to the beach and kids like to read in the summer and grown-ups like reading to,” Conroy said in the letter.
Conroy also pushed for the space to have computers.
In response to the letter, Whitefield Select Board member Sue McKeen approached the school to see if the school library could be run by volunteers during the summer, but Joslyn said plans never materialized.
In 2017, the Arlington Grange allowed volunteers to create a summer library on the first floor of the building. The first election of officers for a building acquisition committee came around early the following year, with McKeen sworn in as president and Joslyn as vice president.
For two summers before moving into the building, Joslyn said a “summer library” was hosted on the main floor with a table full of donated books.
In July 2018, the Whitefield Library Association was granted a nonprofit 501(c)(3) designation. Throughout the year, the committee worked and created design concepts for the Grange building, later dissolving once the work was finished the nonprofit designation was given.
In September 2018, the Whitefield Library Association submitted an $8,000 bid to Maine State Grange for the purchase of the property. The first bid was denied, and a second one was later submitted for $25,000.
On Jan. 3, 2019, the Maine State Grange accepted the bid, which led to the committee tasked with the acquisition to begin fundraising efforts.
“We didn’t know how we were going to raise $25,000 to buy this building,” Joslyn said.
It was in March 2019 when Kennebec Saving Bank donated the total amount needed for the purchase to the library after getting wind of the committee’s efforts through a Kennebec Journal article by George Smith titled “There’s Nothing Like a Library.”
“We got a call from Kennebec Savings Bank and they said ‘We’d like to come out and meet with you,’” Joslyn said. “We thought they were coming out to make us a proposal for borrowing the money from their bank. They came out with a check for $25,000.”
Now with the building and no money left in their account, the committee started brainstorming ways to raise money to start renovations, Joslyn said. Throughout the rest of 2019, the library hosted fundraising efforts such as a dodgeball tournament, art nights, and other events. As work started to roll, the library continued to be operated in the summer, but the building was not ready for year-round use yet.
The first renovation done in the building once it was in the hands of the library association was the removal of a faulty furnace. For the next two years, the building went through a transformation.
In March 2020, as the library paused operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, the committee kept on working, installing new heaters and adding additional support beams, among other tasks.
Joslyn referred to herself and the group of volunteers who did most of the work as “the geezers,” because they were all retired. She said the group was very fortunate to find so many craftsmen around the area to help.
Most of the money for renovations was raised through grants, according to Joslyn, including the Stephen and Tabitha King Grant Award. The David Family Foundation Award, and a Bangor Saving Grant Award.
“We renovated no more than what we had the money granted to us and it wasn’t all grants,” Joslyn said. “We had some very, very good donors from our community who stepped up with some big checks to help.”
In January 2022, the newly renovated Whitefield Library opened to the public. Only the first floor was complete at this point, with a new main room, office, hallway, storage closet, bathroom, and kitchenette.
At Whitefield’s annual town meeting in March 2023, $15,000 was approved to help fund the salaries of the library administrator and the children’s program coordinator, as well as an additional $10,000 for parking lot repairs.
In May 2023, the association received the building permit to begin second floor renovations. Joslyn said the library faced the problem of figuring out how to fund the project until a community member donated $200,000 while advocating for a larger children’s space.
According to Joslyn, many people stopped by when the association was working on the major renovations before opening. One of those people, Niki Janus, offered to fund the remaining renovations.
For the next three years, renovations continued. The second floor received the required permitting to host people in February 2025 and an appreciation celebration was held in September of that year.
With years of hard work, renovations, and hoops to jump through, the Whitefield Library is now a community center used for everything from checking out books, after-school programs, author visits, music groups, and more.
Even with the bigger projects done, Joslyn said the goal is to now prioritize preventative maintenance. She said she also would like to find a way to either install a chair lift or other accessibility tool to help get everyone upstairs.
“We’re thrilled to have such wonderful facilities,” Joslyn said.
For more information about the Whitefield Library, call 549-0170 or go to whitefieldlibrary.org.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting, White House says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed by the White House on Friday and the Kremlin on Saturday. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.
Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the “beginning of hopefully a conversation” on nuclear disarmament “that can be productive going forward,” said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.
But Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to “step up ... to the adult table” on a matter of international importance.
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”
Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.
“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”
___
Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow.

title: Let’s do away with wasteful ranked-choice voting
text:
The delay in announcing the winner of Maine’s 2nd Congressional District came down to ranked-choice voting. This delay gives us another reason to eliminate this method.
Despite the fact that the loser conceded the election and the winner had a 5,400-vote lead, Maine had to spend money and time on proving the obvious. This law is a nightmare for everyone, including voters.
If you included the 6,000 ballots that were blank, the winner’s margin dropped below 50%, requiring all these costly additional steps. What about all the voters who didn’t vote at all? What if they were included in every election?
What happened to common sense? Let’s stop this charade.
Marshall Jarvis
York Harbor
